subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic choice in suspected native valve endocarditis
stem: A 46-year-old man has three weeks of fevers and night sweats. He had a dental extraction five weeks ago and has a bicuspid aortic valve. He has no prosthetic material and does not inject drugs.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, splinter haemorrhages, tender finger pulp nodule
data_table.Investigations: Three blood culture sets drawn; echocardiogram pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antimicrobial regimen?

options.text: Vancomycin alone pending culture and sensitivity results
Benzylpenicillin, flucloxacillin and gentamicin intravenously
Vancomycin, gentamicin and rifampicin for the full course
Ceftriaxone alone for community-acquired sepsis
Withhold antibiotics and repeat blood cultures over 24 hours

subtopic_detail: Duke criteria interpretation for infective endocarditis
stem:
You are the infectious diseases registrar reviewing a 58-year-old woman admitted 3 days ago with fever and malaise. She has a background of a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement 5 years ago and no injecting drug use.

Two separate blood cultures drawn 4 hours apart have both returned positive for Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly Streptococcus bovis). A transoesophageal echocardiogram today demonstrates a 6 mm mobile vegetation on the prosthetic aortic valve with mild new central aortic regurgitation. She has no janeway lesions, no roth spots, and no glomerulonephritis. Her only minor finding is a temperature of 38.2 on admission.

Examination reveals a soft ejection systolic murmur consistent with her prosthesis and a new soft early diastolic murmur. Peripheral pulses are equal. There are no focal neurological signs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 128/72, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.2
data_table.Cultures: Two blood culture sets 4 hours apart both positive for Streptococcus gallolyticus
data_table.Echocardiography: TOE: 6 mm mobile vegetation on prosthetic aortic valve; mild new central aortic regurgitation
data_table.Examination: Soft ejection systolic murmur (prosthesis); new soft early diastolic murmur; no janeway lesions or roth spots

lead_in: How does this case classify under the modified Duke criteria?

options.text: Possible infective endocarditis on the basis of one major criterion and one minor criterion being present in the case
Definite infective endocarditis on the basis of one major and three minor criteria being satisfied together in this case
Rejected diagnosis because prosthetic valve dysfunction alone accounts for both the fever and the new murmur adequately
Definite infective endocarditis on the basis of two major criteria being satisfied by the current findings
Possible infective endocarditis pending a coeliac vascular workup because of the organism identified from the blood culture bottles

subtopic_detail: Surgical referral indication in infective endocarditis
stem: A 52-year-old man is on day 6 of flucloxacillin for mitral valve Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis, cultures clear since day 4. Overnight he developed orthopnoea and pink frothy sputum.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, BP 108/72 mmHg, SpO2 90% on oxygen
data_table.Examination: Crepitations to the mid zones, loud apical pansystolic murmur
data_table.Echocardiogram: Flail posterior mitral leaflet, severe mitral regurgitation, vegetation 8 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Complete 6 weeks of flucloxacillin and defer surgical review until afterwards
Add intravenous gentamicin for synergy against Staphylococcus aureus
Commence non-invasive ventilation and repeat the echocardiogram in 48 hours
Urgent cardiothoracic review for mitral valve surgery on this admission
Change to vancomycin plus daptomycin for suspected persistent bacteraemia

subtopic_detail: Empirical therapy in adult community bacterial meningitis
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 34-year-old woman presents with 8 hours of severe headache, fever, photophobia, and neck stiffness. She has vomited twice.

She has no known immune compromise, no head trauma, no recent neurosurgery, and no ventricular shunt. She is not pregnant.

Examination reveals full Glasgow coma scale 15, no focal neurology, no papilloedema on fundoscopy, and a positive Brudzinski sign. There is no petechial rash. There is no papilloedema or new onset seizure.

Vital signs: pulse 116, blood pressure 108/62, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 39.5. Intravenous access has been secured and two sets of blood cultures have been drawn. Full blood count and biochemistry have been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116, BP 108/62, RR 22, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.5
data_table.Neurology: GCS 15; no focal deficit; no papilloedema; Brudzinski positive; no seizure
data_table.Access: IV access secured; two sets of blood cultures drawn; FBC and biochemistry sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step before the lumbar puncture?

options.text: Perform an urgent non contrast CT brain first before any antibiotic administration to exclude a mass lesion causing raised intracranial pressure
Give ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously alone and defer dexamethasone until cerebrospinal fluid Gram stain results are back from the pathology laboratory
Add benzylpenicillin 1.8 g intravenously 4 hourly to ceftriaxone empirically to cover Listeria monocytogenes in this febrile encephalopathic patient
Give dexamethasone 10 mg intravenously with or immediately before ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously and proceed with lumbar puncture as soon as feasible
Commence intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8 hourly first and defer any antibiotic administration until magnetic resonance imaging excludes temporal lobe changes

subtopic_detail: HSV encephalitis recognition and treatment
stem: A 41-year-old previously well man has 2 days of fever and confusion and had a witnessed generalised tonic clonic seizure overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, T 38.9 degrees C
data_table.Neurology: Disoriented with expressive dysphasia, no neck stiffness
data_table.Imaging: Non contrast CT brain normal
data_table.CSF: 82 lymphocytes x10^6/L, protein 0.8 g/L, glucose 3.6 mmol/L with serum 5.4 mmol/L, no organisms on Gram stain

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Await the cerebrospinal fluid polymerase chain reaction before starting aciclovir
Intravenous aciclovir with ceftriaxone and dexamethasone pending the result
Intravenous ganciclovir as empirical therapy for viral encephalitis
Intravenous ceftriaxone and dexamethasone without antiviral cover
Urgent contrast enhanced MRI, deferring antimicrobial therapy

subtopic_detail: LRINEC and surgical urgency in necrotising soft tissue infection
stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents 18 hours after a gardening scratch to the thigh, with pain out of proportion to the skin change.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/58 mmHg, temperature 39.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Dusky erythema mid thigh to groin, central bulla, crepitus
data_table.Investigations: White cells 21 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, creatinine 148 micromol/L, glucose 16 mmol/L, CRP 320 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin with fluids, marking the erythema
Immediate surgical exploration and debridement with broad antibiotics
Contrast computed tomography of the thigh to confirm soft tissue gas
Hyperbaric oxygen after antibiotics as definitive treatment
Punch biopsy of the bulla, deferring exploration until histology

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis recognition and immediate management
stem: A 38-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency takes hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone daily. She has had 48 hours of vomiting and diarrhoea and has kept neither food nor her hydrocortisone down.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, BP 82/54 mmHg, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, cool peripheries
data_table.Venous gas: pH 7.29, sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg now, with saline and dextrose
Measure serum cortisol and withhold hydrocortisone pending the result
Double her oral hydrocortisone and observe for four hours
Intravenous fludrocortisone and saline, without any glucocorticoid
Intravenous dexamethasone, then a short synacthen test

subtopic_detail: Screening test choice for suspected Cushing syndrome
stem: A 42-year-old woman has 12 months of central weight gain, easy bruising, proximal weakness climbing stairs and new hypertension. She uses no steroid of any form.

data_table.Examination: BP 158/94 mmHg, purple abdominal striae wider than 1 cm, thin skin, supraclavicular fat pad

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line screening investigation?

options.text: Random midday plasma cortisol with plasma adrenocorticotrophic hormone
8 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test with an 8 am cortisol
Corticotrophin releasing hormone test with petrosal sinus sampling
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary with dynamic contrast
1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test with an 8 am cortisol

subtopic_detail: Initial blood pressure control in Stanford type B aortic dissection
stem: A 62-year-old man with hypertension has 40 minutes of sudden severe tearing interscapular pain.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, BP 198/112 mmHg right arm and 194/108 mmHg left arm
data_table.Examination: Equal peripheral and femoral pulses, no aortic regurgitation murmur, no focal neurology
data_table.Imaging: CT aortogram: intimal flap from distal to the left subclavian artery to the diaphragm, no malperfusion or root involvement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Intravenous hydralazine boluses, withholding beta blockade
Immediate endovascular repair without blood pressure control
Intravenous esmolol to a heart rate of 60, then glyceryl trinitrate
Intravenous heparin while awaiting a vascular surgical opinion
Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate with oral amlodipine, then reassess

subtopic_detail: AAA surveillance interval per Australian vascular guidance
stem: A 68-year-old asymptomatic ex-smoker has an incidental fusiform infrarenal aortic aneurysm on ultrasound. He has hypertension on perindopril and takes atorvastatin. He has no back or abdominal pain and no leg claudication.

data_table.Ultrasound: Fusiform infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm, 4.6 cm maximum anteroposterior diameter
data_table.Examination: BP 132/78 mmHg, non-tender mid-abdominal pulsation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate follow up plan?

options.text: Repeat ultrasound in 6 months and optimise cardiovascular risk factors
Refer for open repair now, as 4.6 cm crosses the threshold
Repeat ultrasound in 12 months, referring only at 5.5 cm
Computed tomography aortogram in 3 months before deciding an interval
Commence metoprolol to slow the rate of aneurysm expansion

subtopic_detail: Massive transfusion protocol activation criteria
stem: A 34-year-old man arrives after a motor vehicle collision with a distended tender abdomen and a closed femur fracture. He remains hypotensive after 1 L of prehospital crystalloid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 78/48 mmHg, temperature 35.2 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: FAST positive, Hb 88 g/L (130-180), pH 7.18, lactate 6.8 mmol/L
data_table.Ongoing loss: Over 30 per cent lost, still bleeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in resuscitation?

options.text: Continue crystalloid to at least 3 L before any blood product
Packed red cells alone, reassessing after every 4 units
Recombinant factor VIIa 90 micrograms/kg before components
Tranexamic acid only if still transfusing at 24 hours
Massive transfusion protocol 1:1:1 with tranexamic acid 1 g

subtopic_detail: Warfarin reversal in major bleeding
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 76-year-old man on warfarin for mechanical mitral valve replacement presents 2 hours after a witnessed fall down 5 stairs. He has a new right sided hemiparesis and GCS 12.

Non contrast CT brain shows a 25 mL right frontal intraparenchymal haemorrhage with 4 mm midline shift. There is no intraventricular extension.

His last INR 1 week ago was 2.6 (target 2.5-3.5). Current INR is 3.4. He weighs 82 kg. Renal function is within normal limits and he has no known heparin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 168/94, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.CT brain: 25 mL right frontal intraparenchymal haemorrhage; 4 mm midline shift; no intraventricular extension
data_table.Weight: 82 kg; normal renal function; no heparin allergy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate reversal strategy?

options.text: Give intravenous vitamin K 10 mg alone and await 12 hourly INR checks before considering further reversal with clotting factor concentrates or fresh frozen plasma products
Give fresh frozen plasma 4 units alone as first line reversal without prothrombin complex concentrate to avoid the thrombotic risk of concentrated factor products in this patient
Give recombinant activated factor VII as first line reversal because it acts faster than any other agent and provides complete correction of the coagulopathy on its own
Withhold reversal entirely and observe with 6 hourly INR trends because the current value is close to therapeutic range for the mechanical valve indication
Give prothrombin complex concentrate at a weight based dose according to INR plus intravenous vitamin K 10 mg with immediate neurosurgical referral for review

subtopic_detail: DOAC reversal choice in major bleeding
stem: A 72-year-old woman on apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation has two hours of severe headache and left hemiplegia. Her last dose was 6 hours ago.

data_table.Neurology: GCS 13, dense left hemiplegia, BP 182/104 mmHg
data_table.CT brain: 30 mL right basal ganglia haemorrhage with intraventricular extension

lead_in: What is the most appropriate specific reversal option to request?

options.text: Idarucizumab as two 2.5 g intravenous boluses 15 minutes apart
Andexanet alfa as an intravenous bolus then a 2 hour infusion
Protamine sulfate infused intravenously over 10 minutes
Fresh frozen plasma at 15 mL/kg as first line reversal
Intravenous vitamin K 10 mg as first line reversal

subtopic_detail: Mixed acid base and anion gap interpretation
stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and chronic alcohol use has three days of vomiting after a binge. He last ate 36 hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122/min, RR 32/min
data_table.Examination: Kussmaul respirations
data_table.Biochemistry: Sodium 138 mmol/L, chloride 92 mmol/L, glucose 14 mmol/L, ketones 5.2 mmol/L, lactate 3.1 mmol/L, albumin 34 g/L

lead_in: Which best characterises the acid base disturbance?

options.text: Pure high anion gap metabolic acidosis, fully compensated
Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis
High anion gap metabolic acidosis with a metabolic alkalosis
Primary respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation
Compensated respiratory acidosis with bicarbonate retention

subtopic_detail: Opioid rotation ratio from oral morphine to oral hydromorphone
stem: A 62-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer takes slow release morphine 60 mg twice daily with 10 mg immediate release for breakthrough, about four a day. She has persistent nausea and myoclonus with normal renal function.

data_table.Plan: Rotate to oral hydromorphone at 5 mg morphine to 1 mg hydromorphone, then reduce by 25 to 50 per cent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate new hydromorphone regimen?

options.text: Hydromorphone 16 mg slow release twice daily, 4 mg breakthrough
Hydromorphone 32 mg slow release twice daily, 8 mg breakthrough
Hydromorphone 4 mg slow release twice daily, 1 mg breakthrough
Continue morphine and add metoclopramide with clonazepam
Hydromorphone 8 mg slow release twice daily, 2 mg breakthrough

subtopic_detail: Anticipatory prescribing for terminal secretions
stem: A 78-year-old man with end stage heart failure is dying at home, deeply drowsy. For 4 hours he has had audible upper airway secretions that distress his wife. He is not distressed himself.

data_table.Examination: Not tachypnoeic, no crackles of pulmonary oedema
data_table.Access: Subcutaneous butterfly in situ, receiving morphine for dyspnoea

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticipatory prescription?

options.text: Subcutaneous glycopyrronium as required, with repositioning and explanation to his wife
Subcutaneous furosemide with a glyceryl trinitrate infusion for pulmonary oedema
Deep oropharyngeal suctioning two-hourly and transfer to an inpatient unit
Regular nebulised salbutamol with added nebulised ipratropium to open the airways
Increase the morphine by half and add regular subcutaneous midazolam

subtopic_detail: Chronic Addison disease sick day rules
stem: A 44-year-old man with Addison disease takes hydrocortisone 15 mg morning and 5 mg mid-afternoon plus fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily. He rings with 24 hours of fever and cough. He is eating and drinking normally without vomiting.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 degrees C

lead_in: What is the most appropriate glucocorticoid advice?

options.text: Double the total daily hydrocortisone until 24 hours after the fever settles
Give 100 mg intramuscular hydrocortisone and attend the emergency department
Continue his usual hydrocortisone and add an oral antibiotic only
Quadruple hydrocortisone to 80 mg daily and double the fludrocortisone
Switch to prednisolone 25 mg daily for its longer duration of action

subtopic_detail: Stanford type A dissection recognition
stem: A 58-year-old woman with poorly controlled hypertension has 30 minutes of severe tearing chest pain radiating between her shoulder blades.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, BP 176/94 mmHg right arm and 158/86 left
data_table.Examination: Weak right radial pulse, soft early diastolic murmur
data_table.CT aortogram: Intimal flap from the aortic root through the arch, small pericardial effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous esmolol and glyceryl trinitrate as medical management alone
Emergency percutaneous coronary intervention for acute coronary syndrome
Emergency pericardiocentesis before any imaging or surgical referral
Immediate cardiothoracic referral for repair, with esmolol started now
Intravenous heparin while awaiting a cardiothoracic opinion

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing ACTH dependent from ACTH independent Cushing syndrome
stem: A 46-year-old woman has confirmed hypercortisolism: the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test did not suppress cortisol below 50 nmol/L, and urinary free and late night salivary cortisol were elevated.

data_table.Examination: Moon face, purple abdominal striae, proximal weakness
data_table.ACTH: Morning plasma adrenocorticotrophic hormone 76 ng/L (up to 46)
data_table.Imaging: None to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Computed tomography of the adrenal glands with a dedicated protocol
Computed tomography of the chest for an ectopic source
Pituitary magnetic resonance imaging, then sinus sampling if equivocal
High dose 8 mg dexamethasone suppression test to localise the source
Repeat the 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test to confirm the screen

subtopic_detail: Calcium replacement during massive transfusion
stem: A 42-year-old woman having massive transfusion for postpartum haemorrhage has had 6 units of red cells, 6 of plasma and 1 of platelets in 45 minutes. She is still bleeding on noradrenaline 0.2 micrograms/kg/min.

data_table.Point of care: Ionised calcium 0.82 mmol/L (1.10-1.32), magnesium 0.72 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), fibrinogen 1.4 g/L (2.0-4.0), pH 7.24

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes for the long QT
Sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol to correct the acidosis first
Calcium chloride 10 mL of 10 per cent over 5 to 10 minutes
Escalate noradrenaline to 0.4 micrograms/kg/minute
Cryoprecipitate 10 units for the fibrinogen of 1.4 g/L

subtopic_detail: Acute HIV seroconversion diagnosis
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 27-year-old man presents with 6 days of fevers to 39, sore throat, generalised aching, and a diffuse blanching maculopapular rash on the trunk and upper arms. He is otherwise well.

He returned 4 weeks ago from a 3 month trip through South East Asia and reports several episodes of condomless receptive anal sex with new partners while away. He has no injecting drug use, no dental work, and takes no regular medications.

On examination he has small non-tender cervical and axillary lymph nodes, mild pharyngeal erythema without exudate, and a soft palate with several shallow non-vesicular ulcers. There is no meningism. Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 38.6. Full blood count shows lymphocytes 1.4 x10^9/L (1.5-4.0) with atypical lymphocytes reported on film. Liver enzymes are mildly raised. A fourth generation HIV antigen/antibody combination immunoassay drawn 2 hours ago has just returned negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Examination: Non-tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy; pharyngeal erythema without exudate; shallow non-vesicular palatal ulcers; truncal maculopapular rash
data_table.Sexual history: Multiple episodes of condomless receptive anal sex with new male partners during recent 3 month South East Asia trip; last exposure approximately 3 weeks ago
data_table.Investigations: Lymphocytes 1.4 x10^9/L (1.5-4.0) with atypical lymphocytes; mildly raised transaminases; fourth generation HIV Ag/Ab immunoassay NEGATIVE
data_table.Other testing: EBV IgM pending; syphilis serology pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm or exclude acute HIV infection?

options.text: Quantitative plasma HIV RNA viral load by polymerase chain reaction
HIV Western blot antibody assay on the current serum sample
Repeat fourth generation HIV antigen/antibody immunoassay in 4 weeks
Monospot heterophile antibody test for infectious mononucleosis
CD4 T lymphocyte count with CD4 to CD8 ratio measurement

subtopic_detail: Opportunistic infection prophylaxis by CD4 threshold
stem:
You are the infectious diseases registrar reviewing a 39-year-old man in the HIV clinic. He was diagnosed with HIV 3 weeks ago after presenting with weight loss and oral candidiasis, and antiretroviral therapy with bictegravir-tenofovir alafenamide-emtricitabine was commenced last week.

His baseline CD4 count was 42 cells/microL and HIV RNA 480000 copies/mL. He has no known drug allergies. Chest X-ray on presentation was clear and a QuantiFERON-Plus assay was negative. Cryptococcal serum antigen was negative. Toxoplasma IgG is positive.

He is asymptomatic today apart from mild fatigue. Vital signs are within normal limits. Oral thrush has resolved with fluconazole. Baseline bloods show haemoglobin 128 g/L (135-175), neutrophils 2.6 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 90 mL/min/1.73m^2, and liver enzymes within normal limits. G6PD screening is normal.

data_table.HIV status: New diagnosis 3 weeks ago; baseline CD4 42 cells/microL; HIV RNA 480000 copies/mL; ART commenced 1 week ago (bictegravir-TAF-FTC)
data_table.Screening: CXR clear; QuantiFERON-Plus negative; cryptococcal serum antigen negative; Toxoplasma IgG POSITIVE
data_table.Bloods: Haemoglobin 128 g/L (135-175); neutrophils 2.6 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5); eGFR greater than 90; LFTs within normal limits; G6PD normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate opportunistic infection prophylaxis regimen?

options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole single strength orally once daily as sole agent
Cotrimoxazole double strength orally daily plus azithromycin 1.2 g weekly
Dapsone plus pyrimethamine plus folinic acid orally at standard weekly dosing
Nebulised pentamidine 300 mg once every 4 weeks by respiratory therapist
Fluconazole 200 mg orally daily as long term primary prophylaxis

subtopic_detail: Timing of preventive therapy for latent infection found in pregnancy
stem: A 27-year-old woman at 14 weeks gestation has a positive interferon gamma release assay from antenatal screening. She is asymptomatic, HIV negative, and has had no known contact with anyone with tuberculosis.

data_table.Examination: Well, no cough, no night sweats, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Interferon gamma release assay positive; shielded chest radiograph normal; liver function tests normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Defer preventive therapy until after she has delivered
Start isoniazid with pyridoxine now and continue postpartum
Start rifampicin now and stop it before delivery
Repeat the assay each trimester and treat if rising
Withhold treatment permanently and arrange yearly review

subtopic_detail: Hepatotoxicity monitoring during RIPE therapy
stem: A 58-year-old man is 5 weeks into rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for pulmonary tuberculosis. He has 4 days of nausea and anorexia without jaundice, and remains adherent.

data_table.Examination: No icterus, vital signs normal
data_table.Liver tests: ALT 285 U/L (baseline 32, reference less than 40), bilirubin 22 micromol/L (less than 20), INR 1.1
data_table.Other: Hepatitis A, B and C serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his TB therapy?

options.text: Continue all four drugs and repeat liver tests in 2 weeks
Stop pyrazinamide only, continuing rifampicin, isoniazid and ethambutol
Stop the hepatotoxic drugs, cover with ethambutol and moxifloxacin
Halve the rifampicin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide doses
Admit for N-acetylcysteine and continue current therapy

subtopic_detail: Early rheumatoid arthritis diagnosis and first line DMARD
stem: A 44-year-old woman has 10 weeks of symmetrical swelling of both wrists, all metacarpophalangeal joints and the second and third proximal interphalangeal joints, with 90 minutes of morning stiffness.

data_table.Examination: Synovitis of wrists, MCPs and PIPs, no nail change or dactylitis
data_table.Serology: RF 96 IU/mL, anti-CCP 180 U/mL, ESR 48 mm/h, CRP 24 mg/L
data_table.Screening: Liver enzymes and viral serology normal
data_table.Imaging: Hand radiographs show no erosions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line disease modifying therapy?

options.text: Weekly oral methotrexate, uptitrated, with folic acid
Long term oral prednisolone monotherapy without a DMARD
Subcutaneous adalimumab as first line biologic therapy
Naproxen twice daily with physiotherapy referral alone
Oral hydroxychloroquine as sole disease modifying therapy

subtopic_detail: Pre-biologic screening for latent tuberculosis
stem: A 52-year-old man with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis has active disease after six months of methotrexate, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine. He was born in Vietnam and has no cough, fever or weight loss.

data_table.Screening: Hepatitis B, C and HIV negative; QuantiFERON-Plus positive; chest x-ray small right upper lobe fibronodular scar

lead_in: What should be done before starting the tumour necrosis factor inhibitor?

options.text: Start the inhibitor now and monitor with six monthly chest x-rays
Treat latent tuberculosis with isoniazid and start the biologic at four weeks
Send induced sputum and start four drug antituberculous therapy
Repeat the interferon gamma release assay and computed tomography of the chest
Switch to a Janus kinase inhibitor without tuberculosis therapy

subtopic_detail: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis diagnosis and induction
stem: A 62-year-old man has 6 weeks of bloody nasal crusting, hearing loss and a cough with blood-streaked sputum, and one week of ankle oedema and reduced urine output.

data_table.Examination: Evolving saddle nose deformity, right basal crackles, pitting ankle oedema
data_table.Bloods: Creatinine 245 micromol/L, rising from 90; Hb 96 g/L
data_table.Urine: Dysmorphic red cells with red cell casts, 2+ protein
data_table.Immunology: c-ANCA positive, PR3 145 U/mL, anti-GBM negative
data_table.Imaging: Two peripheral cavitating nodules on chest CT

lead_in: What is the most appropriate induction regimen?

options.text: Weekly subcutaneous methotrexate with oral prednisolone
Intravenous immunoglobulin with oral prednisolone
Plasma exchange alone, pending the renal biopsy result
Oral prednisolone alone, tapered over 6 months
Rituximab with pulsed methylprednisolone then an oral taper

subtopic_detail: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis versus polyarteritis nodosa
stem: A 48-year-old woman has three months of progressive numbness and weakness of the right foot and left hand. She has late onset asthma and adult onset nasal polyposis.

data_table.Examination: Foot drop, wrist drop, palpable purpura on both shins
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 4.8 x10^9/L (less than 0.5), creatinine 78 micromol/L, urine trace blood, no casts
data_table.Immunology: Perinuclear ANCA positive with MPO 45 U/mL; hepatitis B and C negative
data_table.Imaging: Chest CT migratory ground glass infiltrates

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Microscopic polyangiitis with pulmonary renal syndrome
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis with airway involvement
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss)
Polyarteritis nodosa related to chronic hepatitis B
Mixed cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis from hepatitis C

subtopic_detail: McDonald 2017 criteria for multiple sclerosis after clinically isolated syndrome
stem:
You are the neurology registrar. A 29-year-old woman is admitted with 5 days of progressive painful visual blurring in the right eye and worsening on eye movement. She has no headache, no other neurological symptoms, and has never had similar episodes.

She is otherwise well, does not smoke, and is not pregnant. She takes no regular medications. There is no family history of multiple sclerosis.

Examination shows right visual acuity 6/24 (baseline 6/6), reduced red desaturation on the right, and a right relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy is normal (retrobulbar). Cranial nerves are otherwise intact. Motor, sensory, cerebellar, and gait examination are normal. Vital signs are within normal limits.

Investigations: MRI brain with gadolinium shows 6 T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions - one in the corpus callosum (juxtacortical), one periventricular, two infratentorial, and two in the cervical spinal cord; two of the six lesions enhance with gadolinium and four do not. CSF shows a normal cell count, normal protein, negative culture, and oligoclonal bands present in CSF but not in matched serum. Aquaporin-4 IgG (NMO) is negative and MOG antibodies are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Right visual acuity 6/24; red desaturation right; right RAPD; normal fundoscopy; remainder of neurological exam normal
data_table.MRI: 6 T2/FLAIR lesions: 1 juxtacortical corpus callosum, 1 periventricular, 2 infratentorial, 2 cervical cord; 2 enhance with gadolinium, 4 do not enhance
data_table.CSF: Normal cells; normal protein; culture negative; oligoclonal bands present in CSF not in serum

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnosis at this presentation?

options.text: Clinically isolated syndrome without dissemination in time or space
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder based on the optic neuritis
MOG antibody-associated disease with predominant optic neuritis
Relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis meeting McDonald 2017 criteria at first event
Primary progressive multiple sclerosis presenting with optic neuritis

subtopic_detail: JCV testing before natalizumab in multiple sclerosis
stem:
You are the neurology registrar in an MS clinic. A 34-year-old woman with relapsing remitting MS diagnosed 3 years ago has had 2 clinical relapses in the past 12 months and 5 new T2 lesions on annual surveillance MRI despite 2 years of adherence to dimethyl fumarate. Her EDSS has risen from 1.5 to 2.5.

She was previously untreated with immunosuppressants. She has never had chickenpox to her knowledge and has no history of shingles or opportunistic infection. She is not pregnant and uses effective contraception.

Examination: mild bilateral lower limb hyperreflexia, brisk knee jerks, and a slightly wide-based gait; cognition intact. Vital signs are within normal limits.

Her neurologist is considering escalation to natalizumab. Investigations show JC virus antibody index 2.8 (positive; low positive less than 0.9, high positive greater than 1.5), hepatitis B and C serology negative, HIV negative, VZV IgG positive. Baseline MRI brain from 4 months ago is available for future comparison.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mild bilateral lower limb hyperreflexia; brisk knee jerks; wide-based gait; cognition intact
data_table.MS status: 3 years RRMS; 2 clinical relapses in past 12 months; 5 new T2 lesions on annual MRI on dimethyl fumarate; EDSS 1.5 to 2.5
data_table.Screening: JCV Ab index 2.8 (high positive greater than 1.5); HBV, HCV, HIV negative; VZV IgG positive
data_table.Baseline: MRI brain 4 months ago available for future comparison

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding disease modifying therapy?

options.text: Commence natalizumab at standard 4 weekly infusion and repeat MRI in 6 months
Commence natalizumab with extended interval 6 weekly dosing from the first year
Recommend natalizumab as JCV index below 5.0 confers acceptable risk regardless
Switch to ocrelizumab or ofatumumab given the high positive JCV antibody index
Continue dimethyl fumarate and add IV methylprednisolone for each relapse

subtopic_detail: Wearing off in Parkinson disease
stem:
You are the general medical registrar. A 68-year-old man with idiopathic Parkinson disease diagnosed 6 years ago attends for review with his wife. He has been on levodopa-carbidopa 100/25 mg four times daily for 4 years with initially good response.

Over the past 6 months he describes reliable good motor function for about 2.5 hours after each dose, then a return of tremor, stiffness and slow movement about 30 minutes before his next scheduled dose. Symptoms improve within 30 minutes of the next dose. There are no involuntary movements at peak dose. He is fully continent, sleeps well, and has no visual hallucinations or cognitive decline.

His MMSE is 29/30. Postural blood pressure change is minimal. Vital signs are within normal limits. He is otherwise well with no other regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Cognition: MMSE 29/30; no hallucinations; no cognitive complaints
data_table.Motor pattern: Predictable return of tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia 30 min before next dose; symptoms resolve within 30 min of dose; no peak dose dyskinesias
data_table.Medications: Levodopa-carbidopa 100/25 mg four times daily for 4 years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line adjustment to his therapy?

options.text: Add entacapone with each levodopa-carbidopa dose to prolong plasma levodopa
Refer for deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus urgently
Discontinue levodopa and switch to pramipexole or ropinirole monotherapy
Add amantadine 100 mg twice daily for management of dyskinesia symptoms
Add anticholinergic benzatropine 1 mg orally twice daily for tremor control

subtopic_detail: Dementia with Lewy bodies versus Alzheimer disease
stem: A 74-year-old man has 18 months of cognitive change with marked day-to-day fluctuation in alertness, recurrent vivid visual hallucinations, and two years of shouting and kicking in his sleep. He has fallen twice.

data_table.Examination: Masked face, bilateral rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity, stooped shuffling gait
data_table.Cognition: MMSE 22/30 with attention and visuospatial deficits, recall relatively preserved
data_table.Imaging: MRI shows mild generalised atrophy without hippocampal or vascular change
data_table.Bloods: B12 138 pmol/L, TSH and syphilis serology normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Alzheimer disease with an atypical cognitive profile
Dementia with Lewy bodies meeting probable criteria
Vascular dementia from subcortical small vessel disease
Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia with parkinsonism
Parkinson disease dementia following motor onset

subtopic_detail: Fitness to drive in dementia (Austroads)
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 76-year-old man 6 months after a diagnosis of mild Alzheimer disease was confirmed by a geriatrician. He drives a private vehicle only (no commercial licence). He lives with his wife who normally sits in the front passenger seat when he drives.

His MMSE is 24/30 with impairment in orientation and recall. Functional review by his wife reveals he now needs prompting to take his morning medications and has become lost driving home from the local supermarket twice in the last 2 months. He denies any recent motor vehicle collisions. His visual acuity is 6/9 corrected and he has no significant visual field deficit. His car has manual transmission and he wears reading glasses.

Examination shows no focal neurology. Vital signs are within normal limits. He asks you whether he can continue driving.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Cognition: MMSE 24/30; impairment in orientation and recall; needs prompting for medications; getting lost driving home twice in 2 months
data_table.Vision: 6/9 corrected; no significant visual field deficit
data_table.Licence: Private class only; drives with wife in front passenger seat

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding driving?

options.text: Recommend continued driving only when accompanied by his wife and only in daylight hours
Reassure that mild cognitive impairment is compatible with unrestricted driving above MMSE 20
Review him at the next annual dementia review before making any decision about driving
Discharge from your care and advise him to arrange his own transport in future
Advise him to stop driving and arrange formal occupational therapy on-road assessment

subtopic_detail: Guillain-Barre syndrome immunotherapy choice
stem: A 54-year-old man has five days of ascending weakness and can no longer walk without support. He had bloody diarrhoea three weeks ago.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical leg weakness, absent knee and ankle reflexes, stocking sensory loss, cranial nerves intact
data_table.Nerve conduction: Slowed motor conduction with conduction block

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immunotherapy?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily tapered over eight weeks
Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for three days
Intravenous rituximab weekly for four consecutive weeks
Intravenous immunoglobulin for five days or plasma exchange
Supportive care with physiotherapy and thromboprophylaxis alone

subtopic_detail: Respiratory monitoring and ICU criteria in Guillain-Barre syndrome
stem: A 58-year-old woman with Guillain-Barre syndrome, day 4 and on immunoglobulin, becomes breathless overnight. She can count to 15 on one breath, down from 30.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, BP 168/102 mmHg from 130/80, RR 32 /min
data_table.Bedside respiratory: FVC 950 mL at weight 71 kg, accessory muscle use, paradoxical abdominal movement, weak cough, coughs on sips of water
data_table.Neurology: MRC grade 2 in all limbs, quieter voice

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: High flow nasal oxygen and repeat the FVC in 4 hours
Continuous positive airway pressure on the medical ward
A further immunoglobulin loading dose with hourly observations
Intravenous salbutamol with peak expiratory flow monitoring
Urgent intensive care review for elective intubation

subtopic_detail: Managing a bone density in the osteopenic range with no fracture
stem: A 62-year-old woman has densitometry after her sister was treated for osteoporosis. She has never fractured, does not smoke, drinks rarely and walks daily. Menopause was at 52 and her only medicine is an antihistamine in spring.

data_table.Bone density: Femoral neck T-score -1.7; lumbar spine T-score -1.5
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L; vitamin D 80 nmol/L; TSH 1.9 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Weight bearing exercise, dietary calcium and rescanning in two years
Start weekly oral alendronate now to prevent progression to osteoporosis
Begin menopausal hormone therapy for skeletal protection from now
Start six monthly subcutaneous denosumab and review in one year
Repeat the bone density scan in six months before deciding

subtopic_detail: Denosumab discontinuation and rebound vertebral fracture risk
stem: A 73-year-old woman has had denosumab six-monthly for 7 years for osteoporosis. She has been told her bone density is now good and the drug can stop. Her next dose is due in 3 weeks.

data_table.DXA: T-scores lumbar spine -1.8, femoral neck -2.0, improved from baseline
data_table.Bloods: Corrected calcium 2.30 mmol/L, vitamin D 72 nmol/L
data_table.Imaging: No vertebral fracture on spine imaging

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Stop denosumab now that her T-scores have normalised on treatment
Continue denosumab six-monthly with no other change to management
Continue denosumab with closer calcium monitoring and specialist review
Stop denosumab and give intravenous zoledronic acid instead
Stop denosumab and switch to subcutaneous teriparatide daily

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated adult female urinary tract infection
stem:
You are the general practitioner. A 32-year-old non-pregnant woman presents with 2 days of dysuria, urinary frequency, and suprapubic discomfort. She has no fever, no back pain, no vaginal discharge, and no nausea or vomiting.

She has had 2 uncomplicated urinary tract infections in the past 5 years, both successfully treated with a short antibiotic course. She has no history of pyelonephritis, no known urological anomaly, and no diabetes. She is sexually active with a regular male partner, uses condoms, and has no recent hospital admission or urinary catheterisation.

Examination shows suprapubic tenderness only. There is no costovertebral angle tenderness. Vital signs are within normal limits.

Urinalysis is positive for leukocytes and nitrites; midstream urine has been sent for culture. She has no known drug allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Suprapubic tenderness only; no CVA tenderness; no vaginal discharge
data_table.History: 2 days dysuria, frequency, suprapubic discomfort; 2 previous uncomplicated UTIs in 5 years; not pregnant; no diabetes; no urological anomaly; no catheter or recent hospitalisation
data_table.Urinalysis: Leukocytes and nitrites positive; MSU sent for culture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic?

options.text: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally 6 hourly for 5 days as first line agent
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally 12 hourly for 3 days as empirical treatment
Cefalexin 500 mg orally 12 hourly for 5 days as first line antibiotic
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 500/125 mg orally 8 hourly for 5 days empirically
Fosfomycin 3 g orally as a single dose without further follow-up antibiotic

subtopic_detail: Acute pyelonephritis empirical intravenous therapy
stem: A 42-year-old woman has 24 hours of right flank pain, fever, rigors and vomiting after three days of dysuria. She is not pregnant and has had no recent hospital contact.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 degrees C, HR 118/min, BP 96/58 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Right costovertebral angle tenderness, dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.2 x10^9/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L; urine 3+ leukocytes and 3+ nitrites

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin for 7 days with review by her doctor tomorrow
Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam as empirical monotherapy
Intravenous vancomycin with metronidazole as empirical cover
Intravenous meropenem as empirical monotherapy for pyelonephritis
Intravenous amoxicillin with a single weight adjusted gentamicin dose

subtopic_detail: Sepsis hour-1 bundle and vasopressor initiation
stem: A 66-year-old man has 12 hours of productive cough, fever and breathlessness. He is drowsy, oriented to person only.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 78/44 mmHg at arrival, 88/52 mmHg after fluid, pulse 122 /min, T 39.1 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L, lactate 4.6 mmol/L
data_table.Given: Intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin, 30 mL/kg crystalloid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in resuscitation?

options.text: Give a further 2 L crystalloid bolus before considering a vasopressor
Commence intravenous dopamine peripherally as the first line vasopressor
Give intravenous hydrocortisone and hold vasopressors pending the response
Commence intravenous noradrenaline titrated to a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg
Broaden antibiotics to meropenem and vancomycin, deferring haemodynamic support

subtopic_detail: Initial gait and balance assessment after a single non-syncopal fall
stem:
A 79-year-old woman attends your general practice after catching her foot on a rug at home last week. She landed on her hands and got up without help; she did not hit her head.

She lives alone in a single-storey house and manages her own shopping. Her only regular medicine is perindopril. She describes no light-headedness or blackout around the time of the fall.

Heart sounds are dual and her visual acuity is 6/9 in each eye with her glasses on. She steadies herself on the furniture as she walks across the consulting room. Both knees show crepitus and reduced range of movement.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min regular, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg supine and 136/76 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily, paracetamol 1 g as required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial assessment?

options.text: Arrange a non-contrast CT brain to exclude an intracranial cause of falling
Request a 24-hour ambulatory electrocardiogram to look for an intermittent arrhythmia
Perform a timed up-and-go test with direct observation of her gait
Refer her for bone densitometry before undertaking any further clinical assessment
Arrange an echocardiogram to assess her for structural valvular heart disease

subtopic_detail: Primary prevention of delirium in a high-risk surgical admission
stem:
You are the admitting resident for an 83-year-old woman who has fractured the neck of her right femur after a fall at home. She is booked for hemiarthroplasty tomorrow afternoon.

Her daughter reports that she has been forgetting appointments for the past two years but still manages at home with prompting. She wears glasses and two hearing aids, neither of which came in with the ambulance. She has never had an episode of confusion in hospital before.

On assessment she is orientated to time, place and person, and her abbreviated mental test score is 8 out of 10. She has received one dose of intravenous morphine in the emergency department and reports her hip pain as 3 out of 10 at rest.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86/min, blood pressure 132/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, urea and creatinine all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action to reduce her risk of delirium?

options.text: Start a multicomponent program addressing orientation, sleep, mobility and sensory aids
Prescribe regular oral haloperidol 0.5 mg twice daily until after her operation
Prescribe melatonin 2 mg nightly from admission until the day of discharge
Order a non-contrast CT brain and screen for occult infection before theatre
Restrict her analgesia to paracetamol alone to avoid opioid-induced confusion after theatre

subtopic_detail: Hypoactive presentation misattributed to low mood
stem:
An 81-year-old man is on day 4 of treatment for community-acquired pneumonia. The nursing staff ask you to review him because he has become withdrawn, is eating very little and takes a long time to answer questions. They wonder whether he has become depressed since his wife died last year.

His daughter tells you he was managing his own finances and driving to bowls twice a week until this admission, and that he seemed himself when she visited on the day he came in.

At the bedside he is drowsy and loses the thread mid-sentence, but the nursing notes record him as alert and chatting at 8 am. He denies feeling sad and says he simply feels tired.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 124/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 93% on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 12.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 68 mg/L (<5), sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 92 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start mirtazapine 15 mg at night and review his mood again in two weeks
Start regular quetiapine 12.5 mg at night to settle his fluctuating daytime state
Arrange an inpatient psychiatry consultation for assessment of a major depressive disorder
Screen for delirium at the bedside and review his precipitants and medications
Arrange an MRI brain and formal neuropsychological testing before any further treatment

subtopic_detail: Searching for a reversible precipitant before sedating an agitated postoperative patient
stem:
You are the night resident called to an 84-year-old man on day 2 after a hemiarthroplasty for a fractured neck of femur. Since midnight he has been pulling at his intravenous cannula and trying to climb over the bed rails. He was calm and orientated at the evening ward round.

He answers questions in single words and keeps reaching towards his lower abdomen. His indwelling catheter was removed at 10 am and the fluid balance chart records no urine output since.

His analgesia chart shows regular paracetamol only; the oxycodone charted in recovery was ceased when the spinal block wore off.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, blood pressure 156/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 42 mg/L (<5), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give haloperidol 0.5 mg orally now, repeating in two hours if he remains agitated
Assess him for pain and urinary retention, including a bedside bladder scan
Give lorazepam 0.5 mg sublingually and nurse him in a low-stimulus single room
Send a urine culture and start empirical oral trimethoprim for presumed infection
Apply a physical restraint and arrange one-to-one nursing observation through the night

subtopic_detail: Palliative emergency with evolving cord signs
stem:
A 68-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer presents to the emergency department with five days of mid-thoracic back pain that is worse when he lies flat and wakes him at night. For the past two days his legs have felt heavy and he has needed both arms to push himself out of a chair.

He takes slow-release morphine 20 mg twice daily, which has not helped the back pain, and abiraterone with prednisolone.

Power is 4 out of 5 for hip flexion on both sides with normal upper limb power. Knee and ankle reflexes are brisk and both plantar responses are extensor. He last passed urine nine hours ago and says his bladder feels full.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 142/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), prostate specific antigen rising over three months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Arrange an urgent CT of the lumbar spine and review it in the morning
Increase his slow-release morphine and arrange an outpatient MRI within a fortnight
Refer directly for urgent radiotherapy planning without further imaging of the spine
Request urgent neurosurgical review after plain radiographs of the whole spine today
Give dexamethasone 16 mg orally now and arrange urgent MRI of the whole spine

subtopic_detail: Responding to a family request for artificial hydration in the last days of life
stem:
An 88-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer is in a palliative care unit and is recognised to be in her last days of life. She has taken only sips of water for three days and has been unrousable since yesterday morning.

Her son has driven from interstate and is distressed. He asks you to start a drip, saying he cannot bear the thought of his mother dying thirsty.

Her lips and tongue are dry, she is not grimacing or restless, and there has been no jerking of her limbs. She is on a continuous subcutaneous infusion of morphine that has kept her settled for the past 48 hours, with no breakthrough doses required overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 12/min, SpO2 not measured, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No peripheral oedema and no added breath sounds

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Start subcutaneous fluid at one litre over 24 hours and review the effect daily
Start intravenous fluid at 80 mL per hour and monitor her for peripheral oedema
Provide regular mouth care and sips as tolerated, with explanation for family
Insert a nasogastric tube for hydration and continue it until she is more alert
Check her urea and electrolytes and decide on fluid once the results are back

subtopic_detail: Rationalising the medication chart when swallowing is lost in the last days of life
stem:
You visit a 90-year-old man in his residential aged care facility. He has metastatic lung cancer and over the past week has become bed-bound and drowsy, rousing only briefly when his daughter speaks to him. The facility staff report that this morning he coughed and spluttered on his crushed tablets and refused any further medicines.

His current chart is perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, alendronate 70 mg weekly, metformin 500 mg twice daily, aspirin 100 mg daily, slow-release morphine 20 mg twice daily and a daily macrogol sachet.

He grimaces when the staff roll him. His daughter and the facility both wish him to remain there rather than return to hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 93% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Rouses briefly to voice, unable to swallow safely, no urine output recorded for 12 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication plan?

options.text: Cease the whole oral regimen and chart subcutaneous morphine with as-required medicines
Continue all his current medicines by crushing them and giving them in thickened fluid
Insert a nasogastric tube so that his oral regimen can be continued without change
Cease only the statin and the bisphosphonate and continue the other oral medicines
Chart subcutaneous morphine but continue his oral cardiac and diabetes medicines unchanged

subtopic_detail: Predictable procedure-related pain on a stable background opioid
stem:
A 74-year-old woman with locally advanced breast cancer attends the community palliative care clinic. Her chest wall wound is dressed twice weekly by the district nurses.

For the past month her background pain has been controlled on her current slow-release opioid, and she has used no more than one breakthrough dose a week. She reads and gardens between dressing changes and is not drowsy.

During each dressing change she cries out and asks the nurses to stop, and she is tearful for the rest of the visit. Within 20 minutes of the dressing being finished she is comfortable again and back to her usual self.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Slow-release morphine 30 mg twice daily, immediate-release morphine 10 mg as required, macrogol daily, paracetamol 1 g four times daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her analgesia?

options.text: Increase her slow-release morphine to 60 mg twice daily and review weekly
Add regular paracetamol four times daily and continue her current opioid regimen
Add slow-release oxycodone 10 mg twice daily alongside her current morphine dose
Give an immediate-release morphine dose half an hour before each dressing
Add regular amitriptyline 10 mg at night and reassess after the next dressing

subtopic_detail: Non-pharmacological management of chronic breathlessness without hypoxaemia
stem:
A 76-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and metastatic lung cancer is seen at home by the community palliative care service. He has been breathless at rest for three weeks and can no longer walk to his letterbox.

He was started on immediate-release morphine 2.5 mg four-hourly a fortnight ago and reports that it takes the edge off but that he still panics when the breathlessness comes on. His daughter has bought a second-hand oxygen concentrator and wants to know when to turn it on.

His chest is quiet with a prolonged expiratory phase and there is no new focal change. He is not using accessory muscles at rest and speaks in full sentences.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mild ankle oedema, no calf tenderness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Arrange home oxygen at 2 litres per minute by nasal prongs for continuous use
Provide a handheld fan directed at the face with breathing and positioning advice
Start oral prednisolone 25 mg daily for five days and review his symptoms after
Start regular diazepam 2 mg three times daily for his breathlessness-related anxiety
Increase his morphine to 10 mg four-hourly and review the effect in 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Compounded bleeding risk from a recently added agent
stem:
A 77-year-old woman attends for a routine review. She has atrial fibrillation treated with apixaban 5 mg twice daily and takes sertraline 50 mg daily for depression, which has been stable for four years.

She mentions that a locum started her on naproxen 500 mg twice daily three weeks ago for pain in her right knee, and that it has helped her walk to the shops again. Since then she has noticed several large bruises on her forearms and some burning discomfort behind her breastbone after meals.

Her stools are described as normal in colour. Her blood pressure today is 148/84 mmHg, up from 128/76 mmHg at her last visit.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 118 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 42 mL/min/1.73m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication change?

options.text: Stop apixaban and start aspirin 100 mg daily with a proton pump inhibitor
Continue all her medicines and add pantoprazole 20 mg daily with a repeat count
Switch sertraline to mirtazapine and continue naproxen at a reduced daily dose
Switch naproxen to celecoxib 100 mg daily and add pantoprazole 20 mg daily
Stop naproxen and manage the knee pain with paracetamol and topical therapy

subtopic_detail: Choosing the first medicine to stop using time to benefit
stem:
An 84-year-old man with metastatic colorectal cancer is reviewed in the outpatient clinic. Systemic treatment was stopped last month and the oncology team estimate his prognosis in months rather than years.

He spends more than half his waking hours in a chair or in bed and needs help to shower. He tells you he is tired of swallowing so many tablets each day and asks which ones he can let go.

He has aching thighs on most days and no history of vascular disease. His bone pain is well controlled and his bowels open daily. He has never had a fracture or a myocardial infarction.

data_table.Medications: Atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, pantoprazole 20 mg daily, paracetamol 1 g four times daily, colecalciferol 1000 IU daily, macrogol one sachet daily, slow-release oxycodone 10 mg twice daily
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110), liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: Which medicine is most appropriate to cease first?

options.text: Pantoprazole 20 mg daily, which was started for reflux during his recent chemotherapy
Paracetamol 1 g four times daily, taken for his background bone pain
Atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, which was prescribed years ago for primary prevention
Colecalciferol 1000 IU daily, which was prescribed for his bone health
Macrogol one sachet daily, which was prescribed alongside his regular opioid

subtopic_detail: Reviewing long-term antiresorptive therapy after five years
stem:
A 76-year-old woman asks whether she still needs the weekly tablet she has taken since a wrist fracture at the age of 70. She has taken alendronate 70 mg weekly for five and a half years and has not missed a dose.

She walks 3 km most days, has never taken a corticosteroid, and has had no fracture since the wrist. Her height is unchanged on measurement today.

She had repeat densitometry last month and asks whether the result changes anything.

data_table.Investigations: Femoral neck T-score -1.9 (pre-treatment -2.6), lumbar spine T-score -1.7, corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 76 nmol/L (>50)
data_table.Medications: Alendronate 70 mg weekly, colecalciferol 1000 IU daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her osteoporosis therapy?

options.text: Stop alendronate now and reassess her fracture risk with densitometry in two years
Continue alendronate indefinitely on the basis that her fracture risk remains elevated
Switch to denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every six months and continue indefinitely
Switch to daily teriparatide for 18 months and then review her bone mineral density
Stop alendronate now and start calcium 1200 mg daily with no further bone review

subtopic_detail: Stopping a cholinesterase inhibitor when the treatment goal can no longer be met
stem:
You review an 89-year-old woman in her residential aged care facility at the request of her family. She has had Alzheimer dementia for nine years and has taken donepezil daily for the last six.

She no longer uses words, does not recognise her daughter, and is fully dependent for feeding, transfers and continence. Her daughter asks whether the tablets are still doing anything.

Staff report she has lost 6 kg over six months and often refuses food. Her pulse has been persistently low at each of the last three facility observations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 48/min regular, blood pressure 118/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Medications: Donepezil 10 mg daily, paracetamol 1 g three times daily, colecalciferol 1000 IU daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her donepezil?

options.text: Increase donepezil to 15 mg daily and monitor her cognition over three months
Switch to rivastigmine patch 9.5 mg daily to reduce gastrointestinal adverse effects
Add memantine 10 mg twice daily and continue donepezil at her current dose
Taper and cease donepezil, monitoring her for any deterioration over four weeks
Continue donepezil unchanged and refer her for 24-hour ambulatory cardiac monitoring

subtopic_detail: Reversible metabolic cause of deterioration in advanced malignancy
stem:
A 71-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer involving the spine and pelvis is brought in by her husband. Over five days she has become progressively drowsy, has vomited several times a day and has not opened her bowels for a week.

He says she has been drinking glass after glass of water and getting up at night to pass urine, which is new.

She is rousable and orientated to person only. Her mucous membranes are dry and her skin turgor is reduced. Her opioid dose has not changed for six weeks and her pupils are 3 mm and reactive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 102/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 3.28 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), albumin 30 g/L (34-48), creatinine 132 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 36 mL/min/1.73m2, sodium 141 mmol/L (135-145)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Give intravenous furosemide 40 mg after a 500 mL saline bolus and recheck
Give intravenous sodium chloride 0.9% rehydration first and then zoledronic acid
Start oral prednisolone 50 mg daily and restrict her dietary calcium intake
Start subcutaneous calcitonin alone and repeat her serum calcium in 48 hours
Start denosumab 120 mg subcutaneously without first giving any intravenous rehydration

subtopic_detail: Localised metastatic bone pain not responding to opioid escalation
stem:
A 70-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer reports worsening pain over his right hip for six weeks. It is worst when he puts weight through the leg and eases when he sits.

His slow-release morphine has been tripled over that period. He now sleeps through visits from his grandchildren and his daughter says he is not himself, yet he still rates the hip pain at 8 out of 10 on standing.

Pain is reproduced by percussion over the right greater trochanter and there is no pain elsewhere. A recent bone scan showed increased uptake at that site with no other new lesion.

data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.36 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 84 micromol/L (60-110), haemoglobin 116 g/L (130-180)
data_table.Medications: Slow-release morphine 90 mg twice daily, immediate-release morphine 30 mg as required, macrogol daily, paracetamol 1 g four times daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in managing his pain?

options.text: Increase his slow-release morphine by a further 50 per cent and add more aperients
Add regular pregabalin 75 mg twice daily and review his response in two weeks
Start dexamethasone 8 mg daily and continue his current opioid doses unchanged
Rotate from morphine to hydromorphone at an equianalgesic dose reduced by a third
Refer him for palliative external beam radiotherapy directed at the painful site

subtopic_detail: Vitamin D repletion and exercise prescription in a recurrent faller
stem:
An 82-year-old woman has had two falls in the past six months, both indoors and neither causing a fracture. She lives alone, rarely goes outside during winter and covers her arms and legs when she does.

She takes perindopril 5 mg daily and no sedatives. Lying and standing blood pressures show no postural drop and her visual acuity is 6/9 with her current glasses.

She can rise from a chair only by pushing on the armrests, and her timed up-and-go is 16 seconds. She tells you her neighbour was given a large once-a-year vitamin D dose and asks whether she should have the same.

data_table.Investigations: 25-hydroxyvitamin D 38 nmol/L (>50 sufficient), corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 62 mL/min/1.73m2, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Colecalciferol 1000 IU daily plus referral to a supervised balance and strength class
Colecalciferol 500,000 IU orally as a single annual dose, with clinical review in 12 months
Colecalciferol 1000 IU daily alone, with repeat vitamin D testing in three months
Referral to a supervised balance and strength class with no vitamin D treatment
Calcium carbonate 1200 mg daily with colecalciferol 1000 IU daily and hazard review

subtopic_detail: Separating a cardiac cause from a mechanical fall
stem:
A 79-year-old man is brought to your clinic by his wife after his third fall in four months. On this occasion she found him on the kitchen floor and he has no memory of going down.

She says he looked grey and clammy for about a minute and then talked to her normally. He was talking normally within a minute and had no limb jerking. Two of the earlier falls happened while he was carrying washing to the line.

His pulse has a slow upstroke and there is an ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge that radiates to both carotids.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min regular, blood pressure 126/82 mmHg supine and 124/80 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 138 g/L (130-180), creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer him to a community falls prevention program and review in three months
Arrange outpatient 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring and review the resulting trace
Arrange an urgent transthoracic echocardiogram today with a resting 12-lead electrocardiogram
Arrange a non-contrast CT brain with carotid duplex ultrasound within one week
Arrange a tilt-table test and refer him to the syncope clinic next month

subtopic_detail: Identifying the substitute decision-maker under New South Wales law
stem:
An 85-year-old man with severe dementia is admitted to your New South Wales hospital with aspiration pneumonia. He is drowsy, cannot state where he is and cannot retain or weigh any information about treatment. You need consent for a decision about ongoing intravenous antibiotics and the goals of his care.

A search of his records and his home documents finds no advance care directive and no enduring guardian appointment.

Three relatives are at the bedside. His wife separated from him ten years ago and has not seen him since, though they never divorced. His daughter has lived with him and provided his unpaid daily care for the past three years. His brother visits monthly and holds an enduring power of attorney for financial matters.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, blood pressure 118/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 90% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, coarse crackles at the right base

lead_in: Who should you approach as the substitute decision-maker?

options.text: His brother, because he already holds an enduring power of attorney for this patient
The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal, by an urgent application for a guardian
His wife, because she is his spouse regardless of the current state of the relationship
His daughter, as the unpaid carer with a close and continuing relationship with him
The treating team, acting in his best interests without a substitute decision-maker

subtopic_detail: Choosing a starting opioid when glomerular filtration is severely reduced
stem:
An 80-year-old woman with metastatic ovarian cancer describes constant deep abdominal pain rated 7 out of 10 that now wakes her every night. Regular paracetamol 1 g four times daily is no longer helping and she has never taken an opioid.

She lives at home with her daughter, who will supervise her medicines. She weighs 52 kg and eats small amounts.

Her creatinine has risen steadily over three months, attributed to ureteric compression that is not amenable to stenting. She is fully orientated and her liver function is unchanged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 190 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 22 mL/min/1.73m2, potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate analgesic plan?

options.text: Slow-release morphine 10 mg twice daily with immediate-release morphine as required
Immediate-release oxycodone 2.5 mg four-hourly as required with daily telephone review
Transdermal fentanyl 12 micrograms per hour with immediate-release morphine as required
Regular ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with paracetamol and weekly review
Immediate-release morphine 5 mg four-hourly regularly with aperients and daily review

subtopic_detail: Review of antipsychotic therapy prescribed for behavioural symptoms of dementia
stem:
You are the visiting general practitioner for an 84-year-old woman in residential aged care who has Alzheimer dementia. Sixteen weeks ago she was started on risperidone 0.5 mg twice daily after she hit staff repeatedly during showering.

The care plan shows that showering was moved to the afternoon and a familiar carer assigned at the same time the medicine began. Staff record no episode of aggression for the past ten weeks.

Over the last fortnight she has begun shuffling, her handwriting has become small and she had an unwitnessed fall in the corridor last week. Her weight and swallowing are unchanged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 132/74 mmHg supine and 118/68 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her risperidone?

options.text: Continue risperidone at the current dose and place a movement alarm in her room
Switch to olanzapine 2.5 mg at night to reduce her extrapyramidal adverse effects
Halve the risperidone dose and schedule the next formal review in twelve months
Continue risperidone and add benzatropine 1 mg daily to treat her gait change
Taper risperidone with a plan to cease it, monitoring her behaviour each week

subtopic_detail: Managing a narrow therapeutic index drug when renal function falls acutely
stem:
An 83-year-old woman presents with a week of nausea, poor appetite and lethargy. She has permanent atrial fibrillation treated with digoxin 250 micrograms daily and apixaban 5 mg twice daily, and takes indapamide for hypertension.

She had four days of loose stools a fortnight ago after a family barbecue and has been drinking little since. She has not vomited and has no abdominal pain.

She is alert and orientated, her capillary refill is three seconds, and her blood pressure does not fall on standing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 52/min irregularly irregular, blood pressure 118/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Digoxin 3.1 nmol/L (0.5-2.0), creatinine 168 micromol/L (45-90, was 92 six weeks ago), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular response and no ectopy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Withhold digoxin, correct the potassium and magnesium, and repeat the level tomorrow
Give digoxin-specific antibody fragments and admit her for continuous cardiac monitoring
Halve the digoxin dose, replace potassium orally, and repeat the level weekly
Continue digoxin, give intravenous fluid, and repeat renal function in 24 hours
Insert a temporary pacing wire and withhold digoxin until the ventricular rate rises

subtopic_detail: Movement disorder emerging after a recently started antiemetic
stem:
A 78-year-old man is brought in by his wife because he has slowed down over the past three months. He shuffles when he walks, has stopped playing the piano and takes twice as long to dress.

Four months ago he was started on metoclopramide for nausea after an admission with gastritis, and it has been continued since.

On examination there is bradykinesia with equal decrement in finger tapping on both sides and a symmetrical rest tremor of both hands. His wife confirms that his sense of smell is unchanged and that he has never acted out his dreams. His handwriting is smaller than it was a year ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 138/80 mmHg supine and 132/78 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Medications: Metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily, pantoprazole 20 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start levodopa with carbidopa 100/25 mg three times daily and review in six weeks
Arrange a dopamine transporter scan before making any change to his current medicines
Cease the metoclopramide and reassess his movements over the next three months
Start amantadine 100 mg twice daily and continue metoclopramide for his nausea
Add benzatropine 1 mg twice daily and refer him to neurology for further assessment

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation decision in a recurrent faller with atrial fibrillation
stem:
An 86-year-old woman with permanent atrial fibrillation, hypertension and type 2 diabetes is reviewed after her third fall in six months. Each fall happened outdoors on uneven footpaths while she was wearing backless slippers, and none caused a fracture or a head strike.

A locum has written in her notes that her apixaban should be stopped because she keeps falling. Her daughter agrees and asks you to sign the cessation.

She weighs 68 kg and has had no bleeding episode since apixaban was started three years ago. Her blood pressure is recorded supine and again at three minutes standing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min irregularly irregular, blood pressure 148/82 mmHg supine and 124/74 mmHg standing at three minutes, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-165), platelets 244 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 48 mL/min/1.73m2
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily, perindopril 10 mg daily, indapamide 1.5 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her anticoagulation?

options.text: Stop apixaban and start aspirin 100 mg daily to reduce her overall bleeding risk
Continue apixaban at full dose and address her modifiable falls risk factors
Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily given her age and her recurrent falls
Stop apixaban and refer her for percutaneous left atrial appendage closure instead
Stop apixaban for three months while she completes a falls prevention program

subtopic_detail: Converting oral oxycodone to a subcutaneous morphine infusion when the oral route is lost
stem:
A 72-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer is being cared for at home. For the past week his pain has been well controlled on his current oral opioid regimen, and he has needed only one breakthrough dose in the last 48 hours.

Since yesterday he has vomited every oral dose within minutes and has kept nothing down. He remains alert and comfortable at rest, with no myoclonus and pupils of 3 mm.
