His renal and liver function are unchanged from a month ago. A continuous subcutaneous infusion is to be started this afternoon.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 74 micromol/L (60-110), estimated glomerular filtration rate >60 mL/min/1.73m2, liver function tests within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Slow-release oxycodone 30 mg twice daily, immediate-release oxycodone 5 mg as required, macrogol daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate 24-hour subcutaneous morphine regimen to commence?

options.text: Morphine 15 mg over 24 hours, with morphine 2.5 mg subcutaneously hourly as required
Morphine 60 mg over 24 hours, with morphine 10 mg subcutaneously hourly as required
Morphine 45 mg over 24 hours, with morphine 7.5 mg subcutaneously hourly as required
Morphine 30 mg over 24 hours, with morphine 5 mg subcutaneously hourly as required
Morphine 90 mg over 24 hours, with morphine 15 mg subcutaneously hourly as required

subtopic_detail: Agitated delirium in hospital when the admission medication history is incomplete
stem:
A 79-year-old woman is on day 3 of admission after a fall that fractured her left pubic ramus. Overnight she became agitated and tremulous, has not slept for two nights, and tells the nurses there are small animals moving along the curtain rail.

She is drenched in sweat despite being afebrile. There is a fine postural tremor of both outstretched hands. Her chest is clear, her abdomen is soft, and a bladder scan shows a residual of 40 mL. She drinks one glass of wine at Christmas and her breath alcohol on admission was zero.

Her general practitioner's list, faxed this morning, includes diazepam 10 mg nightly prescribed for the past twenty years, which was not charted on admission. She is orientated to person but not to place, and her attention fluctuates through the day.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 158/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 7.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 6 mg/L (<5), sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 82 micromol/L (45-90), corrected calcium 2.36 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), urine dipstick positive for nitrites and leukocyte esterase

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral haloperidol 0.5 mg twice daily and continue it until her agitation settles
Start oral trimethoprim 300 mg at night and repeat the urine culture later
Arrange a non-contrast CT brain and an electroencephalogram before starting any treatment
Start olanzapine 2.5 mg at night and nurse her in a low-stimulus single room
Chart diazepam at her usual dose and plan a slow dose reduction after discharge

subtopic_detail: Proximal weakness with a heliotrope and knuckle rash persisting after statin withdrawal
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 56-year-old woman with 4 months of increasing difficulty rising from a low chair and hanging washing on the line. She has to push up on the arms of her chair and can no longer reach the top shelf of her cupboard.

Her general practitioner stopped her atorvastatin 8 weeks ago for presumed statin related muscle pain, with no improvement since. Over the past 6 weeks she has developed a purple discolouration of both upper eyelids and scaly red plaques over the knuckles of both hands. She has no dysphagia and no breathlessness.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical proximal weakness with power 3 out of 5 at both hip flexors and 4 out of 5 at both shoulder abductors, distal power preserved, reflexes and sensation normal, violaceous discolouration of both upper eyelids, scaly erythematous plaques over the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, no synovitis
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 2840 units/L (30 to 200), ALT 92 units/L (less than 40), ESR 44 mm/h (less than 20), TSH 1.9 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), creatinine 71 micromol/L (45 to 90), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer urgently to rheumatology and arrange malignancy screening
Recheck the creatine kinase in 8 weeks now the statin has stopped
Commence colchicine and refer to dermatology for the skin rash
Arrange nerve conduction studies and electromyography of the legs
Restart a lower dose statin and monitor the creatine kinase level

subtopic_detail: Dysphagia to solids and liquids with nocturnal regurgitation and a normal gastroscopy
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 44-year-old woman with 18 months of food sticking in her lower chest. She initially managed by drinking water with meals, but over the past few months liquids have become just as difficult as solids.

She wakes at night coughing and finds undigested food from the previous evening on her pillow. She has lost 5 kg. She was treated with a proton pump inhibitor for a year without benefit.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21 kg/m2, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, chest clear, no abdominal mass
data_table.Gastroscopy: Dilated oesophageal body containing retained food and saliva, normal mucosa with no stricture, ulcer or mass, gastro-oesophageal junction traversed with mild resistance, biopsies of the distal oesophagus showed no eosinophilic infiltrate
data_table.Barium swallow: Smooth tapering of the distal oesophagus with proximal dilatation and delayed emptying of contrast

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Commence high dose proton pump inhibitor for 8 weeks and review
Refer for laparoscopic fundoplication to control the regurgitation
Arrange computed tomography of the chest with oral contrast
Repeat gastroscopy with biopsies of the distal oesophagus
Arrange high resolution oesophageal manometry studies

subtopic_detail: Food bolus impaction in a young atopic adult with rings and furrows at endoscopy
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar who has just endoscopically relieved a food bolus impaction in a 26-year-old man who could not swallow his own saliva after eating steak. The bolus was pushed through without complication.

He tells you that solid food has caught in his chest intermittently for two years, that he always sits at the end of the table so he can drink water with every mouthful, and that he cuts meat very small. He has asthma treated with an inhaled corticosteroid and seasonal hay fever. Liquids have never been a problem.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Endoscopic findings: Concentric rings throughout the oesophageal body with linear longitudinal furrows and scattered white exudate, no stricture and no mass, normal stomach and duodenum
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count shows eosinophils 0.6 x10^9/L (less than 0.5), other indices within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform balloon dilatation of the oesophagus at the same procedure
Commence a proton pump inhibitor and arrange review in 8 weeks
Arrange a barium swallow to define the length of the narrowing
Refer for skin prick allergy testing to guide an elimination diet
Take multiple oesophageal biopsies from proximal and distal sites

subtopic_detail: Abrupt creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor in a man with widespread atherosclerosis
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 72-year-old man two weeks after starting perindopril 5 mg daily for blood pressure that had remained high on amlodipine. He feels well and has taken every dose.

He smoked 40 pack years, has calf claudication at 200 metres and had a coronary stent 3 years ago. He has twice been admitted overnight with sudden breathlessness that settled quickly with diuretic. He takes no anti-inflammatory medicines and has not been vomiting or had diarrhoea.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74 beats per minute, blood pressure 148/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure not elevated, chest clear, no peripheral oedema, mucous membranes moist, audible bruit in the left upper abdomen, absent posterior tibial pulses bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 186 micromol/L, up from 98 micromol/L six weeks ago (60 to 110), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), sodium 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), bicarbonate 22 mmol/L (22 to 32), urine dipstick trace protein and no blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue perindopril and add furosemide 40 mg daily for the oedema
Cease perindopril and recheck creatinine and potassium in one week
Refer for renal artery angioplasty and stenting within two weeks
Continue perindopril and arrange a renal tract ultrasound this week
Halve the perindopril dose and repeat the blood tests in one month

subtopic_detail: Isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation with localised bone pain and cortical thickening
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 68-year-old man with 6 months of deep aching in his right shin that is worse at night and not related to activity. He has also noticed his hats feel tighter and his hearing has declined on the right.

He takes no regular medications and has had no fractures, no weight loss and no fevers. He worked as a plumber and is otherwise well.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Anterolateral bowing of the right tibia with skin warmth over the shin, no joint effusion, no localised tenderness suggesting fracture, Weber test lateralises to the left
data_table.Investigations: Alkaline phosphatase 640 units/L (30 to 110), gamma glutamyl transferase 28 units/L (less than 50), ALT 22 units/L (less than 40), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10 to 2.55), phosphate 1.1 mmol/L (0.8 to 1.5), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (more than 50), creatinine 82 micromol/L (60 to 110)
data_table.Imaging: Tibial radiograph shows cortical thickening, coarse trabeculae and bowing, nuclear bone scan shows intense uptake in the right tibia and right hemipelvis only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Commence regular paracetamol and review the pain in three months
Commence denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every six months
Give a single intravenous infusion of zoledronic acid 5 mg
Refer for bone biopsy of the tibial lesion before any treatment
Start calcium and colecalciferol supplements and repeat the ALP

subtopic_detail: Second recurrence of toxigenic Clostridioides difficile colitis after vancomycin treatment
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 74-year-old woman with a third episode of watery diarrhoea, now eight times a day with lower abdominal cramping. The first episode followed ceftriaxone for pneumonia four months ago and was treated with oral metronidazole; the second, six weeks ago, settled on a ten day course of oral vancomycin.

Each time her symptoms returned within two weeks of finishing treatment. She has taken no antibiotics since and lives independently.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 17 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent in room air, temperature 37.3 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with mild generalised tenderness, no guarding or rigidity, bowel sounds present, no abdominal distension
data_table.Investigations: Stool toxin gene detected by nucleic acid amplification with toxin detected on enzyme immunoassay, white cell count 12.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), creatinine 88 micromol/L (45 to 90), albumin 34 g/L (35 to 50), lactate 1.2 mmol/L (less than 2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Give intravenous vancomycin 1 g twice daily for ten days
Repeat the ten day course of oral metronidazole 400 mg 8 hourly
Prescribe loperamide to control the stool frequency and review
Commence oral fidaxomicin 200 mg twice daily for ten days
Repeat stool toxin testing at the end of treatment to confirm cure

subtopic_detail: Thyrotoxicosis emerging on long term amiodarone with absent vascularity on colour flow Doppler
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 66-year-old man who has taken amiodarone 200 mg daily for 3 years to maintain sinus rhythm after atrial fibrillation ablation. Over the past 3 months he has lost 7 kg without trying, feels his heart racing, and his atrial fibrillation has returned.

He has never had thyroid disease and no one in his family has. He has not travelled and has not taken any iodine containing supplement or had contrast imaging.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 138/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent in room air, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No palpable goitre and no thyroid bruit, no proptosis, lid retraction or ophthalmoplegia, no pretibial changes, fine tremor present
data_table.Investigations: TSH less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free T4 42 pmol/L (9 to 25), free T3 9.8 pmol/L (3.0 to 5.5), TSH receptor antibody negative, C reactive protein 14 mg/L (less than 5)
data_table.Thyroid ultrasound: Normal gland volume with no nodule, colour flow Doppler shows absent intrathyroidal vascularity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 40 mg daily and monitor thyroid function
Commence carbimazole 40 mg daily and monitor thyroid function
Refer for radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid gland now
Cease amiodarone alone and recheck thyroid function in 6 weeks
Refer for urgent total thyroidectomy under cardiac anaesthesia

subtopic_detail: Acute flaccid paralysis with profound hypokalaemia after a carbohydrate load in an untreated thyrotoxic man
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 28-year-old man who woke at 5 am unable to lift his legs off the bed and only just able to raise his arms. Power has been returning slowly over the past hour.

Last night he trained heavily at the gym and then ate a large rice and noodle meal. He had a milder episode three months ago that resolved by itself before he reached a doctor. He takes no medications, no supplements and no diuretics, and has had no vomiting or diarrhoea. He has lost 5 kg over 6 months and feels hot at night.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 142/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical proximal weakness, power 2 out of 5 in the legs and 4 out of 5 in the arms, reflexes depressed, sensation intact throughout, no goitre palpable, no eye signs, fine tremor present
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 2.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), magnesium 0.85 mmol/L (0.7 to 1.1), phosphate 0.62 mmol/L (0.8 to 1.5), bicarbonate 24 mmol/L (22 to 32), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60 to 110), TSH less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free T4 38 pmol/L (9 to 25)
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus tachycardia with prominent U waves and a prolonged QU interval, no arrhythmia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give 60 mmol of oral potassium chloride immediately and repeat
Give intravenous magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes
Commence carbimazole alone and await the potassium to correct
Give cautious potassium replacement with propranolol and monitor
Arrange urgent nerve conduction studies before any replacement

subtopic_detail: Young adult with hepatitis, new tremor and behavioural change with a disproportionately low alkaline phosphatase
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 24-year-old man referred with 4 months of jaundice and abnormal liver tests. He drinks no alcohol, takes no supplements or herbal preparations, and has had no blood transfusions or tattoos.

His partner adds that for about 6 months his handwriting has become cramped and untidy, he has developed a tremor when holding a cup, and he has been uncharacteristically irritable and impulsive, losing a job he had held for 3 years.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Scleral icterus, liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, spleen tip palpable, coarse postural and action tremor of both hands, mild dysarthria, no asterixis, no confusion
data_table.Investigations: ALT 180 units/L (less than 40), AST 210 units/L (less than 40), bilirubin 48 micromol/L (less than 20), alkaline phosphatase 42 units/L (30 to 110), INR 1.3, haemoglobin 104 g/L (130 to 180) with reticulocytosis, viral hepatitis serology negative, autoimmune and coeliac screens negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Measure ferritin and transferrin saturation with HFE genotyping
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with gadolinium
Refer for percutaneous liver biopsy as the initial investigation
Measure alpha 1 antitrypsin level and phenotype the patient
Measure serum caeruloplasmin and arrange slit lamp examination

subtopic_detail: Visible haematuria beginning within a day of a sore throat with normal complement levels
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 23-year-old man whose urine turned the colour of cola yesterday. His sore throat began the day before that, and the urine change followed within 24 hours of the first symptom.

He had an identical episode a year ago during a chest infection, which cleared after three days and was not investigated. He has no flank pain, no dysuria, no fevers and no rash, has never smoked and takes no medications.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pharyngeal erythema with no exudate, no peripheral oedema, no rash or purpura, no joint swelling, abdominal examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick blood 3 plus and protein 1 plus, urine microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells with red cell casts, urine albumin creatinine ratio 68 mg/mmol (less than 3.5), creatinine 92 micromol/L (60 to 110), C3 and C4 within normal limits, antistreptolysin O titre not raised, antinuclear antibody and ANCA negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to nephrology for consideration of a renal biopsy
Treat with phenoxymethylpenicillin for streptococcal pharyngitis
Repeat the urine dipstick in three months and act on that
Arrange a computed tomography urogram to find a bleeding source
Refer for flexible cystoscopy to exclude a bladder lesion

subtopic_detail: Recurrent peptic ulceration with hypercalcaemia and amenorrhoea pointing to a familial endocrine syndrome
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 38-year-old woman with a fourth episode of epigastric pain and a duodenal ulcer found at gastroscopy. Helicobacter pylori was eradicated two years ago with confirmed clearance, and she takes a proton pump inhibitor daily and no anti-inflammatory medicines.

Separately she has not had a period for 2 years and reports occasional milky discharge from both breasts. Her father had kidney stones in his thirties and died at 54 from what the family were told was a tumour in his pancreas.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Epigastric tenderness, expressible bilateral milky nipple discharge, visual fields full to confrontation, no neck mass palpable
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.82 mmol/L (2.10 to 2.55), phosphate 0.68 mmol/L (0.8 to 1.5), parathyroid hormone 9.8 pmol/L (1.6 to 6.9), creatinine 76 micromol/L (45 to 90), prolactin 3960 mIU/L (less than 500), TSH 1.7 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), beta hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for parathyroidectomy and defer further investigation for now
Repeat Helicobacter pylori testing and re-treat if it is positive
Refer for germline genetic testing and first degree family screening
Commence cabergoline and review the serum calcium in six months
Arrange gallium labelled somatostatin receptor imaging of the abdomen

subtopic_detail: Resuscitation strategy in septic shock complicated by severe fixed left ventricular outflow obstruction
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar managing a 76-year-old man brought in with rigors and confusion. He has severe aortic stenosis and is on the waiting list for transcatheter valve implantation, with a recent echocardiogram showing a valve area of 0.8 cm2, a mean gradient of 48 mmHg and preserved ejection fraction.

He has had 500 mL of compound sodium lactate and his first dose of intravenous antibiotics. Urine cultures have been sent and the source appears urinary. Your resident has drawn up a further 2 litres to complete a 30 mL per kilogram bolus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute in sinus rhythm, blood pressure 82/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 percent on 4 litres per minute, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Warm peripheries with capillary refill 3 seconds, jugular venous pressure 3 cm above the sternal angle, ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, bibasal crackles to the mid zones, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 mmol/L (less than 2.0), creatinine 148 micromol/L from a baseline of 92 (60 to 110), haemoglobin 118 g/L (130 to 180), white cell count 19.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0)
data_table.Bedside echocardiogram: Hyperdynamic hypertrophied left ventricle with a small end diastolic cavity, heavily calcified aortic valve, no regional wall motion abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to his haemodynamic resuscitation?

options.text: Complete a 30 mL per kilogram crystalloid bolus over the next hour
Give 250 mL boluses with reassessment and start early noradrenaline
Start a dobutamine infusion to augment the cardiac output now
Give metoprolol 2.5 mg intravenously to slow the ventricular rate
Restrict fluids entirely and start an intravenous furosemide infusion

subtopic_detail: Brief positional spinning with torsional upbeating nystagmus provoked by a positioning manoeuvre
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old woman who has had episodes of the room spinning for the past week. Each episode comes on when she rolls onto her right side in bed or tips her head back to hang out washing, builds over a few seconds and settles within half a minute if she stays still.

She feels unsteady and nauseated for a while afterwards but is completely well between episodes. She has no hearing loss, no ringing in the ears and no feeling of fullness in either ear, and no headache. She has had no double vision, slurred speech, weakness or numbness.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 per minute, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg lying with no postural drop, respiratory rate 15 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right Dix Hallpike manoeuvre provokes upbeating torsional nystagmus after a latency of about five seconds that fatigues within thirty seconds and reproduces her vertigo, left Dix Hallpike negative, no spontaneous nystagmus on sitting, cranial nerves intact, gait and limb coordination within normal limits, whispered voice test normal in both ears
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe regular prochlorperazine to be taken for the next two weeks
Commence betahistine at a standard dose and review her symptoms in a month
Request magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with attention to the posterior fossa
Perform a canalith repositioning manoeuvre at this consultation and reassess
Refer for a course of vestibular rehabilitation exercises with a physiotherapist

subtopic_detail: Paroxysmal electric shock facial pain triggered by light touch with an entirely normal neurological examination
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 62-year-old man who describes sudden bursts of pain in his right cheek and along his upper jaw that he likens to an electric shock. Each burst lasts a second or two, comes in runs of several minutes, and happens twenty or thirty times a day.

It is set off by shaving, by cold wind on his face and by brushing his teeth, and he has stopped shaving that side and eats only on the left. He has no pain between the attacks, no facial numbness, no ear or eye symptoms and no headache. He saw his dentist last month, who found no dental cause and took radiographs that were normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Light touch and pinprick sensation equal over all three trigeminal divisions bilaterally, corneal reflex present and symmetrical, masseter and temporalis bulk and power within normal limits, facial movement symmetrical, hearing normal, no cerebellar signs
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea creatinine and electrolytes, liver function and inflammatory markers all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Commence amitriptyline at night and increase the dose slowly over four weeks
Commence carbamazepine and check the sodium and liver function before starting
Commence gabapentin and titrate the dose upwards over the next three weeks
Commence modified release oxycodone regularly and review the dose in two weeks
Refer to a neurosurgeon for microvascular decompression of the affected nerve

subtopic_detail: Proximal muscle aching weeks after starting high intensity statin therapy with a mildly raised creatine kinase
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 64-year-old man who had a myocardial infarction and a drug eluting stent placed three months ago and was discharged on atorvastatin, aspirin, ticagrelor, metoprolol and perindopril.

For the past six weeks he has had a dull ache across both thighs and shoulders that is worse after walking the dog and eases with rest. He has no dark urine, no muscle tenderness and no difficulty rising from a chair. He has started no new medication, takes no supplements, and does not drink grapefruit juice. He tells you he has read that statins ruin muscles and wants to stop the tablet permanently.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 62 per minute, blood pressure 124/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No proximal weakness on formal testing, no muscle tenderness or swelling, no rash, reflexes symmetrical, able to rise from a chair without using his arms
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 320 U/L (less than 200), urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, vitamin D within normal limits, low density lipoprotein cholesterol 1.4 mmol/L (target less than 1.8 after an event)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop the atorvastatin permanently and commence ezetimibe as a replacement
Continue the atorvastatin unchanged and reassure him that the ache is unrelated
Add coenzyme Q10 supplementation and continue the current statin dose unchanged
Request antibodies to hydroxymethylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase before deciding
Withhold the statin briefly and rechallenge at a lower dose or with another agent

subtopic_detail: Girdle pain with prolonged morning stiffness and a high inflammatory response without weakness or cranial symptoms
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 71-year-old woman with six weeks of pain across both shoulders and both hips that came on over a few days. She says she cannot lift her arms to wash her hair and has to roll out of bed sideways, and that it takes well over an hour each morning before she can move freely.

She has had no jaw ache when chewing, no scalp tenderness when brushing her hair, and no visual disturbance of any kind. She has lost two kilograms and feels generally unwell but has had no fevers, night sweats or cough. She takes no statin and no new medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 per minute, blood pressure 136/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Painful restriction of active shoulder abduction bilaterally with full passive range, no synovitis of the small joints, power 5 out of 5 in all limbs on formal testing, temporal arteries non-tender with normal pulsation, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 68 mm/h (less than 30), C reactive protein 54 mg/L (less than 5), creatine kinase within normal limits, full blood count shows a normocytic anaemia with haemoglobin 112 g/L (115-155), rheumatoid factor and anti cyclic citrullinated peptide negative, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Commence prednisolone 15 mg daily and review the response within one week
Commence prednisolone 60 mg daily and arrange urgent temporal artery biopsy
Commence ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily and review again in four weeks
Commence methotrexate 10 mg weekly with folic acid on the following day
Commence paracetamol 1 g four times daily and refer her to a physiotherapist

subtopic_detail: Periprocedural planning before iodinated contrast in a diabetic patient with moderately reduced kidney function
stem:
You are the medical registrar asked to advise before a 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes attends for a computed tomography coronary angiogram with iodinated contrast next week.

He takes metformin, perindopril and rosuvastatin, and has stable exertional chest tightness under investigation. He is eating and drinking normally, has had no vomiting or diarrhoea, and is on no diuretic or non-steroidal anti inflammatory drug. He has had contrast for a computed tomography scan two years ago without any problem.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70 per minute, blood pressure 134/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no peripheral oedema, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-110) with estimated glomerular filtration rate 38 mL/min/1.73m2 stable across three measurements over a year, potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), bicarbonate 24 mmol/L (22-28), haemoglobin A1c 52 mmol/mol, urine albumin creatinine ratio 18 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate periprocedural plan?

options.text: Withhold the metformin for 48 hours before and 48 hours after the contrast study
Give oral N acetylcysteine on the day before and the day of the contrast study
Give intravenous isotonic saline around the study and continue the metformin
Give an infusion of isotonic sodium bicarbonate instead of saline before the study
Cancel the contrast study and request a stress echocardiogram in its place

subtopic_detail: Request to discontinue a six monthly antiresorptive injection after several years of improving bone density
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 73-year-old woman who has had six monthly denosumab injections for four years after a wrist fracture. Her most recent bone density scan shows the T score at the lumbar spine has improved from minus 3.1 to minus 2.2.

She has had no further fractures, takes calcium in her diet and a daily vitamin D supplement, and walks daily. She tells you she feels the problem is now fixed, dislikes injections, and has decided not to have the next one, which is due in three weeks. She takes no corticosteroid and has had no dental problems.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Height unchanged from two years ago, no thoracic kyphosis, no spinal tenderness, gait steady with no falls in the past year
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.20-2.65), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (greater than 50), creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate within normal limits, bone density T score minus 2.2 at the lumbar spine and minus 2.4 at the femoral neck

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Agree to stop the injections now and repeat her bone density scan in two years
Explain that stopping requires transition to a bisphosphonate to prevent bone loss
Extend the interval between injections to twelve months as a compromise measure
Stop the injections and continue calcium and vitamin D as her only treatment
Continue the injections indefinitely without any planned review of treatment

subtopic_detail: Prolonged fever with hepatitis and negative blood cultures in an abattoir worker with no travel history
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 38-year-old man from a regional New South Wales town with twelve days of daily fevers to 39 degrees Celsius, drenching night sweats, severe frontal headache and aching in his thighs and back.

He works on the slaughter floor of an abattoir processing sheep and cattle and has done so for six years. He has not travelled outside Australia, has no recent tick bite and has seen no rash. He has had no cough, no breathlessness, no diarrhoea and no dysuria. His general practitioner gave him amoxicillin a week ago with no effect.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Unwell and sweaty, no rash and no eschar, no lymphadenopathy, liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin and mildly tender, no splenomegaly, no murmur, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), platelets 128 x10^9/L (150-400), alanine aminotransferase 186 U/L (less than 40), alkaline phosphatase 148 U/L (30-110), bilirubin within normal limits, C reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5), two sets of blood cultures sterile at 72 hours, malaria thick and thin films negative, chest radiograph normal, transthoracic echocardiogram shows no vegetation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence intravenous ceftriaxone and repeat the blood cultures before dosing
Commence oral azithromycin to cover atypical community-acquired pneumonia
Arrange percutaneous liver biopsy to establish the cause of the hepatitis
Withhold antimicrobial treatment until the serological results become available
Commence oral doxycycline and request acute and convalescent phase serology

subtopic_detail: Progressive thoracic back pain with a sensory level and upper motor neurone signs in metastatic prostate cancer
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 68-year-old man with prostate cancer on androgen deprivation therapy who has had three weeks of mid back pain. The pain is worse at night, wakes him, and is aggravated by coughing and by lying flat.

Over the past four days his legs have felt heavy and he has begun holding the rail to climb the stairs at home. He is passing urine normally with no hesitancy or incontinence and has had no constipation. His last prostate specific antigen three months ago was rising.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 per minute, blood pressure 132/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tenderness on percussion over the mid thoracic spine, power 4 out of 5 in hip flexion and knee extension bilaterally, knee and ankle reflexes brisk with bilateral extensor plantar responses, sensory level to pinprick at the level of the umbilicus, normal anal tone, bladder not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.44 mmol/L (2.20-2.65), full blood count and renal function within normal limits, alkaline phosphatase 310 U/L (30-110), post-void bladder scan shows 40 mL residual

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give high dose dexamethasone now and arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine within the next 24 hours
Request plain radiographs of the thoracic spine and a whole body bone scan
Refer for urgent radiotherapy to the painful vertebral level before any imaging
Prescribe opioid analgesia and arrange outpatient imaging within the coming week

subtopic_detail: Severe cavitating pneumonia in a poorly controlled diabetic during the tropical wet season after soil exposure
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a Darwin hospital admitting a 52-year-old man in February with five days of fever, productive cough and pleuritic chest pain that have worsened rapidly over the past day.

He has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin and gliclazide and last had his glycated haemoglobin measured a year ago. He operates earthmoving machinery and has been clearing flooded ground for the past fortnight, and he has several healing abrasions on both shins from working in the mud. He has had no overseas travel and is not immunosuppressed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 126 per minute, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 per minute, SpO2 89 per cent on 6 L per minute via face mask, temperature 39.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Confused and peripherally shut down, bronchial breathing at the right upper zone, several healing abrasions on both shins with no surrounding cellulitis, no murmur, no rash
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110), lactate 3.6 mmol/L (less than 2.0), glucose 18.2 mmol/L, glycated haemoglobin 84 mmol/mol, chest radiograph shows dense right upper lobe consolidation with an early cavity, blood cultures taken and pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin with intravenous doxycycline
Intravenous ceftriaxone with intravenous azithromycin
Intravenous flucloxacillin with intravenous vancomycin
Intravenous meropenem with trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole
Intravenous ticarcillin with clavulanate and gentamicin

subtopic_detail: Core temperature in the twenties with bradycardia and a J wave on the electrocardiogram after a night outdoors
stem:
You are the emergency registrar receiving a 74-year-old man found at dawn on a park bench after an overnight minimum of 2 degrees Celsius. He had left his nursing home the previous afternoon and had been missing for about sixteen hours.

He is drowsy and confused but opens his eyes to voice and moves all four limbs. He is no longer shivering. His clothing is damp and has been removed and he has been covered with blankets.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 38 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 8 per minute, SpO2 unable to be recorded reliably due to poor peripheral perfusion, oesophageal temperature 28.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 12, cold and pale peripheries with no shivering, muscle tone increased, pupils sluggish and equal, no head injury, no focal neurology, no signs of frostbite
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia at 38 per minute with a positive deflection at the junction of the QRS complex and the ST segment in the lateral leads, potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), glucose 6.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), venous pH 7.28, thyroid function pending, alcohol not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give atropine intravenously to correct the bradycardia and repeat if needed
Apply transcutaneous pacing to raise the heart rate towards a normal range
Begin active external rewarming with warmed intravenous fluid and minimal handling
Insert a central venous catheter via the subclavian route for warmed fluid delivery
Immerse him in a hot water bath to raise the core temperature as quickly as possible

subtopic_detail: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia after parathyroidectomy with a low phosphate and a high alkaline phosphatase
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the surgical ward two days after a 62-year-old woman underwent parathyroidectomy for primary hyperparathyroidism. She complains of tingling around her mouth and in her fingertips and says her hands keep cramping.

Before surgery she had bone pain, a corrected calcium of 3.12 mmol/L and a markedly elevated parathyroid hormone, and imaging had shown a single enlarged gland. She takes no other medication and has had no wound problems, no fever and no voice change.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 per minute, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Trousseau sign positive after one minute of cuff inflation, Chvostek sign present, no stridor, no wound haematoma, no carpopedal spasm at rest
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 1.68 mmol/L (2.20-2.65), phosphate 0.54 mmol/L (0.80-1.50), magnesium 0.58 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), alkaline phosphatase 620 U/L (30-110), parathyroid hormone 2.4 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 46 nmol/L, electrocardiogram shows a corrected QT interval of 490 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral calcium carbonate alone and recheck the calcium in the morning
Return her to theatre for exploration of the remaining parathyroid glands
Commence teriparatide by daily subcutaneous injection to replace the missing hormone
Treat as surgical hypoparathyroidism with calcium and calcitriol and monitor daily
Give intravenous calcium gluconate with calcitriol and replace the magnesium

subtopic_detail: Visual blurring and mucosal bleeding with dilated segmented retinal veins and a very high immunoglobulin M paraprotein
stem:
You are the haematology registrar seeing a 71-year-old man referred with six weeks of headache, blurred vision and ringing in his ears, along with nosebleeds and gums that bleed when he cleans his teeth. He has lost four kilograms and is breathless climbing a flight of stairs.

The referring doctor has arranged two units of red cells to be transfused this afternoon for the anaemia and has asked you to review him afterwards. He has no chest pain, no melaena and no haematuria, and takes no anticoagulant or antiplatelet drug.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 per minute, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale, with non-tender lymphadenopathy in both axillae and a spleen palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, fundoscopy shows dilated tortuous retinal veins with segmental constrictions and scattered flame haemorrhages, no focal neurology, chest clear with no added heart sounds
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 72 g/L (130-180), white cell count 6.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400), blood film shows marked rouleaux, erythrocyte sedimentation rate greater than 140 mm/h, total protein 112 g/L (60-80) with albumin 32 g/L (35-50), serum immunoglobulin M paraprotein 58 g/L, creatinine and corrected calcium within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent plasma exchange and defer the planned red cell transfusion
Proceed with the two units of red cells and reassess the symptoms afterwards
Commence rituximab today as definitive treatment of the underlying disease
Commence high dose dexamethasone alone and arrange a bone marrow biopsy tomorrow
Perform therapeutic venesection to lower the viscosity before any other treatment

subtopic_detail: Persistent fever and a unilateral effusion during treated pneumonia whose aspirate shows a low pH and low glucose without frank pus
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 61-year-old man on day four of intravenous benzylpenicillin for a community-acquired pneumonia. He was improving until yesterday and now has recurrent fevers, worsening right sided pleuritic pain and increasing breathlessness.

He has no chest wall injury and no history of malignancy, and his renal function has remained normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 92 percent on 2 L/min nasal prongs, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Stony dull percussion note over the right base with absent breath sounds to the mid zone, reduced expansion on the right, no tracheal deviation, no clubbing, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 268 mg/L (less than 5), chest radiograph shows a moderate right pleural effusion with a meniscus, bedside ultrasound shows a septated effusion of approximately 700 mL, diagnostic aspirate is turbid straw coloured fluid with pH 7.08, glucose 1.6 mmol/L, lactate dehydrogenase 1840 U/L and Gram stain showing no organisms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the current antibiotic and repeat the chest radiograph in 48 hours
Perform a therapeutic aspiration of 1.5 litres and reassess him afterwards
Add an antifungal agent and send the fluid for fungal culture and cytology
Refer directly for video assisted thoracoscopic decortication of the pleural space
Insert an intercostal catheter for drainage and broaden the antibiotic cover

subtopic_detail: Young adult with years of night time back pain easing with movement, restricted lumbar flexion and sacroiliac inflammation on imaging
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 27-year-old plasterer with four years of low back pain that wakes him in the second half of the night and forces him out of bed to move about. He is stiff for well over an hour each morning, the pain eases as he works through the day, and rest over a long weekend makes it worse rather than better.

He had a painful red eye eighteen months ago that an optometrist referred urgently and which settled with drops. There is no history of trauma, no leg pain, no weakness and no bladder or bowel disturbance, and he has lost no weight.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Reduced lumbar flexion with a modified Schober measurement of 3.5 cm, tenderness over both sacroiliac joints, chest expansion 4 cm, no peripheral joint swelling, no dactylitis, no psoriatic skin or nail changes, straight leg raise negative bilaterally, normal lower limb power reflexes and sensation
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 28 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 34 mm/h (less than 20), rheumatoid factor and cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody negative, full blood count normal, plain radiograph of the pelvis shows no definite erosive change, magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints shows bilateral subchondral bone marrow oedema

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Oral prednisolone at a moderate dose with a taper over three months
Oral methotrexate weekly with folic acid and monitoring of blood counts
Regular non-steroidal treatment with a structured exercise program
Simple analgesia with advice to stay active and review in three months
Test for the HLA B27 antigen and base the treatment decision on it

subtopic_detail: Acute hot swollen knee in an older inpatient with linear cartilage calcification and positively birefringent rhomboid crystals
stem:
You are the medical registrar asked to review an 81-year-old woman on day three after a hemiarthroplasty for a fractured neck of femur. Overnight her right knee, which was not operated on, became hot swollen and too painful to move.

She has chronic kidney disease with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 32 mL/min/1.73m2 and takes an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor. Her surgical wound is clean and dry with no surrounding erythema.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 37.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right knee warm with a tense effusion, exquisitely tender, held at 20 degrees of flexion with any movement resisted, overlying skin red without a defined border, no lymphangitis, no tophi, no other joint involved, operative wound clean and dry
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 142 mg/L (less than 5), serum urate 0.29 mmol/L (0.15 to 0.45), knee radiograph shows linear calcification of the meniscal cartilage, joint aspirate yields cloudy fluid with a white cell count of 32 x10^9/L predominantly neutrophils, Gram stain no organisms seen, polarised microscopy shows rhomboid positively birefringent crystals, cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Commence a non-steroidal anti inflammatory drug with a proton pump inhibitor
Inject the joint with a corticosteroid once culture results exclude infection
Commence allopurinol at a low dose and titrate against the serum urate
Commence colchicine at standard dosing until the symptoms have fully resolved
Commence intravenous flucloxacillin and arrange urgent surgical joint washout

subtopic_detail: Older adult with a magnetic shuffling gait, urinary urgency and slowed thinking with enlarged ventricles disproportionate to cortical atrophy
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 76-year-old man brought by his wife over twelve months of change. She says he walks as though his feet are stuck to the floor, takes small steps and struggles to turn, needing several shuffles to come about.

He has started wetting himself on the way to the toilet, which distresses him, and she says he is slower to answer questions and has lost interest in his woodwork, although he still knows the family, remembers recent conversations when given time, and finds his way around town. He takes no antipsychotic or antiemetic medication and has had no head injury, meningitis or subarachnoid haemorrhage.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits with no postural drop
data_table.Examination: Broad based short stepped gait with reduced foot clearance and a multistep turn, arm swing preserved, no resting tremor, no cogwheel rigidity, no cerebellar signs, Romberg negative, power and reflexes normal with downgoing plantars, Montreal Cognitive Assessment 23 out of 30 with losses in attention and executive domains, no visual hallucinations
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid stimulating hormone, vitamin B12 and syphilis serology all within normal limits, computed tomography of the brain shows ventriculomegaly with an Evans index of 0.37 and narrowed sulci at the vertex, with only mild cortical atrophy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start levodopa and assess the gait response after six weeks of treatment
Start a cholinesterase inhibitor and arrange review of cognition in three months
Arrange urodynamic assessment of his bladder and treat the incontinence first
Refer to neurosurgery for assessment including a high volume lumbar drainage test
Refer to a falls and balance service for gait retraining and home modification

subtopic_detail: Middle aged man with fatigue, joint pain and a raised transferrin saturation with a high ferritin and minimal alcohol intake
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 48-year-old man who has come in with eighteen months of fatigue and aching in both second and third knuckles that makes gripping his tools uncomfortable. His skin has gradually darkened over the same period although he works indoors.

He drinks four standard drinks a week, takes no supplements and no regular medication, and has never had a blood transfusion. His older brother has been told he has a liver problem but has not been investigated.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26 kg/m2, generalised slate grey skin pigmentation, tenderness and bony swelling at the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints of both hands, liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin and smooth, no splenomegaly, no ascites, no spider naevi, testicular volume normal
data_table.Investigations: Fasting transferrin saturation 68 percent (15 to 45), ferritin 1180 micrograms/L (30 to 300), alanine aminotransferase 78 U/L (less than 45), bilirubin within normal limits, international normalised ratio 1.0 (0.8 to 1.2), albumin 40 g/L (35 to 50), full blood count normal, glucose 6.1 mmol/L (3.0 to 5.4), hepatitis B and C serology negative, autoimmune liver screen negative, hand radiographs show hook shaped osteophytes at the second and third metacarpal heads

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence therapeutic venesection weekly and monitor the ferritin response
Commence an oral iron chelating agent and refer to a haematologist for review
Request HFE genotyping and arrange assessment of hepatic fibrosis
Attribute the ferritin rise to inflammation and repeat the iron studies in six months
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the liver to quantify hepatic iron content

subtopic_detail: Commercial heavy vehicle driver with witnessed apnoeas, marked daytime sleepiness and a near miss at the wheel
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 52-year-old man who drives interstate freight and has come for his commercial driving medical. When you ask about sleep he tells you his wife has moved to the spare room because of the snoring, and that she has watched him stop breathing and then gasp.

He admits he nodded off at a set of lights three weeks ago and was woken by the horn behind him, and that he pulls over most trips because he cannot keep his eyes open. He has hypertension treated with two agents and has gained 12 kg in four years.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 37 kg/m2, neck circumference 45 cm, crowded oropharynx with a Mallampati score of 4, nasal airway patent, chest clear, no peripheral oedema, no elevation of the jugular venous pressure
data_table.Investigations: Epworth Sleepiness Scale 18, full blood count normal, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), glycated haemoglobin 6.2 percent (less than 6.0), electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a weight loss program and reassess his symptoms in three months
Trial an oral mandibular advancement device and review after it is fitted
Certify him fit to drive and arrange a sleep study within the next few months
Start continuous positive airway pressure empirically and certify him once settled
Refer urgently for a diagnostic sleep study and advise him not to drive meanwhile

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulated patient with a falling haemoglobin and a markedly prolonged international normalised ratio after a minor fall
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 74-year-old woman brought in after slipping on a wet floor three hours ago and striking her right flank. She now has severe right sided abdominal and back pain and feels faint on sitting up.

She takes warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve replacement performed nine years ago, and finished a course of trimethoprim for a urinary infection two days ago. She has had no vomiting or melaena.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale and clammy, tender fullness in the right flank with guarding, bruising over the right loin, abdomen otherwise soft, no external bleeding, no focal neurological deficit, Glasgow Coma Scale 15
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 78 g/L (115 to 155), falling from 124 g/L three months ago, platelets 212 x10^9/L (150 to 400), international normalised ratio 7.4 (target 2.5 to 3.5), activated partial thromboplastin time prolonged, creatinine 96 micromol/L (45 to 90), computed tomography shows a large right retroperitoneal haematoma with active contrast extravasation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous vitamin K with prothrombin complex concentrate and resuscitate
Give fresh frozen plasma with intravenous vitamin K and resuscitate with blood
Give intravenous vitamin K alone and recheck the coagulation profile in six hours
Give a specific reversal antibody and arrange interventional radiology assessment
Withhold warfarin, transfuse red cells, and observe her in a monitored bed

subtopic_detail: Young adult with positional chest pain after a viral illness whose electrocardiogram shows widespread ST elevation with PR depression and a normal troponin
stem:
You are the emergency department resident seeing a 29-year-old man with two days of central chest pain that is sharp, worse when he lies flat and when he takes a deep breath, and relieved by sitting forward. He had a sore throat and coryza a fortnight ago.

He has no cardiac history, does not smoke, has no family history of premature coronary disease, and takes no medication or supplements. He has had no fever, no leg swelling and no recent travel or immobility.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg with no pulsus paradoxus, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: A scratchy triphasic sound heard at the left sternal edge in expiration with the patient leaning forward, heart sounds otherwise dual with no murmur, jugular venous pressure not elevated, chest clear, calves soft and non-tender, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram shows widespread concave upward ST elevation in leads I, II, aVL, aVF and V2 to V6 with PR segment depression, PR elevation in aVR and no reciprocal ST depression, high sensitivity troponin 8 ng/L (less than 14) on presentation and 9 ng/L at three hours, C reactive protein 42 mg/L (less than 5), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits, chest radiograph normal, echocardiogram shows normal biventricular function with a trivial pericardial effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Activate the catheter laboratory for immediate coronary angiography and intervention
Commence therapeutic anticoagulation and arrange computed tomography pulmonary angiography
Commence oral prednisolone with a taper and review him in the cardiology clinic
Commence high dose anti inflammatory treatment with colchicine and restrict exercise
Arrange urgent pericardiocentesis and admit him to the coronary care unit

subtopic_detail: Smoker with proximal leg weakness that improves briefly after sustained effort, absent reflexes returning after exercise, and dry mouth
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 63-year-old man with four months of difficulty climbing the stairs at home and getting out of a low chair. He has smoked 30 cigarettes a day since he was 18.

He says his legs feel strongest a few minutes after he has been walking about and worst first thing, that his mouth is constantly dry, and that he has become constipated. He denies double vision, drooping eyelids, difficulty swallowing and slurred speech, and there is no bulbar fatigue on prolonged talking during the consultation. He has lost 3 kg without trying.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits with no postural drop
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical proximal weakness of hip flexion and knee extension graded 4 out of 5, waddling gait, knee reflexes absent at rest but obtainable after ten seconds of sustained quadriceps contraction, no ptosis, full eye movements with no fatigable diplopia, no facial or bulbar weakness, sensation intact throughout, no fasciculations, dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 142 U/L (less than 200), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 22 mm/h (less than 20), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.2 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), electrolytes calcium and vitamin D within normal limits, acetylcholine receptor antibody negative, nerve conduction studies show a low compound muscle action potential amplitude at rest that more than doubles after brief maximal exercise

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence prednisolone for an inflammatory myopathy and monitor the creatine kinase
Arrange computed tomography of the chest to look for an underlying malignancy
Commence pyridostigmine and assess the symptomatic response over two weeks
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine to assess for radiculopathy
Refer for muscle biopsy of the quadriceps to establish a histological diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Frail older patient with recurrent falls on rising, a substantial postural blood pressure drop and several agents contributing to it
stem: An 84-year-old man has fallen three times in two months, each within a minute of standing, with the room greying out and no loss of awareness. He takes perindopril, amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide and prazosin.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/78 mmHg lying, 94/54 at three minutes standing with symptoms; pulse 74 to 78
data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic, no focal deficit, no parkinsonism
data_table.Investigations: Holter shows no pause or arrhythmia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add fludrocortisone daily and review the postural drop
Refer for cardiology assessment and permanent pacemaker insertion
Computed tomography of the brain and carotid duplex ultrasound
Advise compression stockings with increased salt and fluid
Cease the alpha blocker and the thiazide, then repeat the reading

subtopic_detail: Painful spreading rash with erosions at two mucosal sites and epidermal shearing three weeks after starting a new medication
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 58-year-old man with a rash that began on his trunk two days ago and has spread to his limbs. He says his skin feels as though it has been scalded and is more painful than it looks, and that his eyes are gritty and his mouth is too sore to eat.

He started allopurinol three weeks ago after a second attack of gout. He has chronic kidney disease with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 38 mL/min/1.73m2 and takes no other new medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dusky macules with central blistering over the trunk and proximal limbs affecting an estimated 7 percent of body surface area, lateral pressure on adjacent normal looking skin produces epidermal shearing, haemorrhagic crusting of the lips with buccal erosions, bilateral conjunctival injection with erosions, no genital involvement, no facial oedema, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) with no eosinophilia, alanine aminotransferase 48 U/L (less than 45), creatinine 168 micromol/L (60 to 110), sodium 133 mmol/L (135 to 145), C reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5), blood cultures taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue the allopurinol and add an oral antihistamine with topical emollient
Commence intravenous flucloxacillin for a presumed staphylococcal skin infection
Stop the allopurinol and arrange urgent transfer to a burns or specialist unit
Stop the allopurinol and commence high dose oral corticosteroid on the ward
Stop the allopurinol and arrange dermatology review in the outpatient clinic

subtopic_detail: Patient with advanced cancer and declining renal function who develops twitching and drowsiness while pain control on a strong opioid is deteriorating
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 67-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer whose abdominal pain has been controlled on regular oral morphine for six weeks. Over the past four days her family report she has become drowsy, jumps and twitches when resting, and yet says her pain is worse than before.

She has vomited intermittently for a week and her oral intake has fallen. She is not confused about where she is, has no neck stiffness and no headache, and is not taking any new medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable and oriented, frequent multifocal myoclonic jerks of the limbs at rest, pupils 2 mm and reactive, mucous membranes dry with reduced skin turgor, abdomen soft with hepatomegaly, no focal neurological deficit, no hyperreflexia and no clonus, no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 218 micromol/L (45 to 90) rising from 92 three weeks ago, estimated glomerular filtration rate 21 mL/min/1.73m2 (greater than 60), urea 18 mmol/L (3.0 to 8.0), corrected calcium 2.44 mmol/L (2.20 to 2.60), sodium 134 mmol/L (135 to 145), glucose 6.2 mmol/L (3.0 to 5.4), liver function stable from previous results

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Rotate to an alternative opioid at a reduced equianalgesic dose with rehydration
Increase the morphine dose because her reported pain has become worse
Give naloxone to reverse the opioid effect and reassess her conscious state
Commence intravenous bisphosphonate treatment for hypercalcaemia of malignancy
Add regular levetiracetam to suppress the myoclonic jerks and continue the morphine

subtopic_detail: Screening for a mineralocorticoid excess state in resistant hypertension with hypokalaemia while the patient is already taking a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 46-year-old woman whose blood pressure remains 168/104 mmHg despite perindopril 10 mg, amlodipine 10 mg and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, all of which she takes reliably according to her dispensing record.

Her potassium has been between 3.0 and 3.3 mmol/L on three occasions over the past year, and a colleague added spironolactone 25 mg daily six weeks ago. She has no episodic sweating, palpitations or pallor. She drinks no liquorice tea and takes no over the counter preparations. Her renal function is normal and there is no bruit over either renal artery. She has never smoked and has no family history of early vascular disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 168/104 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg per square metre, no abdominal or flank bruit, no Cushingoid features, no radiofemoral delay, fundi with grade 1 hypertensive changes
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 143 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 72 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate above 90 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, bicarbonate 30 mmol/L (22-32), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.4 milliunits per litre (0.4-4.0), urine albumin to creatinine ratio 4.2 mg per mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her assessment?

options.text: Measure the aldosterone to renin ratio on a morning sample later this week
Request computed tomography of the adrenal glands before any blood testing
Request a renal artery duplex ultrasound to assess for arterial narrowing
Substitute verapamil for spironolactone and measure the ratio six weeks later
Measure plasma free metanephrines on a sample taken after 30 minutes supine

subtopic_detail: Negative urea breath test performed while the patient was still taking a daily proton pump inhibitor for upper abdominal burning
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old man with eight months of burning upper abdominal discomfort that is worse when his stomach is empty and eases after meals. He has no dysphagia, no vomiting, no weight loss and no anaemia, and there is no family history of gastric cancer.

He bought esomeprazole over the counter and has taken 20 mg every morning for the past three months, which helps while he takes it and returns within a week of stopping. You referred him for a urea breath test, which he had four days ago while still taking the tablet, and the result has come back negative. He takes no nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and no aspirin, and he drinks four standard drinks a week.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 25 kg per square metre, abdomen soft with mild epigastric tenderness, no mass, no hepatosplenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, rectal examination not indicated with no melaena reported
data_table.Investigations: Urea breath test negative taken while on a proton pump inhibitor, haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180), ferritin 96 micrograms per litre (30-300), coeliac serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start a week of triple eradication therapy despite the negative test result
Refer for gastroscopy with biopsy on the next available endoscopy list
Stop the acid suppressing medication for two weeks and repeat the same test
Request serology for immunoglobulin G antibodies against the organism instead
Accept the result, label the symptoms functional and continue the current tablet

subtopic_detail: Two centimetre segment of columnar lined lower oesophagus with intestinal metaplasia and no dysplasia on index endoscopy
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the gastroenterology clinic reviewing a 54-year-old man who had his first gastroscopy last month for fifteen years of reflux. The endoscopist described a 2 cm tongue of salmon coloured mucosa extending above the gastro-oesophageal junction, and four quadrant biopsies confirmed intestinal metaplasia with no dysplasia on review by a second pathologist.

His symptoms are well controlled on esomeprazole 20 mg daily. He has no dysphagia, no weight loss and no anaemia. He stopped smoking eight years ago and his body mass index is 31 kg per square metre. He has no family history of oesophageal cancer. He asks how often he will need another camera test and whether anything can remove the abnormal lining.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 31 kg per square metre, abdomen soft and non-tender, no supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Gastroscopy with a 2 cm columnar lined segment above the gastro-oesophageal junction, four quadrant biopsies every 2 cm showing intestinal metaplasia without dysplasia, confirmed by a second pathologist, haemoglobin 152 g/L (130-180)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing management?

options.text: Continue acid suppression and plan repeat endoscopy in twelve months' time
Continue acid suppression and plan repeat endoscopy in three to five years
Refer for endoscopic radiofrequency ablation of the abnormal segment this year
Refer for laparoscopic fundoplication to prevent progression of the abnormal lining
Stop acid suppression and discharge him with no further endoscopic surveillance

subtopic_detail: Two years of abdominal pain relieved by defaecation with alternating stool form, a normal faecal calprotectin and a brother with Crohn disease
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 28-year-old woman with two years of crampy lower abdominal pain that she notices most when she is stressed at work. The pain eases after she opens her bowels, and her stools swing between hard pellets and loose motions from week to week.

She has no rectal bleeding, has not lost weight and wakes at night only to pass urine. Her brother was diagnosed with Crohn disease at 22 and she is frightened she has the same thing. Her periods are regular and not painful. Examination is normal apart from mild tenderness in the left iliac fossa. Her coeliac serology is negative on a gluten containing diet and her faecal calprotectin, sent because of the family history, is 28 micrograms per gram.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg per square metre, abdomen soft with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no guarding, no mass, no perianal skin tags fissures or fistulae, no mouth ulcers, no clubbing
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 134 g/L (115-155), C reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), faecal calprotectin 28 micrograms per gram (less than 50), coeliac serology negative on a gluten containing diet, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.7 milliunits per litre (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for colonoscopy with terminal ileal biopsies because of the family history
Refer for hydrogen breath testing to assess for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth
Request computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with oral contrast medium
Make the diagnosis positively and start dietary and symptom directed treatment
Start a two week course of rifaximin and review her bowel symptoms afterwards

subtopic_detail: Six weeks of bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain with two hours of morning stiffness and markedly raised inflammatory markers in a woman over 70 with no cranial symptoms
stem: A 74-year-old woman has six weeks of aching across both shoulders and hips with two hours of morning stiffness. She has no headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or visual symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Painful restricted active shoulder abduction with full passive range
data_table.Investigations: ESR 78 mm/h (less than 30), CRP 62 mg/L, creatine kinase 92 U/L, rheumatoid factor negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily, reviewed within the week
Oral methotrexate weekly with folic acid, reviewed in six weeks
Oral naproxen twice daily with a proton pump inhibitor
Temporal artery biopsy before any corticosteroid is started
Oral prednisolone 15 mg daily, reviewed within the week

subtopic_detail: Fever and diffuse abdominal tenderness in a man with alcohol related cirrhosis whose diagnostic ascitic tap shows a neutrophil count above the threshold with a rising creatinine
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 58-year-old man with alcohol related cirrhosis and longstanding ascites who has had two days of fever and generalised abdominal discomfort. He has become slower in his responses over the same period.

He last drank alcohol four months ago. He has had no vomiting, no diarrhoea and no localised pain, and his abdomen is diffusely tender without guarding or rebound. He has not had an endoscopy or any instrumentation recently. A diagnostic paracentesis performed in the emergency department has just been reported. He takes spironolactone and furosemide and has never had an episode like this before.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Jaundiced with mild asterixis, abdomen distended with shifting dullness and diffuse tenderness, no guarding or rebound, bowel sounds present, no cellulitis or other visible infective focus, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear cell count 480 per cubic millimetre with no organisms seen on Gram stain, ascitic albumin 8 g/L, serum albumin 26 g/L (35-50), bilirubin 68 micromol/L (less than 20), international normalised ratio 1.8 (0.9-1.3), creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-110) rising from 92, white cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Start intravenous ceftriaxone now and give intravenous albumin as well
Start intravenous ceftriaxone now and withhold albumin pending the culture
Start oral norfloxacin now and arrange a repeat paracentesis in 48 hours
Arrange a large volume therapeutic paracentesis now with albumin replacement
Await ascitic fluid culture results before committing to any antibiotic therapy

subtopic_detail: Three centimetre adrenal nodule with low unenhanced attenuation found incidentally on imaging for renal colic in a normotensive man
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 52-year-old man who had a computed tomogram last week for left sided loin pain. He passed a 4 mm stone and the pain has settled, but the report also describes a 3 cm nodule in the right adrenal gland with an unenhanced attenuation of 8 Hounsfield units and a smooth margin.

He feels well. He has never had hypertension and his blood pressure today is normal, and he has had no episodes of sweating, headache or palpitations. He has not gained weight, has no striae and no proximal weakness, and there is no easy bruising. He has never had a cancer diagnosis and has never smoked. His potassium and renal function are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 70 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26 kg per square metre, no supraclavicular fat pad, no purple striae, no proximal myopathy, no hirsutism, no palpable abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography showing a 3 cm right adrenal nodule with an unenhanced attenuation of 8 Hounsfield units and smooth margins, potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange image guided percutaneous biopsy of the nodule to obtain a tissue diagnosis
Refer for laparoscopic adrenalectomy because the nodule measures more than 3 cm
Screen for hormone excess with an overnight dexamethasone test and metanephrines
Repeat the computed tomogram in twelve months with no biochemical testing now
Arrange positron emission tomography to characterise the nodule before further testing

subtopic_detail: Abrupt severe hypertension with rising creatinine, fragmented red cells and a bland urinary sediment weeks after starting moderate dose corticosteroid for early diffuse skin thickening
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 44-year-old woman admitted with a three day headache and blurred vision. Her hands and forearms have become tight and thickened over the past eight months and she has had cold painful colour changes in her fingers for a year.

Her rheumatologist started prednisolone 20 mg daily five weeks ago for troublesome joint pain. She has no fever, no rash and no recent diarrhoea. Her blood pressure was 126/78 mmHg at her clinic visit two months ago and is now 214/122 mmHg. Her creatinine has risen from 68 to 212 micromol/L over three weeks.
