The blood film shows fragmented red cells and her platelet count has fallen, while her urinalysis shows no casts and only a trace of protein.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 214/122 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Skin thickening over the fingers, hands and forearms extending above the elbows, digital pitting scars, bilateral papilloedema on fundoscopy, no rash, no synovitis, chest clear, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 212 micromol/L (45-90) risen from 68 three weeks ago, haemoglobin 92 g/L (115-155), platelets 84 x10^9/L (150-450), blood film with fragmented red cells, lactate dehydrogenase 620 units per litre (120-250), urinalysis with trace protein and no red cell casts, ADAMTS13 activity 62 per cent, antinuclear antibody positive with a nucleolar pattern

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Start an intravenous labetalol infusion and titrate against the blood pressure response
Start oral captopril and increase the dose rapidly against the blood pressure response
Start intravenous methylprednisolone pulses and increase her maintenance prednisolone
Start daily plasma exchange and give intravenous methylprednisolone alongside it
Start intravenous cyclophosphamide and arrange urgent percutaneous renal biopsy

subtopic_detail: Uniform swelling of an entire toe with asymmetric large joint involvement, nail pitting and negative rheumatoid serology after six weeks of an anti-inflammatory drug
stem: A 38-year-old man has four months of joint pain. His left second toe is swollen along its whole length and six weeks of naproxen gave only partial relief.

data_table.Examination: Whole left second toe uniformly swollen, right knee effusion, synovitis of two distal interphalangeal joints, nail pitting, scaly plaques behind the ears
data_table.Investigations: CRP 28 mg/L, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP negative, urate 0.32 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase the anti-inflammatory dose and review him
Start a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor as first treatment
Start weekly methotrexate with folic acid and review
Start allopurinol after checking his renal function
Inject the swollen knee with corticosteroid and review

subtopic_detail: Large unilateral exudative pleural effusion in a former power station worker that has recurred after drainage with malignant cells not found on two separate fluid samples
stem: A 68-year-old never-smoker has three months of breathlessness and constant right chest ache. He was a power station fitter in the 1970s and has lost 5 kg. A drained right effusion has reaccumulated.

data_table.Examination: Stony dullness to the mid zone on the right
data_table.Investigations: Pleural fluid exudative, cytology negative twice, cultures and acid fast bacilli negative
data_table.Imaging: Nodular circumferential pleural thickening including the mediastinal surface

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Local anaesthetic thoracoscopy with biopsy of the thickened pleura
A third large volume aspiration with cytology on more fluid
Blind percutaneous pleural biopsy with an Abrams needle
Bronchoscopy with washings and transbronchial biopsy of the lower lobe
Talc pleurodesis through an intercostal catheter without further sampling

subtopic_detail: New firm persistent unilateral parotid enlargement over three months in a woman with established sicca syndrome, a falling C4 and a new paraprotein
stem: A 57-year-old woman with eight years of dry eyes and dry mouth and anti-Ro antibodies has had painless left parotid enlargement over three months, unchanged by antibiotics, with night sweats and 3 kg weight loss.

data_table.Examination: Firm non-tender 4 cm left parotid, spleen tip palpable
data_table.Investigations: Complement C4 0.08 g/L (0.15-0.45), fallen from 0.22; new immunoglobulin M kappa monoclonal band

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Another antibiotic course with sialogogues, reviewing in eight weeks
Start hydroxychloroquine and review her symptoms in three months
Start oral prednisolone and review the gland in one month
Labial salivary gland biopsy to reassess the infiltration
Urgent imaging with biopsy of the enlarged parotid gland

subtopic_detail: Enlarging hands and feet with new snoring, carpal tunnel symptoms and difficult to control diabetes and hypertension in a man in his forties
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 46-year-old man whose wedding ring had to be cut off last year and who has gone up three shoe sizes in a decade. He has come today about numbness in both hands that wakes him at night.

His wife says he has begun snoring heavily and stops breathing at times. His blood pressure has needed a third agent this year and his glycated haemoglobin has risen from 7.1 to 8.4 per cent despite metformin and good adherence. He has a persistent headache most mornings and has noticed his teeth feel further apart. Photographs from ten years ago show a visibly different face with finer features and a less prominent jaw.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 156/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Broad spade like hands with doughy soft tissue, prominent supraorbital ridges and mandible with interdental separation, macroglossia, Tinel sign positive at both wrists, visual fields full to confrontation, no galactorrhoea, skin tags over the neck
data_table.Investigations: Glycated haemoglobin 8.4 per cent, fasting glucose 9.2 mmol/L, phosphate 1.6 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), calcium and thyroid function within normal limits, prolactin 620 milliunits per litre (less than 500)

lead_in: Which investigation should be performed first?

options.text: Measure a random serum growth hormone level on a morning fasting blood sample
Measure serum insulin like growth factor 1 against an age matched reference range
Measure growth hormone during a 75 gram oral glucose tolerance test this week
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa with gadolinium contrast
Arrange overnight polysomnography to quantify the severity of his sleep disordered breathing

subtopic_detail: Palpable purpura on the legs with arthralgia and a mildly abnormal sensory examination in a man with untreated chronic hepatitis C, a low C4 and a positive rheumatoid factor
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 55-year-old man with six months of crops of raised purple spots over both shins that come and go, leaving brown staining behind. He also has aching in both wrists and a numb patch over the outer side of the left calf.

He was diagnosed with hepatitis C fifteen years ago after injecting drug use, has never been treated and has not injected for twelve years. He has no ascites, no encephalopathy and no varices on a gastroscopy last year, and his transient elastography reading was in the mild fibrosis range. His creatinine is normal and his urine shows no blood or protein. He takes no regular medication and has had no recent infection or new drug exposure.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura over both shins with haemosiderin staining, no ulceration or digital infarcts, wrists tender with no synovitis, reduced pinprick sensation over the left lateral calf with normal power and reflexes, no hepatosplenomegaly, no ascites
data_table.Investigations: Hepatitis C antibody positive with detectable hepatitis C ribonucleic acid at 1.2 million international units per millilitre, genotype 1a, complement C4 0.04 g/L (0.15-0.45), C3 0.98 g/L (0.80-1.80), rheumatoid factor positive at high titre, cryoglobulins detected, creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), urinalysis with no blood or protein, albumin 39 g/L (35-50), international normalised ratio 1.0 (0.9-1.3), platelets 186 x10^9/L (150-450)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Start rituximab infusions first and add antiviral therapy once the vasculitis settles
Start high dose oral prednisolone alone and taper it over the next several months
Start pegylated interferon with ribavirin for a twenty four week treatment course
Start direct acting antiviral therapy for the underlying chronic viral infection
Start colchicine with graduated compression stockings and review him in three months

subtopic_detail: Rings and linear furrows seen at endoscopy for a food bolus obstruction in a young man with atopy and no biopsies taken
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 24-year-old man the morning after an emergency endoscopy for a steak bolus that had been stuck for four hours. The bolus was pushed through and he is now eating without difficulty.

On questioning he tells you he has cut steak and crusty bread out of his diet over the past two years, always drinks water with meals and is usually the last to finish. He has asthma, hay fever and childhood eczema. The endoscopy report describes concentric rings and fine longitudinal furrows through the whole oesophagus, with no stricture, no ulceration and no mass, and records that no biopsies were taken.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Well and comfortable, body mass index 23 kg per square metre, abdomen soft and non-tender, no cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count shows an eosinophil count of 0.7 x10^9/L (0.0 to 0.5), urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, C reactive protein within normal limits, endoscopy reports concentric rings and linear furrows throughout the oesophagus with no stricture, ulceration or mass and no biopsies taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start a proton pump inhibitor and review his symptoms in eight weeks
Arrange a barium swallow and review once the study has been reported
Repeat endoscopy and biopsy the proximal and distal oesophagus
Arrange oesophageal manometry and review once it has been reported
Start a topical corticosteroid and review his symptoms in eight weeks

subtopic_detail: Eighteen months of dysphagia to solids and liquids together with regurgitation of undigested food and a normal endoscopy
stem:
You are the physician seeing a 52-year-old woman with eighteen months of food sticking behind the sternum. She says it has been just as hard to get water down as bread from the very beginning, and that she has to stand up and arch her back to make things go through.

She brings up undigested food from hours earlier, sometimes onto her pillow, and has lost 6 kg. A proton pump inhibitor prescribed by her general practitioner made no difference. Endoscopy performed last week showed retained food and saliva in the oesophagus with a snug but passable gastro-oesophageal junction, normal mucosa and no mass, and gastric and duodenal biopsies were normal. A barium swallow shows a dilated oesophagus tapering smoothly to a narrow segment at the junction.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21 kg per square metre having fallen from 23, chest clear on auscultation, abdomen soft and non-tender, no supraclavicular lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, endoscopy shows retained food and saliva with normal mucosa, a passable gastro-oesophageal junction and no mass, gastric and duodenal biopsies normal, barium swallow shows a dilated oesophagus tapering smoothly at the junction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange high resolution oesophageal manometry to confirm the diagnosis
Start a proton pump inhibitor and review her symptoms in eight weeks
Refer for laparoscopic myotomy without further physiological testing
Arrange computed tomography of the chest and abdomen, then reassess
Refer for oesophageal dilatation at the next available endoscopy list

subtopic_detail: An incidental immunoglobulin G kappa paraprotein of 12 g per litre with a normal free light chain ratio and normal end organ markers
stem:
You are the physician reviewing a 68-year-old man referred after a paraprotein was found on blood tests ordered because of a raised total protein on a routine panel. He feels entirely well, walks 5 km most days and has kept his weight steady.

He reports no bone pain and no night sweats. On examination the lymph node areas, the abdomen and the axial skeleton are unremarkable, and pinprick and vibration sense are intact in both feet. Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation identifies an immunoglobulin G kappa paraprotein of 12 g/L, the serum free light chain ratio is within the normal range, and his haemoglobin, calcium and creatinine are all normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no bony tenderness, no peripheral neuropathy on testing pinprick and vibration sense, no macroglossia
data_table.Investigations: Immunoglobulin G kappa paraprotein 12 g/L, serum free light chain ratio within the normal range, haemoglobin 142 g/L (130 to 180), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.20 to 2.60), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60 to 110), immunoglobulin A and immunoglobulin M within normal limits, urine protein electrophoresis shows no Bence Jones protein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for bone marrow biopsy and skeletal survey before further review
Start bortezomib based therapy and refer to the haematology clinic
Arrange whole body magnetic resonance imaging and review in six months
Repeat the paraprotein, blood count and renal function in six months
Reassure him that no further monitoring of any kind will be needed

subtopic_detail: A haematocrit of 0.58 with itching after a hot shower and a palpable spleen in a man whose oxygen saturation is normal
stem:
You are the physician seeing a 58-year-old man referred because three separate blood counts over four months have shown a haemoglobin around 190 g/L. He mentions in passing that he has developed intense itching for about half an hour after a hot shower, which he has been treating with moisturiser.

He has never smoked, sleeps well without snoring and his partner has not noticed any pauses in his breathing. He is not on testosterone or any other medication. His oxygen saturation is 98 per cent breathing room air, both at rest and after walking briskly along the corridor. On examination his face is plethoric and the splenic edge is palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 148/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Plethoric facies, conjunctival suffusion, splenic edge palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin, no hepatomegaly, no clubbing, no cyanosis, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 192 g/L (130 to 180), haematocrit 0.58 (0.40 to 0.52), white cell count 13.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), platelets 512 x10^9/L (150 to 400), ferritin 18 micrograms/L (30 to 300), urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, oxygen saturation 98 per cent at rest and on exertion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange overnight oximetry on 2 consecutive nights and review the report
Measure serum erythropoietin and test for the JAK2 V617F mutation
Arrange renal tract ultrasound and review once it has been reported
Start venesection of 450 mL and review his blood count in four weeks
Repeat the full blood count in three months and review him after that

subtopic_detail: An acutely hot swollen knee in a seventy six year old with chondrocalcinosis on radiograph and a temperature of 37.8 degrees
stem:
You are the physician called to see a 76-year-old woman who developed a painful swollen right knee overnight. She has had two similar episodes in the past three years, each settling over a week or so with anti inflammatory tablets.

She takes hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension and has stage 3 chronic kidney disease. There has been no injury and no recent travel. The knee is warm, swollen and tense with a large effusion, and she will not let you flex it beyond 20 degrees. A radiograph taken in the emergency department shows fine linear calcification within the meniscal cartilage of both knees. Her temperature is 37.8 degrees Celsius.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right knee warm and swollen with a tense effusion and patellar tap, flexion limited to 20 degrees by pain, overlying skin intact with no break or cellulitis, no other joint involved, no tophi
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 118 mg/L (less than 5), serum urate 0.34 mmol/L (0.16 to 0.42), creatinine 128 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 42 mL/min/1.73m2, knee radiograph shows linear calcification of the meniscal cartilage in both knees

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Aspirate the joint for cell count, culture and polarised light microscopy
Start oral colchicine and review her again in forty eight hours
Start oral prednisolone and review her again in forty eight hours
Start intravenous flucloxacillin and review her response overnight
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the knee and then reassess

subtopic_detail: A magnetic wide based gait with urinary urgency and ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cortical atrophy in a seventy four year old
stem: A 74-year-old man has 18 months of walking as though his feet are stuck to the floor, with en bloc turns. He has had falls and now reaches the toilet too late.

data_table.Examination: Wide based gait, preserved arm swing, no tremor, Montreal Cognitive Assessment 23 out of 30
data_table.Investigations: Reversible screens normal; computed tomography shows an Evans index of 0.36 with mild sulcal widening

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor and review in three months
Refer directly for ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion
Start an anticholinergic for the urinary symptoms and review
Large volume lumbar puncture with gait assessment
Arrange carotid duplex ultrasound and review the report

subtopic_detail: Proximal weakness and bone pain with an alkaline phosphatase of 340 and a bone density T score of minus 2.8 in a housebound woman
stem:
You are the physician seeing a 64-year-old woman referred after a bone density scan requested by her general practitioner returned a lumbar spine T score of minus 2.8. The referral asks you to start treatment for osteoporosis.

She has been largely housebound for three years since a stroke left her with a mild left hemiparesis, and she goes outside only for appointments. She describes aching in her hips and thighs and says she now has to push up on the arms of the chair to stand. Her gait is waddling when she walks with her stick. She takes no calcium or vitamin D supplement and eats little dairy.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mild residual left hemiparesis, proximal weakness of hip flexion and shoulder abduction graded 4 out of 5 bilaterally, waddling gait, tenderness on firm pressure over both anterior tibiae and the sternum, no joint swelling
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.08 mmol/L (2.20 to 2.60), phosphate 0.71 mmol/L (0.75 to 1.50), alkaline phosphatase 340 U/L (30 to 110), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 11 nmol/L (greater than 50), parathyroid hormone markedly elevated, creatinine 74 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 60 mL/min/1.73m2, liver function tests otherwise within normal limits, bone density lumbar spine T score minus 2.8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Start alendronate weekly and review her bone density in two years
Start denosumab six monthly and review her bone density in two years
Replace vitamin D and calcium, then reassess before any antiresorptive
Start teriparatide daily and review her bone density in eighteen months
Start calcitriol daily and review her bone density in eighteen months

subtopic_detail: Deranged liver enzymes with a new tremor and deteriorating handwriting in a twenty four year old whose caeruloplasmin is low
stem:
You are the physician seeing a 24-year-old man referred with four months of abnormal liver enzymes found when he was investigated for tiredness. He drinks about four standard drinks a week and takes no regular medication, supplements or protein powders.

His girlfriend has persuaded him to come because his handwriting has become small and untidy over the same period and he has started dropping things. He has also become withdrawn and irritable and has dropped out of his university course. On examination there is a coarse tremor of both outstretched arms that worsens when he holds them flexed in front of his chest, and his speech is slightly slurred. His caeruloplasmin is 0.08 g/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Coarse proximal tremor of both arms worse on sustained posture, mild dysarthria, no asterixis, no jaundice, liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, spleen not palpable, no ascites, gait normal
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 168 U/L (less than 45), aspartate aminotransferase 194 U/L (less than 40), alkaline phosphatase 42 U/L (30 to 110), bilirubin 28 micromol/L (less than 20), international normalised ratio 1.2 (0.9 to 1.3), caeruloplasmin 0.08 g/L (0.20 to 0.60), haemoglobin 108 g/L (130 to 180) with a negative direct antiglobulin test, hepatitis B and C serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Measure serum alpha 1 antitrypsin and review when the result returns
Measure serum ferritin and transferrin saturation, then review the result
Arrange liver biopsy for histology before any other investigation
Measure 24 hour urinary copper and arrange slit lamp examination
Measure autoantibodies and immunoglobulins, then review the result

subtopic_detail: Increased left ventricular wall thickness with low voltage electrocardiogram complexes and nephrotic range proteinuria in a sixty seven year old
stem: A 67-year-old man has six months of exertional breathlessness, oedema to the thighs and light headedness on standing. He has never been hypertensive and his urine froths.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 104/66 mmHg lying, 86/58 mmHg standing
data_table.Examination: JVP 7 cm, enlarged tongue, periorbital purpura
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein to creatinine ratio 620 mg/mmol, albumin 24 g/L
data_table.ECG and echocardiogram: Low voltage complexes in all limb leads, left ventricular wall thickness 16 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Measure serum free light chains with immunofixation
Arrange coronary angiography and review the report
Start an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor and review
Arrange cardiac magnetic resonance imaging before blood testing
Refer for renal biopsy before any other investigation

subtopic_detail: A persistent platelet count of 780 with a normal C reactive protein and ferritin in a sixty two year old who has had a transient ischaemic attack
stem:
You are the physician reviewing a 62-year-old woman six weeks after an episode of right arm weakness and slurred speech that resolved completely within an hour. Carotid imaging, echocardiography and prolonged rhythm monitoring during that admission were all normal.

Her platelet count was 762 x10^9/L at the time and has been between 740 and 790 on four counts over the eight months before the event. She has no bleeding, no recent surgery and no inflammatory symptoms. On examination the splenic edge is palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. Her C reactive protein and ferritin are both normal, a blood film shows large platelets with occasional giant forms, and JAK2 V617F testing is positive.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No residual neurological deficit, splenic edge palpable 2 cm below the left costal margin, no lymphadenopathy, no bruising or petechiae, no livedo or digital ischaemia
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 780 x10^9/L (150 to 400), haemoglobin 134 g/L (115 to 155), white cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein within normal limits, ferritin 92 micrograms/L (30 to 200), blood film shows large platelets with occasional giant forms, JAK2 V617F positive, BCR-ABL1 not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start low dose aspirin alone and repeat the blood count in six months
Start aspirin and refer for cytoreductive therapy with hydroxycarbamide
Start oral iron replacement and repeat the blood count in three months
Start therapeutic anticoagulation and repeat the blood count in six months
Repeat the blood count in three months before any treatment is started

subtopic_detail: An ulcer with a violaceous undermined border that doubled in size after debridement in a woman with ulcerative colitis and sterile wound cultures
stem: A 44-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis has a painful left shin ulcer that began at a cannula site three weeks ago. Antibiotics gave no benefit and it doubled in size after debridement eight days ago.

data_table.Examination: 8 cm ulcer with a violaceous undermined border, pain out of proportion, no crepitus
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 1.1 mmol/L, deep tissue cultures no growth, edge biopsy neutrophilic infiltrate without organisms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent surgical debridement with intravenous antibiotics
Intravenous vancomycin and wound review in 48 hours
Systemic corticosteroid with no further debridement
Negative pressure wound therapy and review in 48 hours
Repeat wound swab and review when cultures return

subtopic_detail: Painless burns on the fingers with loss of pain and temperature over both shoulders and preserved vibration sense in a thirty two year old
stem:
You are the neurologist seeing a 32-year-old chef referred because he keeps burning his fingers on pans without noticing until he sees the blister. He has also dropped several plates over the past year and says his hands feel clumsy.

He mentions a dull ache at the back of his head that comes on when he coughs or strains and lasts a few seconds. He had a whiplash injury in a car accident eight years ago. On examination he cannot feel pinprick or the cold of a tuning fork across both shoulders, the upper chest and the outer arms, while light touch, vibration and joint position sense are entirely normal in the same distribution. There is wasting of both hands with absent biceps and supinator reflexes, and the knee and ankle reflexes are brisk.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Loss of pinprick and temperature sensation over both shoulders, upper chest and outer arms with preserved light touch, vibration and joint position sense in the same distribution, wasting of the small muscles of both hands, absent biceps and supinator reflexes, brisk knee and ankle reflexes with equivocal plantar responses, healed painless burns on several fingers, no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, serum copper within normal limits, glycated haemoglobin within normal limits, syphilis serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies and review once they are reported
Arrange computed tomography of the cervical spine, then reassess him
Measure vitamin B12 and copper, then review once the results return
Refer for carpal tunnel decompression and review him postoperatively
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the spine and craniocervical junction

subtopic_detail: Back pain for two years that wakes a young man at four in the morning and eases with movement, with normal pelvic radiographs
stem:
You are the general physician seeing a 26-year-old man referred with two years of lower back pain. He has been treated with physiotherapy and intermittent ibuprofen with partial benefit.

The pain wakes him at around four in the morning and he has to get out of bed and move about before he can settle. He has an hour of stiffness each morning before he loosens up, and the pain improves with exercise rather than rest. He had one episode of a painful red eye treated with steroid drops eighteen months ago. His father has psoriasis. On examination his lumbar flexion is reduced with a modified Schober measurement of 3.5 cm and there is tenderness over both sacroiliac joints. Plain radiographs of the pelvis are reported as showing normal sacroiliac joints. His C reactive protein is 14 mg/L (less than 5) and HLA-B27 is positive.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Reduced lumbar flexion with modified Schober measurement 3.5 cm, tenderness on direct pressure over both sacroiliac joints, chest expansion 4.5 cm, no peripheral joint swelling, no dactylitis, no psoriatic skin or nail changes, no enthesitis at the Achilles insertions
data_table.Investigations: Plain radiographs of the pelvis reported as normal sacroiliac joints, C reactive protein 14 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 28 mm/h (less than 15), HLA-B27 positive, full blood count within normal limits, rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints
Repeat plain radiographs of the pelvis in twelve months
Computed tomography of the lumbar spine and sacroiliac joints
Dual energy X-ray absorptiometry of the spine and hip
Nuclear medicine whole body bone scan with delayed images

subtopic_detail: Joint aches and tiredness in a man whose ferritin is 1250 with a transferrin saturation of 68 per cent and two copies of the common iron loading variant
stem: A 48-year-old man has six months of fatigue and aching second and third metacarpophalangeal joints. He drinks four standard drinks weekly.

data_table.Examination: Liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 1250 micrograms/L (30 to 300), transferrin saturation 68 per cent, alanine aminotransferase 74 U/L (less than 40), HFE genotype homozygous C282Y

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral deferasirox and monitor his ferritin every three months
Advise a low iron diet avoiding red meat and vitamin C
Begin weekly venesection and assess him for liver fibrosis
Repeat the iron studies in six months before starting treatment
Refer for magnetic resonance imaging to quantify cardiac iron

subtopic_detail: An alkaline phosphatase of 620 with normal liver enzymes and bone pain over one shin in a man whose hearing has declined
stem: A 71-year-old man has a raised alkaline phosphatase and eighteen months of deep ache over his right shin. His hearing has declined and his hat feels tighter.

data_table.Examination: Warm bowed right tibia, right conductive hearing loss
data_table.Investigations: Alkaline phosphatase 620 U/L (30 to 110) with normal transaminases and bilirubin
data_table.Radiograph: Coarsened trabeculae with cortical thickening and a flame shaped lytic front

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Bone biopsy of the tibial lesion before starting treatment
Serum electrophoresis and a skeletal survey for myeloma
Replace vitamin D and recheck the alkaline phosphatase in three months
Start six monthly denosumab and arrange bone density measurement
A single intravenous zoledronic acid infusion after dental review

subtopic_detail: An alkaline phosphatase still twice the upper limit after fourteen months of weight based ursodeoxycholic acid taken reliably, with a normal bilirubin
stem: A 54-year-old woman was diagnosed with primary biliary cholangitis fourteen months ago and takes ursodeoxycholic acid 14 mg/kg daily; dispensing records confirm adherence. She still has fatigue and nocturnal itch.

data_table.Examination: Excoriations and mild xanthelasma, no jaundice, ascites or asterixis
data_table.Investigations: Alkaline phosphatase 248 U/L (30 to 110), down from 410 U/L at diagnosis; bilirubin 12 micromol/L; albumin 39 g/L; ALT 52 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Add a second line agent and continue the ursodeoxycholic acid
Increase her ursodeoxycholic acid dose above 20 mg/kg daily
Start prednisolone with azathioprine as for autoimmune hepatitis
Refer urgently for magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography
Continue current treatment and repeat the liver tests yearly

subtopic_detail: A positive breath test six weeks after completing a week of amoxicillin, clarithromycin and a proton pump inhibitor for a duodenal ulcer
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 52-year-old woman who had a duodenal ulcer found on gastroscopy three months ago with a positive gastric biopsy for Helicobacter pylori. She completed seven days of esomeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin and reports she took every dose.

Her epigastric pain improved but has returned over the past fortnight. She stopped her proton pump inhibitor two weeks before testing and has taken no antibiotics since the eradication course. A urea breath test performed six weeks after finishing treatment is positive. Her appetite, weight and swallowing are unchanged and her haemoglobin and ferritin are within normal limits. She tolerates penicillins and has previously taken clarithromycin twice for chest infections.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mild epigastric tenderness without guarding, no mass, no hepatosplenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Urea breath test positive six weeks after completing eradication therapy with the proton pump inhibitor withheld for two weeks beforehand, haemoglobin within normal limits, ferritin within normal limits, gastroscopy three months ago showing a 10 mm duodenal ulcer with biopsy positive for Helicobacter pylori and no malignancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer for repeat gastroscopy with biopsy for antibiotic susceptibility testing
Repeat the identical seven day regimen for a further fourteen days
Prescribe second line therapy that avoids the antibiotic already used
Continue long term proton pump inhibitor therapy without further antibiotics
Repeat the breath test in three months before any further treatment

subtopic_detail: Grittiness in both eyes and a mouth so dry she carries water to swallow bread, with bilateral parotid swelling and a positive anti-Ro
stem: A 53-year-old woman has two years of gritty eyes and a mouth too dry to swallow bread. She has had painless swelling in front of both ears and six new dental caries.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-tender parotid enlargement, dry fissured tongue, no synovitis or rash
data_table.Investigations: Antinuclear antibody 1 in 640, anti-Ro and anti-La positive, ESR 34 mm/h (less than 20)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start hydroxychloroquine and arrange baseline ophthalmology screening
Start prednisolone 25 mg daily and taper over three months
Refer for parotid biopsy before starting any treatment
Trial pilocarpine with intensive dental and ocular care
Quantify dryness objectively and screen for organ involvement

subtopic_detail: Difficulty rising from a chair with a violaceous rash over the knuckles and upper back in a woman whose creatine kinase is 1800
stem: A 61-year-old woman has ten weeks of progressive difficulty rising from a chair and lifting her arms, with 4 kg of weight loss and dysphagia for solids.

data_table.Examination: Violaceous scaly papules over the metacarpophalangeal joints, violaceous erythema across the upper back and periorbital region, proximal power 3 out of 5
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 1800 U/L (less than 200), anti-Mi-2 antibody positive, myopathic electromyography

lead_in: What is the most important next step alongside corticosteroid treatment?

options.text: Age-appropriate malignancy screening with computed tomography
Muscle biopsy of the most affected proximal muscle group
Nerve conduction studies for a coexisting peripheral neuropathy
Immediate plasma exchange and intravenous immunoglobulin
Ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring for myocarditis

subtopic_detail: Visible blood in the urine appearing on the second day of a sore throat in a young man with protein of 1.2 grams per day and normal complement
stem: A 24-year-old man has had three episodes of cola-coloured urine over two years, each starting on the second day of a sore throat and clearing within four days. He is well between episodes.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/88 mmHg on two readings
data_table.Investigations: Dysmorphic red cells with red cell casts, protein 1.2 g per day, C3 and C4 normal, antistreptolysin O not raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start high dose prednisolone and cyclophosphamide without delay
Arrange cystoscopy and computed tomography urography to exclude a tumour
Start renin angiotensin blockade and refer for renal biopsy
Give a course of penicillin and repeat his urinalysis in six weeks
Reassure him and arrange annual urinalysis and blood pressure checks

subtopic_detail: Eight loose motions a day with abdominal cramping six weeks into pembrolizumab for melanoma, with negative stool cultures
stem: A 64-year-old man six weeks into pembrolizumab for melanoma has five days of diarrhoea, now eight loose motions a day including two overnight, with cramping pain and blood in the stool.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98, BP 118/70 mmHg, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, generalised tenderness, no guarding
data_table.Investigations: Stool culture and Clostridioides difficile toxin negative, computed tomography shows diffuse colonic wall thickening

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral vancomycin empirically, repeating the toxin assay in 48 hours
Urgent colonoscopy with biopsies before any treatment
Intravenous fluids, electrolyte replacement and review in 24 hours
Loperamide regularly, continuing immunotherapy as scheduled
Withhold immunotherapy and start high dose corticosteroid

subtopic_detail: Jaundice and a tender enlarged liver three weeks after a heavy drinking period with a bilirubin of 280 and an international normalised ratio of 1.9
stem: A 47-year-old man has become progressively jaundiced over three weeks after months of drinking 20 standard drinks daily. He stopped eight days ago.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, temperature 37.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Deep jaundice, tender liver edge, mild ascites, no asterixis
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 280 micromol/L, AST 186 U/L, ALT 74 U/L, INR 1.9, albumin 26 g/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, ascitic neutrophils 120 per mm3

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: N-acetylcysteine infusion with monitoring of liver function
Prednisolone 40 mg daily with nutritional support and thiamine
Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily for bacterial peritonitis
Urgent transjugular liver biopsy before starting any treatment
Lactulose three times daily with dietary protein restriction

subtopic_detail: Morning confusion relieved by orange juice with a glucose of 2.1, raised insulin and C-peptide and a negative sulfonylurea screen
stem:
You are the general physician seeing a 39-year-old woman with six months of episodes in which she becomes confused, sweaty and tremulous, mostly before breakfast or if a meal is delayed. Her husband says she becomes vague and cannot follow a conversation, and that a glass of orange juice reverses it within minutes.

She has gained 7 kg because she now eats every two hours to prevent episodes. She has no diabetes, works as a florist, and no one in the household has diabetes or access to insulin or tablets for it. During a supervised 72 hour fast she became symptomatic at 14 hours with a plasma glucose of 2.1 mmol/L. Samples taken at that moment show insulin inappropriately detectable, C-peptide raised, proinsulin raised and beta hydroxybutyrate suppressed. Her sulfonylurea and meglitinide screen is negative, her morning cortisol is within normal limits and her insulin antibodies are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits between episodes
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 29 kg/m2, no hyperpigmentation, no hepatomegaly, no abdominal mass, normal neurological examination between episodes, no lipohypertrophy or injection sites
data_table.Investigations: At the point of symptomatic hypoglycaemia during supervised fasting: plasma glucose 2.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 7.8), insulin inappropriately detectable, C-peptide raised, proinsulin raised, beta hydroxybutyrate suppressed; sulfonylurea and meglitinide screen negative; insulin antibodies negative; morning cortisol within normal limits; short synacthen test normal; liver function tests and creatinine within normal limits; HbA1c 4.7 per cent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Reassure her and advise frequent small meals with a bedtime snack
Start diazoxide and review her symptom diary again in three months
Measure insulin like growth factor 2 and screen for an occult malignancy
Arrange pancreatic imaging to localise the lesion for surgical resection
Begin hydrocortisone replacement for probable adrenal insufficiency

subtopic_detail: Creatinine rising from 98 to 186 ten days after perindopril was started in a smoker with bruits over both flanks
stem: A 71-year-old man with hypertension needing four agents and peripheral vascular disease had perindopril added ten days ago. He feels well and is not volume depleted.

data_table.Examination: JVP 2 cm with no postural drop, flank bruits, absent foot pulses
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 186 micromol/L, up from 98; potassium 5.4 mmol/L; urinalysis bland
data_table.Ultrasound: Right kidney 11.2 cm, left kidney 8.4 cm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Intravenous fluids for presumed prerenal acute kidney injury
Stop the perindopril and arrange imaging of the renal arteries
Continue the perindopril and repeat the biochemistry in four weeks
High dose prednisolone for probable acute interstitial nephritis
Renal biopsy to establish the cause before changing drugs

subtopic_detail: Ringing ears, deep rapid breathing and agitation after a large ingestion of tablets for arthritis, with a pH of 7.44 and a bicarbonate of 12
stem: A 34-year-old woman is brought in four hours after taking an unknown number of her mother's arthritis tablets. She is agitated and reports ringing in her ears.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 /min, RR 34 /min, T 38.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Deep rapid breathing, diaphoretic, confused but rousable
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.44, pCO2 18 mmHg, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, Na 140 mmol/L, K 3.2 mmol/L, Cl 102 mmol/L, salicylate 720 mg/L and rising

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intubate and ventilate her now to protect her airway from aspiration
Give activated charcoal and repeat the salicylate in four hours
Start intravenous sodium bicarbonate and defer dialysis until the pH falls
Start sodium bicarbonate with potassium replacement and refer for dialysis
Give intravenous fluids with active cooling and observe in the department

subtopic_detail: Eighteen months of difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids with regurgitation and a normal endoscopy
stem:
You are the general physician seeing a 42-year-old woman referred with eighteen months of food sticking. She describes the sensation behind the lower sternum and says it happens just as much with water as with steak, and that she now eats standing up and drinks fizzy water to push food down.

She brings up undigested food on the pillow at night and has lost 5 kg. She was treated for reflux with esomeprazole for six months with no benefit. She has never smoked and takes no other medicines.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21 kg/m2, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, chest clear on auscultation, abdomen soft and non-tender with no mass, no oral candidiasis
data_table.Investigations: Gastroscopy reporting retained saliva and food residue in the oesophagus, a normal oesophageal mucosa with no rings, furrows or stricture, and mild resistance on passing the scope through the gastro-oesophageal junction that yields with gentle pressure, biopsies from the distal oesophagus showing no eosinophilic infiltrate, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: High resolution oesophageal manometry with assessment of relaxation at the gastro-oesophageal junction
Twenty four hour ambulatory oesophageal pH and impedance monitoring off acid suppressing therapy
Computed tomography of the chest and upper abdomen with intravenous contrast to look for an infiltrating lesion
A further eight week course of a high dose proton pump inhibitor taken twice daily before meals
A timed barium swallow with fluoroscopic screening of the oesophagus and gastro-oesophageal junction

subtopic_detail: Recurrent food bolus obstruction in a young atopic man planned for endoscopy after spontaneous passage
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 26-year-old man in clinic after his second presentation to the emergency department with meat lodged in his oesophagus, which passed spontaneously after an hour both times.

Between episodes he eats slowly, chews carefully and avoids bread and steak at restaurants. He has asthma treated with an inhaled corticosteroid, hay fever each spring, and had eczema as a child. Acid suppression for three months made no difference to his swallowing. You are booking his gastroscopy.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, chest clear with no wheeze, no cervical lymphadenopathy, no oral lesions, abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count with eosinophils 0.6 x10^9/L (0.0 to 0.5), previous gastroscopy report from another centre describing linear furrows and concentric rings with no stricture and no biopsies taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Arrange a timed barium swallow to define the calibre of the oesophagus before any further endoscopic procedure
Proceed to gastroscopy and take at least six oesophageal biopsies from both the proximal and the distal oesophagus
Refer him for skin prick testing to common foods and start an elimination diet based on the results obtained
Arrange high resolution oesophageal manometry to assess peristalsis and relaxation at the gastro-oesophageal junction
Start a topical swallowed corticosteroid preparation now and reassess his symptoms in the clinic after eight weeks

subtopic_detail: Persistent watery diarrhoea after stopping the implicated drug in a woman whose colonoscopy was macroscopically normal
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 68-year-old woman eight weeks after her colonoscopy. She has had six months of watery diarrhoea, six to eight times a day including at night, with urgency but no blood.

Her colonoscopy looked normal to the eye and random biopsies showed a thickened subepithelial collagen band with a lymphocytic infiltrate. She stopped the diclofenac she had been taking for knee pain the day after the procedure and has had no improvement in eight weeks. Her weight is stable and she has coeliac serology that was negative with a normal immunoglobulin A.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender with no mass, no perianal disease, no oedema, no goitre, no clubbing
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, faecal calprotectin within normal limits, stool culture and Clostridioides difficile toxin negative, colonic biopsies showing a thickened subepithelial collagen band with chronic inflammation and preserved crypt architecture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Commence mesalazine 3 g daily and review her stool frequency and inflammatory markers after 8 weeks
Prescribe loperamide 2 mg titrated to stool frequency and review her in the outpatient clinic in 3 months
Arrange a repeat colonoscopy with extensive random biopsies from the right and left colon to confirm the diagnosis
Commence oral budesonide at 9 mg daily for eight weeks and then taper according to her symptomatic response
Commence a bile acid sequestrant and arrange a selenium homocholic acid taurine scan if she does not respond

subtopic_detail: Postprandial vomiting of recognisable food with erratic glucose readings in long standing type 1 diabetes and a normal endoscopy
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar seeing a 38-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes of twenty two years who has four months of fullness after a few mouthfuls, nausea and vomiting of recognisable food several hours after eating.

Her continuous glucose monitor shows lows two hours after her meal boluses and highs four to six hours later, and she has stopped bolusing before meals because of the lows. She takes no opioid or anticholinergic medicine and has never used a glucagon like peptide 1 agonist. Her most recent haemoglobin A1c was 9.4 per cent.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits with no postural drop in blood pressure
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg/m2, abdomen soft with a succussion splash and no organomegaly or mass, absent ankle reflexes with reduced vibration sense to the mid shin bilaterally, background diabetic retinopathy on fundoscopy, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Gastroscopy reporting retained food in the stomach with no ulcer, stricture or outlet obstruction, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, coeliac serology negative with normal immunoglobulin A, haemoglobin A1c 9.4 per cent (target under 7.0 per cent), urine albumin creatinine ratio 18 mg/mmol (less than 2.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Computed tomography of the abdomen with oral and intravenous contrast to exclude a mechanical cause for her symptoms
A twenty four hour ambulatory oesophageal pH study performed after her acid suppressing therapy has been withheld
Antroduodenal manometry to characterise the contractile pattern of the gastric antrum and the proximal small bowel
A urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori with repeat gastroscopy and antral biopsies if the breath test is positive
Solid phase gastric emptying scintigraphy performed over four hours with her glucose in the target range on the day

subtopic_detail: A shallow ulcer above the medial malleolus with oedema and pigmentation in a woman with palpable foot pulses
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 68-year-old woman with a shallow ulcer above the inner ankle that has been present for ten weeks. It weeps clear fluid, aches at the end of the day and eases when she puts her legs up.

She has hypertension and a body mass index of 34 kg/m2, and she had a deep vein thrombosis in that leg after a knee replacement twelve years ago. A practice nurse has been dressing it weekly with a foam dressing and has asked you whether antibiotics are needed.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Shallow ulcer of 4 cm by 3 cm above the medial malleolus with a flat granulating base and irregular sloping edges, surrounding brown pigmentation with induration of the gaiter area, pitting oedema to the mid calf, varicose veins in the great saphenous distribution, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable bilaterally, normal sensation to monofilament testing, no surrounding warmth beyond the ulcer margin and no purulent discharge
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin A1c 5.4 per cent (under 6.0 per cent), full blood count within normal limits, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), wound swab growing mixed skin flora

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Prescribe oral flucloxacillin for seven days on the basis of the mixed growth from her wound swab
Prescribe pentoxifylline and continue the current weekly dressing regimen with review of the ulcer in six weeks
Refer her for a split skin graft to the ulcer bed and arrange the procedure through the plastic surgery service
Measure the ankle brachial pressure index and commence graduated multilayer compression bandaging
Arrange a punch biopsy of the ulcer edge to exclude malignancy before any compression therapy is commenced

subtopic_detail: Macrocytic anaemia with neutropenia and dysplastic changes on the film in an older man with normal vitamin levels
stem: A 78-year-old man has four months of increasing breathlessness and two chest infections this winter. He takes perindopril and atorvastatin.

data_table.Examination: Pale, no organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Hb 84 g/L, MCV 106 fL, white cells 3.1 x10^9/L (neutrophils 1.2), platelets 92 x10^9/L, reticulocytes 22 x10^9/L, film hypogranular neutrophils with bilobed nuclei, B12 and folate normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Hydroxocobalamin and folate, repeating the count in six weeks
Upper and lower endoscopy to find occult blood loss
Transfuse two units of red cells and review in three months
Cease atorvastatin and perindopril and recheck in one month
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetic studies

subtopic_detail: An incidental sustained lymphocytosis of twenty two in a well man with no lymphadenopathy or cytopenias
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 67-year-old man whose blood count was taken as part of a preoperative check before a cataract operation. He feels entirely well, plays golf twice a week and has lost no weight.

He has had no fevers, drenching night sweats or unusual infections. A count taken eight weeks ago showed a lymphocyte count of 19 x10^9/L, and today's shows 22 x10^9/L. He has hypertension treated with amlodipine and no other medical history.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No cervical, axillary or inguinal lymphadenopathy, no hepatomegaly, spleen not palpable, no pallor, no bruising or petechiae, no skin lesions, tonsils not enlarged
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L (130 to 180), white cell count 26.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) with lymphocytes 22.1 x10^9/L and neutrophils 3.6 x10^9/L, platelets 212 x10^9/L (150 to 400), blood film showing small mature lymphocytes with scattered smudge cells and no blasts, lactate dehydrogenase within normal limits, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Peripheral blood flow cytometry to immunophenotype the circulating lymphocytes and confirm clonality
Excisional lymph node biopsy of an accessible node with histology and immunohistochemistry to classify the lymphoid disorder
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy with cytogenetic studies to assess the degree of marrow infiltration present
Computed tomography of the neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis with contrast to stage the extent of nodal involvement
Repeat the full blood count with a film in twelve months and refer him only if the lymphocyte count has risen further

subtopic_detail: Acute kidney injury with a very high creatine kinase after an older man spent a night on the floor
stem: An 82-year-old man fell in the night and was found on his bathroom floor this morning. He has passed no urine since.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/64 mmHg after prehospital fluid
data_table.Examination: Tender swollen left thigh, soft compartments, dark urine
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 42000 U/L, creatinine 218 micromol/L (84 six months ago), potassium 5.8 mmol/L, dipstick positive for blood, no red cells

lead_in: What is the most important next step after treating his hyperkalaemia?

options.text: Sodium bicarbonate titrated to a urine pH above 6.5
Intravenous mannitol to flush pigment casts through the tubules
Intravenous furosemide to convert to non oliguric injury
Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride titrated to urine output
Urgent haemodialysis to clear myoglobin before further damage

subtopic_detail: Three weeks of fever with headache and hepatitic liver enzymes in an abattoir worker with culture negative blood
stem: A 45-year-old abattoir worker has three weeks of daily fevers, drenching sweats and severe retro-orbital headache, with 4 kg of weight loss. He has had no antibiotics.

data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, no rash or eschar, tender liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 132 x10^9/L, ALT 186 U/L, ALP 168 U/L, three sets of blood cultures sterile, echocardiogram without vegetation
data_table.Imaging: Small right lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin, repeating cultures at 48 hours
Oral prednisolone for inflammatory hepatitis, with liver biopsy
Oral azithromycin for atypical pneumonia, reviewing in five days
Positron emission tomography for fever of unknown origin
Coxiella burnetii serology with a convalescent sample, starting doxycycline

subtopic_detail: A rapidly enlarging painful leg ulcer with a violaceous undermined border that worsened after surgical debridement
stem: A 52-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis has a shin ulcer that has trebled in size over three weeks, with pain nine out of ten. Flucloxacillin changed nothing and it expanded after surgical debridement.

data_table.Examination: 7 cm ulcer with a violaceous undermined border, exquisitely tender, fresh ulceration along the debridement incision, pedal pulses palpable
data_table.Investigations: Cultures sterile including mycobacteria and fungi, biopsy shows a dense neutrophilic infiltrate without vasculitis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Further surgical debridement with negative pressure wound therapy
Systemic corticosteroid at an immunosuppressive dose, avoiding further surgery
Intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam and repeat tissue cultures
Multilayer graduated compression bandaging with weekly community dressings
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy, continuing the current dressing regimen

subtopic_detail: Sudden profound proximal weakness on waking with a potassium of two point zero and a suppressed thyrotropin
stem: A 28-year-old man woke unable to get out of bed after a large late meal and beers following heavy exercise. He has had three similar milder episodes and has lost 6 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112 /min
data_table.Examination: Power 2/5 proximally and 4/5 distally, fine tremor, small goitre
data_table.Investigations: K 2.0 mmol/L, magnesium 0.86 mmol/L, TSH less than 0.01 mIU/L with free T4 38 pmol/L, urine potassium to creatinine ratio low, ECG with prominent U waves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management of his weakness?

options.text: A large oral potassium load then an infusion to normalise the level
An infusion of glucose with insulin to shift potassium into cells
Small doses of intravenous potassium with a non selective beta blocker
Intravenous magnesium sulfate, withholding potassium until magnesium is normal
Oral carbimazole, deferring potassium replacement until thyroid tests repeat

subtopic_detail: Eight months of abdominal pain relieved by opening the bowels with alternating stool form and a normal faecal calprotectin
stem:
You are the general medical registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman referred with eight months of lower abdominal cramping. She tells you the pain eases once she has opened her bowels and that her motions swing between hard pellets and loose stools from week to week, often with bloating that worsens through the day.

She has not lost weight, has never woken at night with the pain and has never seen blood. Nobody in her family has had bowel cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. She has brought printouts about bowel cancer and wants a colonoscopy.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2 with no documented weight change, abdomen soft with mild non localised tenderness and no mass, no perianal disease, no clubbing, no mouth ulcers, no abdominal distension on examination
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), ferritin 68 micrograms/L (30 to 200), coeliac serology negative with a normal total immunoglobulin A, faecal calprotectin 26 micrograms/g (less than 50), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer her for colonoscopy to exclude an organic cause before committing to any symptomatic treatment for her abdominal symptoms
Arrange a gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies to exclude coeliac disease despite the negative serology and reassess her symptoms afterwards
Explain the positive diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome and refer her to a dietitian for a supervised trial of a low fermentable carbohydrate diet
Commence a proton pump inhibitor for eight weeks and review her abdominal pain and bloating in the clinic once the course is complete
Request a faecal occult blood test and repeat it in three months to provide her with reassurance about the possibility of bowel cancer

subtopic_detail: Two years of recurrent painful lumps in both armpits and the groin with rope like scarring and discharging tunnels
stem:
You are the general medical registrar seeing a 24-year-old woman referred after four courses of flucloxacillin in the past year. She describes painful lumps in both armpits and her groin that swell, burst and discharge, then come back in a slightly different spot a few weeks later.

She has stopped wearing sleeveless tops and has taken sick leave because of the pain and the smell. She smokes fifteen cigarettes a day. She has no fever and feels systemically well between episodes.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 34 kg/m2, multiple tender inflammatory nodules in both axillae and both groins with several double headed open comedones, rope like scarring across the left axilla and two sinus tracts discharging on gentle pressure, no involvement of the face or trunk, no fever
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein 18 mg/L (less than 5), swab from a discharging lesion growing mixed skin flora, fasting glucose 5.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a further two week course of flucloxacillin and advise her to return promptly if the lesions recur again after treatment
Refer her directly for wide surgical excision of both axillae and both groins as the definitive treatment for her recurrent lesions
Arrange incision and drainage of each fluctuant lesion under local anaesthetic and review her in the surgical clinic in six weeks
Prescribe topical mupirocin to both axillae and the groin and arrange nasal decolonisation for her and her household contacts
Commence oral doxycycline for at least three months with smoking cessation support and refer her to a dermatology service for ongoing care

subtopic_detail: Isolated raised alkaline phosphatase with a warm bowed shin and progressive hearing loss in a man in his seventies
stem:
You are the general medical registrar seeing a 72-year-old man referred with an abnormal blood test found when his general practitioner investigated tiredness. He mentions a dull ache in his right shin that has been present for about a year and is worse at night, and says he has needed the television louder over the past two years.

He has no history of cancer and has not lost weight. He takes no regular medications and drinks two standard drinks a week.

data_table.Examination: Anterior bowing of the right tibia with skin over it warmer than the left, no localised bony tenderness to percussion over the spine, conductive pattern hearing loss on the right with Rinne negative on that side, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, normal power and sensation in both legs
data_table.Investigations: Alkaline phosphatase 412 U/L (30 to 110), gamma glutamyl transferase 24 U/L (less than 60), bilirubin and transaminases within normal limits, corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.60), phosphate 1.1 mmol/L (0.8 to 1.5), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 72 nmol/L (greater than 50), creatinine 84 micromol/L (60 to 110), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Measure serum parathyroid hormone to establish whether the bone turnover is being driven by parathyroid overactivity
Request serum and urine protein electrophoresis with serum free light chains to look for a monoclonal paraprotein as the underlying cause
Request plain radiographs of the symptomatic tibia together with a whole body radionuclide bone scan to define the distribution of disease
Arrange a computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis to search for a primary malignancy with skeletal metastatic disease
Commence oral alendronate weekly and recheck the alkaline phosphatase level in three months to confirm a response to treatment

subtopic_detail: Fasting triglycerides above 20 mmol/L found incidentally in a man with poorly controlled diabetes and heavy alcohol use
stem:
You are the general medical registrar seeing a 45-year-old man in a diabetes clinic. He has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin alone and admits he has not been taking it consistently for the past year.

He drinks six standard drinks most evenings. He has no abdominal pain now and has never been admitted with pancreatitis, and he has no personal or family history of cardiovascular disease. The laboratory has telephoned because his fasting lipid sample was grossly lipaemic.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 33 kg/m2, waist circumference 112 cm, eruptive xanthomata over both elbows and the extensor surfaces of the forearms, no hepatomegaly, no abdominal tenderness, no corneal arcus, no tendon xanthomata
data_table.Investigations: Fasting triglycerides 22.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0), total cholesterol 9.8 mmol/L (less than 5.5), high density lipoprotein cholesterol 0.7 mmol/L (greater than 1.0), low density lipoprotein cholesterol not calculable, glycated haemoglobin 10.2 per cent (less than 7.0 for treated diabetes), lipase 38 U/L (less than 60), liver function tests showing an alanine aminotransferase of 68 U/L (less than 40), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological management of his lipid abnormality?

options.text: Refer him urgently for therapeutic plasma exchange to clear the circulating triglycerides before starting any oral lipid lowering therapy
Commence a high intensity statin as the sole lipid lowering agent and reassess his full lipid profile again in three months
Commence ezetimibe and review whether his total cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations have fallen when he returns in three months
Commence a high dose omega 3 fatty acid preparation as the only agent and review his triglyceride level again in three months
Commence a fibrate alongside intensified glycaemic control and a structured plan to reduce his alcohol intake substantially

subtopic_detail: Bruising and mouth bleeding in a young adult with pancytopenia, a very low reticulocyte count and no organomegaly
stem: A 22-year-old woman has three weeks of tiredness, easy bruising and bleeding gums. She takes no medications.

data_table.Examination: Pallor, shin petechiae, no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 76 g/L, white cells 1.9 x10^9/L with neutrophils 0.6 x10^9/L, platelets 11 x10^9/L, reticulocytes 6 x10^9/L (20 to 100), film no blasts or dysplastic forms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral prednisolone for presumed immune destruction, reviewing counts weekly
Transfuse red cells and platelets with haematology review in two weeks
Oral iron and a multivitamin, repeating the count in four weeks
Same day haematology assessment for bone marrow aspirate and trephine
Computed tomography of chest, abdomen and pelvis for malignancy

subtopic_detail: Four months of dry tickly cough in a man with a clear chest and normal spirometry who began a blood pressure tablet last year
stem: A 58-year-old man has four months of a dry tickly cough with no sputum, wheeze or heartburn. He smokes five cigarettes a day. His blood pressure medication was changed eleven months ago and the cough began afterwards.

data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no lymphadenopathy, normal oropharynx
data_table.Investigations: Normal chest radiograph, spirometry FEV1 92 per cent predicted with ratio 0.78 and no bronchodilator response

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: A proton pump inhibitor twice daily for eight weeks, then review
Computed tomography of the chest to exclude an underlying thoracic malignancy
A trial of inhaled corticosteroid for suspected cough variant asthma
Substitute the angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor with a receptor blocker
Intranasal corticosteroid with an oral antihistamine for eight weeks

subtopic_detail: Severe wet season pneumonia in a Top End man with diabetes and heavy alcohol use growing a Gram negative bacillus
stem: A 52-year-old man in Darwin in February has five days of fever and cough. He works in mud on a market garden, has diabetes and drinks heavily, and has deteriorated on ceftriaxone and azithromycin.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/54 mmHg, SpO2 91% on 8 L/min oxygen
data_table.Investigations: Right upper lobe consolidation with a cavity, blood cultures growing a Gram negative bacillus with bipolar staining

lead_in: What change to his antimicrobial therapy is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue ceftriaxone and add doxycycline for zoonotic cover
Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for a three week course
Intravenous gentamicin with amoxicillin for Gram negative cover
Intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam for Gram negative bacteraemia
Intravenous meropenem, then months of oral eradication therapy

subtopic_detail: Vomiting with yellow green visual disturbance and bradycardia in an older woman weeks after two new cardiac drugs were added
stem: A 78-year-old woman on long term digoxin has four days of vomiting and says everything has a yellow green haze. Two new blood pressure and rate tablets were added three weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 42 /min, BP 104/62 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: K 6.4 mmol/L, creatinine 194 micromol/L (from 92), digoxin 4.6 nanomol/L (0.5 to 1.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate to stabilise the myocardium against the hyperkalaemia
An insulin and dextrose infusion as sole treatment for the hyperkalaemia
A temporary transvenous pacing wire while the drug is cleared naturally
Urgent haemodialysis to clear the drug and correct the potassium
Intravenous digoxin specific antibody fragments, monitoring rhythm and potassium

subtopic_detail: Shock with a raised blood glucose after a large modified release calcium channel blocker ingestion unresponsive to calcium and atropine
stem: A 32-year-old man took about thirty modified release verapamil tablets three hours ago. Fluids, atropine 1.2 mg and two doses of calcium gluconate have not improved him.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 38 /min, BP 72/40 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Alert, cool peripheries, capillary refill 5 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 13.8 mmol/L with no diabetes, lactate 4.4 mmol/L, corrected calcium 2.74 mmol/L, ECG junctional bradycardia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Repeated calcium gluconate boluses targeting a calcium above normal
An intravenous lipid emulsion infusion as circulatory rescue
An adrenaline infusion titrated to blood pressure as sole therapy
High dose insulin euglycaemic therapy with dextrose and monitoring
A single dose of activated charcoal and four hours of observation

subtopic_detail: Severe cramping pain, sweating and hypertension developing half an hour after a barely noticed sting off a north Queensland beach
stem: A 28-year-old woman swimming off Cairns in January felt a barely noticeable scratch on her shoulder. Thirty minutes later she had severe cramping back and abdominal pain, vomiting and a sense of impending death. Morphine 5 mg gave little relief.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 126 /min, BP 188/112 mmHg, RR 26 /min
data_table.Examination: Restless, piloerection, profuse sweating, faint erythema with no tentacle marks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Intravenous box jellyfish antivenom, repeated if needed
Pressure immobilisation bandage until the symptoms settle
Immerse the limb in hot water at 45 degrees C for twenty minutes
Escalating intravenous opioid with an antiemetic and cardiac monitoring
Intramuscular adrenaline for a severe allergic reaction

subtopic_detail: Unclottable blood one hour after a garden bite in a well patient with a correctly applied first aid bandage still in place
stem: A 43-year-old man was bitten on the ankle an hour ago and did not see the snake. A pressure bandage and splint are in place and he feels well. The tertiary hospital is two hours away.

data_table.Examination: Bandage intact, no ptosis or weakness, no bleeding
data_table.Investigations: INR greater than 12, APTT greater than 180 seconds, fibrinogen undetectable, D-dimer markedly elevated, arrival profile normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Remove the bandage and repeat coagulation studies
Plasma and cryoprecipitate, with antivenom only if he bleeds
Venom detection to select a monovalent antivenom
Road transfer to the tertiary hospital, deferring antivenom
Antivenom now, with the bandage left until it is running

subtopic_detail: Ringing ears, fever and confusion with a mixed acid base disturbance six hours after an uncounted analgesic ingestion
stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought in six hours after being found with an empty aspirin bottle. She has vomited, has ringing in her ears and is breathing deeply, and has become confused in the past hour.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, RR 34 /min, T 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Confused with GCS 13, deep sighing respirations, diaphoretic
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.41, pCO2 20 mmHg, bicarbonate 13 mmol/L, K 3.1 mmol/L, glucose 3.3 mmol/L, creatinine 118 micromol/L, salicylate 4.9 mmol/L rising from 3.6 mmol/L two hours earlier

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Rapid sequence intubation with standard lung protective ventilation
Repeated activated charcoal, repeating the level in four hours
Sodium chloride with potassium replacement and a repeat level
Intravenous acetylcysteine by the standard weight based protocol
Sodium bicarbonate with potassium replacement and urgent dialysis

subtopic_detail: Thyrotoxicosis after eighteen months of an antiarrhythmic where the gland shows absent vascularity and no antibodies
stem: A 64-year-old man has six weeks of palpitations, tremor and 7 kg weight loss. He has taken amiodarone for eighteen months for atrial fibrillation, and no history of thyroid disease.

data_table.Examination: Fine tremor, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: TSH less than 0.01 mIU/L, free thyroxine 46 pmol/L, thyroid peroxidase and thyrotropin receptor antibodies negative, ultrasound normal gland with absent vascularity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: High dose carbimazole titrated on thyroid function tests
Radioactive iodine ablation after beta blockade controls symptoms
Potassium perchlorate added to a thionamide, reviewed in six weeks
Cease the amiodarone and observe, with a beta blocker
High dose oral corticosteroid, with cardiology advice on amiodarone

subtopic_detail: Two exacerbations in a year on dual bronchodilator therapy with blood eosinophils of 0.4
stem: A 66-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and forty pack years has had two exacerbations this year needing prednisolone and antibiotics. He uses a combined long-acting muscarinic antagonist and beta agonist inhaler correctly.

data_table.Investigations: Post bronchodilator FEV1 45% predicted with ratio 0.58, blood eosinophils 0.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5)

lead_in: What change to his inhaled therapy is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue the current inhaler and add maintenance azithromycin three times weekly
Change to an inhaled corticosteroid with a long-acting beta agonist
Change to one inhaler with corticosteroid, muscarinic antagonist and beta agonist
Continue the current inhaler and add maintenance oral prednisolone
Continue the current inhaler and add oral theophylline with monitoring

subtopic_detail: Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder and weight loss in a seventy year old
stem: A 70-year-old woman has three weeks of painless jaundice with itch, dark urine and pale stools. She has lost 7 kg over two months. She takes no medications and drinks minimal alcohol.

data_table.Examination: Jaundiced with scratch marks, smooth non-tender palpable gallbladder
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 210 micromol/L, ALP 620 U/L, GGT 480 U/L, ALT 96 U/L, INR 1.1
data_table.Ultrasound: Dilated intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts, distended gallbladder, no stones

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Percutaneous liver biopsy, with staging imaging once histology returns
Pancreatic protocol computed tomography before biliary intervention
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with brushings
Repeat fasting ultrasound focused on the distal bile duct
Carbohydrate antigen 19-9 and carcinoembryonic antigen measurement

subtopic_detail: Eligibility for lung cancer screening in a current smoker with a thirty five pack year history
stem:
