You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old woman for a routine review. She smokes fifteen cigarettes a day and has done so since she was seventeen, giving about thirty five pack years, and she has tried to quit twice.

She has no cough, no haemoptysis, no chest pain and no weight loss, and she is otherwise well with no significant medical history. Her sister was recently diagnosed with lung cancer and she has read that scans are now available to detect it early. She asks what she should do and whether a chest X ray would be enough.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Chest clear on auscultation with no wheeze, no clubbing, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, body mass index 26 kg/m2, no hoarseness
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal function and liver function within normal limits, spirometry shows a ratio of 0.74 with a forced expiratory volume in one second of 88 per cent predicted

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: She should have an annual chest radiograph instead, since it involves less radiation exposure and is more accessible in general practice than a computed tomography scan
She is not eligible for screening because she has no respiratory symptoms, so she should be reviewed if cough, weight loss or haemoptysis develops
She should be referred for sputum cytology and a serum tumour marker panel, with computed tomography arranged only if either of those results is abnormal
She should be referred directly to a respiratory physician for bronchoscopy given her family history, with imaging arranged by the specialist afterwards
She is eligible for low dose computed tomography through the national screening program, and you should also offer her structured smoking cessation support

subtopic_detail: Postural dizziness and two falls in a frail older man taking eleven regular medicines
stem: An 88-year-old man has had two falls at home this month, both on standing from a chair. He takes perindopril, amlodipine, furosemide, metoprolol, doxazosin, mirtazapine, temazepam, oxybutynin, atorvastatin, aspirin and pantoprazole.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 148/70 mmHg lying, 106/58 mmHg standing, pulse 58 /min
data_table.Examination: Frail, prolonged timed up and go, no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Na 133 mmol/L, K 3.4 mmol/L, eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Brain computed tomography and carotid ultrasound before reviewing his medicines
Withdraw the medicines causing postural hypotension in a staged plan
Start fludrocortisone and continue his current regimen, reviewing in six weeks
Compression stockings and advice to rise slowly, continuing all medicines
Refer for a permanent pacemaker, deferring the medication review

subtopic_detail: Large primary spontaneous pneumothorax with minimal symptoms in a stable young man
stem: A 23-year-old tall slim man had sudden left sided chest discomfort four hours ago. He has no lung disease and is comfortable at rest. He lives nearby with housemates.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 124/72 mmHg, SpO2 98 per cent
data_table.Examination: Reduced breath sounds at the left apex, trachea central
data_table.Chest radiograph: Left pneumothorax, interpleural rim about 3 cm at the hilum, no mediastinal shift

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis during this admission
Admit for high flow oxygen and a radiograph tomorrow
Observe several hours, then outpatient review with return advice
Insert an intercostal catheter until the lung has reexpanded
Needle aspiration now, then discharge with follow up advice

subtopic_detail: Symptomatic hypercalcaemia with a raised parathyroid hormone and preserved renal function
stem:
You are the physician seeing a 52-year-old primary school teacher referred with a high calcium level found when she was investigated for tiredness. She describes constipation, low mood and two episodes of loin pain over the past year, the second of which passed a stone she collected.

She takes no supplements, no thiazide diuretic and no lithium. Her mother had a parathyroid operation in her sixties. A bone density scan performed last month showed a T score of minus 2.1 at the distal third of the radius. She has had no fractures.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Well appearing with no palpable neck mass, no bony tenderness, no proximal weakness, abdomen soft with no renal angle tenderness, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.90 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), parathyroid hormone 11.8 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), phosphate 0.68 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate above 90 mL/min/1.73m2, twenty four hour urinary calcium raised, vitamin D 68 nmol/L (above 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Observe with annual calcium, renal function and bone density measurement, advising generous fluid intake and avoidance of calcium supplements
Start an oral bisphosphonate to protect her skeleton and review the calcium in three months before deciding whether any further treatment is required
Check the urinary calcium to creatinine clearance ratio and reassure her if it is low, since this pattern suggests a benign familial condition needing no treatment
Refer her for parathyroidectomy after localisation imaging, since she has symptomatic disease with a kidney stone and reduced bone density
Start cinacalcet to lower the calcium level and monitor her calcium and renal function every six months in the outpatient clinic thereafter

subtopic_detail: Worsening bulbar weakness with a falling vital capacity and normal oxygen saturation
stem: A 54-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine was admitted yesterday with a chest infection and an antibiotic started. Her voice is now nasal and she coughs when drinking.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 22 /min, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: Weak cough, cannot count past fifteen in one breath
data_table.Investigations: Forced vital capacity 1.4 L, 2.6 L this morning; arterial pH 7.42, pCO2 42 mmHg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone now, reassessing in the morning
Urgent intensive care review with serial vital capacity
Increase the pyridostigmine and reassess her in two hours
Repeat the blood gas in four hours before escalating
Oxygen to keep saturation above 94% with hourly observation

subtopic_detail: Confusion and vomiting with a suppressed parathyroid hormone in a smoker who has lost weight
stem:
You are the emergency physician seeing a 68-year-old man brought in by his wife because he has become muddled over the past week. He has vomited several times today and has been drinking large volumes of water.

He has smoked since his teens, has lost 9 kg in three months and has a cough that he attributes to the smoking. He takes no supplements, no thiazide and no lithium, and has no history of kidney stones or fractures. His wife says he was completely independent a month ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 per cent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes with reduced skin turgor, drowsy and disoriented to time, no focal neurological deficit, no neck mass, reduced air entry at the right apex, no palpable lymph nodes
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 3.42 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), parathyroid hormone less than 0.5 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), phosphate 1.32 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), creatinine 156 micromol/L (60-110), albumin 31 g/L (35-50), electrocardiogram shows a shortened QT interval

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Arrange urgent parathyroid ultrasound and sestamibi scanning to localise an adenoma, with rehydration commenced while those investigations are organised
Begin intravenous normal saline rehydration and give high dose corticosteroids as the specific treatment for the hypercalcaemia, then arrange imaging of the chest
Arrange urgent haemodialysis against a low calcium bath as the fastest method of lowering the level, with rehydration continued during the dialysis session
Begin intravenous normal saline rehydration, then give intravenous zoledronic acid, and arrange imaging to identify the underlying malignancy
Begin intravenous normal saline rehydration with intravenous furosemide from the outset to promote calcium excretion, then arrange imaging of the chest

subtopic_detail: Paraesthesiae with a normal mean cell volume and a borderline vitamin B12 in a long term metformin user
stem: A 64-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has taken metformin for eleven years and a proton pump inhibitor. He has six months of tingling in both feet and unsteadiness in the dark.

data_table.Examination: Vibration sense absent at the ankles, Romberg positive, reflexes brisk, plantars equivocal
data_table.Investigations: Hb 141 g/L, MCV 88 fL, vitamin B12 172 pmol/L (150-700), HbA1c 6.8 per cent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Measure methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, treating if either is raised
Attribute this to diabetic neuropathy and review him in six months
Repeat the vitamin B12 in six months and treat if lower
Stop the metformin and reassess the vitamin level after three months
Start oral cyanocobalamin now and arrange nerve conduction studies

subtopic_detail: Intracerebral haemorrhage in a patient taking apixaban for atrial fibrillation
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 76-year-old woman brought in after her husband found her confused with a weak right arm. She takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation and took her morning dose about five hours ago.

She takes no antiplatelet agent and has not had recent surgery. A computed tomography scan of the brain performed twenty minutes ago shows a 3 cm left basal ganglia haemorrhage with mild surrounding oedema and no intraventricular extension. The neurosurgical registrar has reviewed the images and advises that no operation is indicated at present but asks you to reverse the anticoagulation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute and irregular, blood pressure 188/96 mmHg, respiratory rate 17 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 13 with confusion, right arm weakness with a right facial droop, pupils equal and reactive, no neck stiffness, no external signs of trauma
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155), platelets 224 x10^9/L (150-400), international normalised ratio 1.3 (0.9-1.3), activated partial thromboplastin time 34 seconds (25-38), creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), computed tomography shows a 3 cm left basal ganglia haemorrhage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reversal treatment?

options.text: Give intravenous idarucizumab and withhold all further anticoagulant doses, with blood pressure lowered concurrently while awaiting neurosurgical review
Give a platelet transfusion with intravenous tranexamic acid and withhold all further anticoagulant doses, with blood pressure lowered concurrently
Give intravenous protamine sulfate and withhold all further anticoagulant doses, with blood pressure lowered concurrently and hourly neurological observations
Give a prothrombin complex concentrate intravenously and withhold all further anticoagulant doses, with blood pressure lowered concurrently
Give intravenous vitamin K with fresh frozen plasma and withhold all further anticoagulant doses, with blood pressure lowered concurrently

subtopic_detail: Persisting bloody diarrhoea on day three of intravenous corticosteroid treatment for severe colitis
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 26-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis admitted three days ago. She presented with ten bloody bowel actions a day, and stool testing for infection including Clostridioides difficile was negative.

She has received intravenous hydrocortisone since admission with thromboprophylaxis and intravenous fluids. Today she reports eight bloody bowel actions in the past twenty four hours including two overnight, and she still has cramping before each one. Her abdomen is soft without guarding, and an abdominal radiograph this morning shows no colonic dilatation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale and tired, abdomen soft with mild generalised tenderness and no guarding, bowel sounds present, no abdominal distension, no perianal disease
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-155), white cell count 13.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5), albumin 27 g/L (35-50), abdominal radiograph with no colonic dilatation and no thumbprinting

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Start azathioprine at a weight based dose alongside the corticosteroid and reassess her stool frequency and inflammatory markers in a further three days
Start broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics alongside the corticosteroid and reassess her stool frequency and inflammatory markers in a further three days
Start rescue therapy with infliximab or ciclosporin after colorectal surgical review, continuing the corticosteroid while the decision is implemented
Continue the intravenous corticosteroid for a further three days before reassessing, since response in this illness commonly takes about a week to appear
Start oral mesalazine at a high dose alongside the corticosteroid and reassess her stool frequency and inflammatory markers in a further three days

subtopic_detail: Encephalopathy with an arterial pH of 7.28 after a staggered paracetamol ingestion over two days
stem: A 31-year-old woman took eight to ten grams of paracetamol daily for two days and was presented eighteen hours ago. Acetylcysteine has run since arrival. The bloods follow fluid resuscitation. The nearest liver transplant unit is ninety minutes by air.

data_table.Examination: Drowsy, disoriented, asterixis, jaundiced
data_table.Investigations: Arterial pH 7.28, INR 4.2, alanine aminotransferase 8400 U/L, creatinine 184 micromol/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop the acetylcysteine, as the standard course is complete
Fresh frozen plasma to correct the coagulopathy before transfer
Activated charcoal by nasogastric tube to limit absorption
Urgent haemodialysis to clear the drug and correct the metabolic acidosis
Continue acetylcysteine, telephone the transplant unit, correct the glucose

subtopic_detail: Three weeks of fever and weight loss with splinter haemorrhages in a man with a bioprosthetic aortic valve
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 67-year-old man with three weeks of fevers, drenching night sweats and a six kilogram weight loss. He has become breathless climbing the stairs at home over the past week.

He had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement four years ago and takes no anticoagulation. He had a dental extraction seven weeks ago. He has no intravenous drug use, no indwelling lines and no recent travel. Three sets of blood cultures were taken from separate sites before any antibiotic was given.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 per cent in room air, temperature 38.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge not documented previously, splinter haemorrhages in three nail beds, two tender nodules on the finger pulps, bibasal inspiratory crackles, spleen not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 102 g/L (130-180), white cell count 14.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 156 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110), urinalysis shows non visible haematuria, transthoracic echocardiogram reports a poorly visualised prosthetic valve with no definite vegetation, chest radiograph shows mild pulmonary congestion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the transthoracic echocardiogram in one week and withhold antibiotics until a vegetation is demonstrated
Start oral amoxicillin and arrange outpatient cardiology review once the blood culture results become available
Arrange computed tomography of the chest abdomen and pelvis to search for an occult malignancy causing the fevers
Give a single dose of intravenous antibiotic and repeat the blood cultures four hours later to improve the yield
Arrange transoesophageal echocardiography and start empirical intravenous antibiotics for prosthetic valve infection

subtopic_detail: Vomiting and hypotension in a woman on long term replacement who halved her dose during a diarrhoeal illness
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 44-year-old woman with two days of vomiting and light headedness. She has primary adrenal insufficiency diagnosed nine years ago and normally takes hydrocortisone twice daily with fludrocortisone each morning.

She developed diarrhoea three days ago and, worried about keeping food down, halved her hydrocortisone dose to make the tablets last. She has vomited four times today and has not kept down this morning's tablets. She has no abdominal pain, no fever and no urinary symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg lying with a fall to 64/40 mmHg on standing, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill three seconds, buccal and palmar crease pigmentation, abdomen soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds, no rash, alert and oriented
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 126 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), urea 12.4 mmol/L (2.5-8.0), creatinine 124 micromol/L (45-90), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.0), venous pH 7.30 (7.32-7.42), C reactive protein 8 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Take a random serum cortisol and a short synacthen test, withholding steroid until the results are available
Restart her usual oral hydrocortisone dose with an antiemetic and observe her in the short stay unit overnight
Give intravenous fluids with insulin and dextrose to correct the hyperkalaemia before addressing the hypotension
Give broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics for presumed sepsis and arrange blood cultures with a septic screen
Give intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately with intravenous sodium chloride and glucose replacement

subtopic_detail: Plan to stop denosumab after four years of treatment in a woman whose bone density has normalised
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 71-year-old woman who has received six monthly denosumab injections for four years after a wrist fracture from standing height. Her repeat bone density scan shows a lumbar spine T score improved from minus 2.8 to minus 1.6 and a femoral neck T score of minus 1.9.

She has had no further fractures. She tells you she is tired of injections, is pleased that her scan has improved and would like to stop treatment altogether. She takes calcium and vitamin D, walks daily and has no falls. She has no renal impairment and no dental problems.

data_table.Examination: Height 161 cm with no loss recorded over four years, body mass index 24 kg/m2, no kyphosis, no spinal tenderness, gait steady with normal tandem walking
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (greater than 50), creatinine 74 micromol/L with estimated glomerular filtration rate 72 mL/min/1.73m2, thyroid stimulating hormone and parathyroid hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Stop the denosumab now and repeat her bone density scan in two years to confirm that the gains have been maintained
Stop the denosumab and commence calcium and vitamin D at higher doses with a supervised exercise program
Extend the dosing interval to twelve monthly injections as a way of gradually weaning her off the treatment
Continue denosumab indefinitely and explain that a normalised density scan is not a reason to reconsider treatment
Transition to a bisphosphonate starting around six months after her last injection rather than stopping outright

subtopic_detail: Unilateral effusion with a pleural protein of 34 and serum protein of 62 in a man taking diuretics for heart failure
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 74-year-old man with three weeks of breathlessness on exertion. He has chronic heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction and takes furosemide, which was increased by his general practitioner a fortnight ago.

He has also lost four kilograms without trying and has a dry cough. He worked as a boilermaker in his twenties. He has no fever, no chest pain and no haemoptysis. A diagnostic pleural aspiration has been performed under ultrasound guidance.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Stony dull percussion note with absent breath sounds over the right lower zone, trachea central, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no peripheral oedema, no clubbing, no palpable lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Pleural fluid protein 34 g/L with serum protein 62 g/L, pleural lactate dehydrogenase 280 U/L with serum lactate dehydrogenase 420 U/L and a laboratory upper limit of normal of 250 U/L, pleural fluid glucose 4.2 mmol/L, pleural pH 7.38, no organisms on Gram stain, chest radiograph shows a moderate right sided effusion with no visible mass

lead_in: How should this fluid be interpreted and what should follow?

options.text: Transudate from cardiac failure, so increase the diuretic dose and repeat the chest radiograph in four weeks
Transudate that has been concentrated by diuresis, so withhold diuretics for a week and repeat the aspiration
Exudate consistent with empyema, so insert an intercostal catheter and commence intravenous antibiotic therapy
Exudate requiring further investigation, so arrange contrast computed tomography of the chest and cytological analysis
Indeterminate fluid, so calculate the serum to pleural albumin gradient and manage as cardiac failure if it exceeds 12

subtopic_detail: International normalised ratio of 8.4 with fresh melaena in a man on warfarin who started an antibiotic five days ago
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 79-year-old man who has passed three black tarry stools since last night and feels dizzy on standing. He takes warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve replacement and his control has been stable for years.

Five days ago he was prescribed trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection by an after hours service. He takes no antiplatelet agent and no non-steroidal anti inflammatory drugs. He has had no vomiting and no abdominal pain.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, melaena on rectal examination, abdomen soft and non-tender, mechanical click audible on cardiac auscultation, no peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 8.4 (target 2.5-3.5), haemoglobin 84 g/L (130-180) down from 138 g/L three months ago, platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), urea 14.2 mmol/L (2.5-8.0), creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management of his anticoagulation?

options.text: Withhold warfarin and recheck the international normalised ratio in 24 hours, giving red cell transfusion as needed
Give oral vitamin K 5 mg and withhold warfarin, arranging endoscopy on the next available elective list
Give fresh frozen plasma at 15 mL/kg as the primary reversal agent alongside resuscitation and urgent endoscopy
Give protamine sulfate with intravenous vitamin K and arrange urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy after transfusion
Give intravenous vitamin K with prothrombin complex concentrate, with resuscitation and urgent endoscopy alongside

subtopic_detail: Worsening weakness with a forced vital capacity of 14 mL/kg two days after a pyridostigmine dose increase
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the ward to see a 63-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis, admitted yesterday with increasing limb weakness and difficulty swallowing. Her pyridostigmine dose was increased two days ago by her neurologist over the telephone.

She has become weaker through the afternoon and now cannot lift her head from the pillow. She reports abdominal cramps and has had loose stools twice today. Her voice has become nasal and she has coughed twice while drinking water.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 58 beats per minute, blood pressure 134/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bilateral ptosis, weak neck flexion against gravity, proximal limb weakness worse on repetition, pupils constricted at 2 mm, skin moist with visible salivation, fine fasciculations over the deltoids, single breath count of 12
data_table.Investigations: Forced vital capacity 14 mL/kg having been 22 mL/kg this morning, venous carbon dioxide 44 mmHg (41-51), chest radiograph clear, potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), C reactive protein 6 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Increase the pyridostigmine dose further and reassess her strength after the next dose has taken effect
Administer an edrophonium test at the bedside to distinguish myasthenic from cholinergic weakness before acting
Commence high dose oral prednisolone and arrange plasma exchange to begin on the ward the following morning
Give supplemental oxygen by face mask to maintain saturations above 94 per cent and repeat the vital capacity overnight
Withhold pyridostigmine and transfer to intensive care for airway protection and ventilatory support assessment

subtopic_detail: Facial oedema with eosinophilia and a rising creatinine four weeks after starting an anticonvulsant
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 52-year-old woman with a widespread rash and fever. She was started on carbamazepine four weeks ago for trigeminal neuralgia and has taken no other new medication.

The rash began on her trunk five days ago and has spread to her limbs. Her husband says her face looks swollen. She feels generally unwell with aching and has had no diarrhoea and no cough. She has no history of atopy or drug allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 38.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform eruption over trunk and limbs affecting about sixty per cent of body surface, marked periorbital and facial oedema, no mucosal erosions, no blistering, Nikolsky sign negative, tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 16.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with eosinophils 1.9 x10^9/L (less than 0.5) and atypical lymphocytes on film, alanine aminotransferase 268 U/L (less than 35), creatinine 142 micromol/L (45-90) from a baseline of 72, C reactive protein 68 mg/L (less than 5), blood cultures negative at 24 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue carbamazepine with an oral antihistamine, treating this as a self-limiting morbilliform drug eruption
Cease carbamazepine and treat as toxic epidermal necrolysis with transfer to a specialised burns unit for care
Continue carbamazepine and commence intravenous antibiotics for a presumed systemic bacterial infection with rash
Cease carbamazepine immediately, commence systemic corticosteroid and monitor liver renal and thyroid function
Cease carbamazepine and substitute phenytoin to maintain control of her facial pain while the rash settles

subtopic_detail: Sodium rising from 108 to 126 over fifteen hours in a malnourished woman on thiazide who was volume deplete
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 61-year-old woman admitted overnight with confusion and one generalised seizure. She takes a thiazide diuretic for hypertension, drinks around forty standard drinks a week and eats poorly.

She received two 100 mL boluses of 3 per cent sodium chloride in the emergency department for the seizure, which terminated, followed by 0.9 per cent sodium chloride running at 125 mL/hour overnight. She has passed 2.8 litres of urine since midnight. She is now awake, oriented and asking for breakfast.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Moist mucous membranes, jugular venous pressure visible at 3 cm, no peripheral oedema, no ascites, body mass index 18 kg/m2, no focal neurological deficit, normal speech and comprehension
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 126 mmol/L (135-145) having been 108 mmol/L on admission fifteen hours ago, potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), urea 3.1 mmol/L (2.5-8.0), urine osmolality now 92 mOsm/kg having been 480 mOsm/kg on admission, thyroid function and morning cortisol within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue the saline infusion at the current rate, since her sodium remains below the lower reference limit
Give a further 100 mL bolus of 3 per cent sodium chloride to protect against a recurrence of her seizure
Commence tolvaptan to control the rate of rise and correct the residual hyponatraemia in a more controlled fashion
Stop the saline, give 5 per cent glucose with desmopressin and recheck the sodium every two hours to relower it
Restrict fluid to one litre daily and repeat the electrolytes in the morning before making any further changes

subtopic_detail: Pulmonary oedema and a blood pressure of 230/130 forty minutes after a beta blocker given for episodic palpitations
stem:
You are the medical registrar called urgently to a ward where a 48-year-old man has deteriorated. He was admitted this morning for investigation of six months of episodic headache, palpitations and drenching sweats, during which his blood pressure has been recorded between 190/110 and 230/125 mmHg, settling to normal in between.

Forty minutes ago the covering resident prescribed oral metoprolol for a pulse of 130 beats per minute. He is now acutely breathless, sitting bolt upright and coughing pink froth. He has no history of ischaemic heart disease and an echocardiogram two weeks ago showed a structurally normal heart with preserved systolic function.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 230/130 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, SpO2 84 per cent on fifteen litres per minute via reservoir mask, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Cool mottled peripheries with a pale diaphoretic face, widespread inspiratory crackles to the apices, pink frothy sputum, jugular venous pressure raised at 6 cm, no murmur audible over the respiratory noise
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with lateral ST depression and no ST elevation, high sensitivity troponin 148 ng/L (less than 14), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110), glucose 12.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.0), plasma free metanephrines requested on admission and still pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Give intravenous phentolamine and start a sodium nitroprusside infusion with intensive care involvement
Give a further dose of intravenous metoprolol to control the tachycardia driving the pulmonary oedema
Give intravenous furosemide and morphine and arrange urgent coronary angiography for a presumed acute coronary event
Give intravenous labetalol as a combined alpha and beta blocking agent to lower the pressure in a balanced way
Start a glyceryl trinitrate infusion alone and titrate it against the blood pressure while awaiting the biochemistry

subtopic_detail: choosing antiresorptive therapy after a vertebral fracture when the estimated glomerular filtration rate sits below the bisphosphonate cut-off
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 78-year-old woman in the fracture liaison clinic. She tripped on a rug three weeks ago, landed on her buttocks, and has had band-like mid-back pain since. Imaging of the thoracolumbar spine shows a wedge deformity at T12 with loss of about a third of the anterior vertebral height, and no other fracture.

She takes perindopril and a thiazide for blood pressure and has never taken a bone-specific medication. She has been on colecalciferol for six months and drinks two glasses of milk daily. Her bloods today show a corrected calcium of 2.32 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), phosphate 1.1 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (>50), creatinine 152 micromol/L (45-90) and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 28 mL/min/1.73m2, unchanged across three readings over the past two years. Parathyroid hormone and serum protein electrophoresis are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Focal tenderness over the T12 spinous process, no neurological deficit in either leg
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (>50), eGFR 28 mL/min/1.73m2, parathyroid hormone within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Thoracolumbar radiographs: T12 wedge deformity with about one third anterior height loss, no other vertebral fracture

lead_in: Which pharmacological therapy would you start for her bone health?

options.text: Six monthly subcutaneous denosumab 60 mg with calcium and vitamin D supplementation
Annual intravenous zoledronic acid 5 mg with calcium and vitamin D supplementation
Daily subcutaneous teriparatide 20 micrograms with calcium and vitamin D supplementation
Continued calcium and vitamin D alone with a repeat bone density scan in two years
Weekly oral alendronate 70 mg with calcium and vitamin D supplementation

subtopic_detail: glucocorticoid replacement adjustment in a patient on long term steroid replacement who presents with vomiting and cannot keep tablets down
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 41-year-old man with a ten year history of primary adrenal insufficiency arrives with eighteen hours of vomiting and watery stools after a family barbecue. He took his morning hydrocortisone but vomited within twenty minutes and has kept nothing down since, including his afternoon dose and his fludrocortisone.

He is alert and answering fully, with dry mucous membranes and a capillary refill of three seconds. His pulse rate is 108 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg lying and 78/50 mmHg on standing, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air and temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius. Bedside glucose is 4.1 mmol/L. Sodium is 129 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2) and creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110), up from a baseline of 76. He carries an emergency card and an ampoule of hydrocortisone he has not used.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg lying and 78/50 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill three seconds, abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 129 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110), glucose 4.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give 100 mg hydrocortisone intravenously now and restrict fluids given the sodium of 129 mmol/L
Give 100 mg hydrocortisone intravenously now and start intravenous sodium chloride 0.9 per cent
Give a double dose of oral hydrocortisone now and observe him for four hours before deciding
Give intravenous fluids and antiemetics now and take a random cortisol before any steroid
Give calcium gluconate and an insulin dextrose infusion now for the potassium of 5.4 mmol/L

subtopic_detail: interpreting pleural fluid biochemistry when the serum protein is low enough to make the absolute fluid protein misleading
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 69-year-old man admitted with four weeks of increasing breathlessness. He has alcohol related cirrhosis and has had two previous admissions for ascites, and he stopped drinking eight months ago. He has smoked twenty cigarettes daily for forty years.

A chest radiograph shows a moderate right pleural effusion, and you perform a diagnostic aspiration. The pleural fluid protein is 28 g/L and pleural lactate dehydrogenase is 176 units/L. His serum protein is 48 g/L (60-80), serum albumin 24 g/L (35-50) and serum lactate dehydrogenase is 310 units/L (120-250). Pleural fluid appearance is straw coloured, pleural glucose is 5.2 mmol/L, and the pleural fluid cell count shows a lymphocyte predominance. There is no fever and the white cell count is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Stony dull percussion note and reduced breath sounds at the right base, moderate ascites, no peripheral stigmata of malignancy
data_table.Pleural fluid: Protein 28 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 176 units/L, glucose 5.2 mmol/L, lymphocyte predominant, straw coloured
data_table.Serum: Protein 48 g/L (60-80), albumin 24 g/L (35-50), lactate dehydrogenase 310 units/L (120-250)

lead_in: How should you classify this effusion and what follows from it?

options.text: Indeterminate, because the glucose is 5.2 mmol/L, so repeat the aspiration in seventy two hours
Exudative, because the fluid protein exceeds 30 g/L, so arrange pleural biopsy
Exudative, because the fluid to serum protein ratio exceeds 0.5, so investigate for malignancy
Transudative, because the fluid to serum lactate dehydrogenase ratio is below 0.6, so treat the ascites
Transudative, because the serum albumin is 24 g/L, so start diuretics and repeat the radiograph

subtopic_detail: fitness to hold a commercial vehicle licence in a driver with severe sleep apnoea who reports falling asleep at the wheel
stem:
You are the general physician seeing a 52-year-old man referred by his general practitioner. He drives a semi-trailer on the interstate route and holds a commercial licence. His wife reports loud snoring with witnessed pauses, and he tells you that three weeks ago he crossed the rumble strip after nodding off on a straight stretch near Dubbo, and that he now stops for coffee every ninety minutes to stay awake.

His body mass index is 38 kg/m2, neck circumference 46 cm, and his Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 17 out of 24. A laboratory polysomnogram performed last week shows an apnoea hypopnoea index of 48 events per hour with oxygen desaturation to 78 per cent. His thyroid function and haemoglobin are within normal limits, and he takes no sedating medication. He tells you he cannot afford to stop driving and asks you to keep this between the two of you.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 38 kg/m2, neck circumference 46 cm, Mallampati class 4, no retrognathia
data_table.Investigations: Polysomnography: apnoea hypopnoea index 48 per hour, minimum SpO2 78 per cent; thyroid function and haemoglobin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Arrange bariatric surgery referral and defer any driving decision until the weight has fallen
Respect his request for confidentiality and review him in the clinic again in three months
Prescribe modafinil for residual sleepiness and permit continued driving under regular review
Start continuous positive airway pressure and advise him not to drive commercially until treated
Start continuous positive airway pressure and allow driving with a two hourly rest break schedule

subtopic_detail: reversal strategy for a supratherapeutic warfarin level accompanied by intracranial bleeding rather than isolated laboratory derangement
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department resuscitation bay. A 74-year-old woman on warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve was found on her bathroom floor by her son about an hour ago. She had struck her head on the vanity, and she now opens her eyes to voice, is confused in speech and localises to pain.

Her pulse rate is 58 per minute, blood pressure 178/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air and temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. A non-contrast computed tomography of the head performed ten minutes ago shows a 12 mm right subdural collection with 4 mm of midline shift. Her international normalised ratio is 5.8, haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), platelets 210 x10^9/L (150-400) and creatinine 88 micromol/L (45-90). She last took warfarin yesterday evening and the neurosurgical team has been called.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 58 per minute, blood pressure 178/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Glasgow Coma Scale 12, pupils equal and reactive, no limb weakness, boggy right parietal scalp haematoma
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 5.8, haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), platelets 210 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 88 micromol/L (45-90)
data_table.Imaging: Non-contrast head computed tomography: 12 mm right subdural collection with 4 mm midline shift

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reversal strategy?

options.text: Prothrombin complex concentrate alone, withholding vitamin K given her mechanical mitral valve
Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg with intravenous vitamin K 5 to 10 mg given together now
Intravenous vitamin K 5 to 10 mg alone with a repeat international normalised ratio in six hours
Withhold warfarin and give tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously with a repeat scan in six hours
Prothrombin complex concentrate with intravenous vitamin K 5 to 10 mg given together now

subtopic_detail: selecting an anticoagulant for a first venous thrombosis occurring during chemotherapy for an upper gastrointestinal tumour
stem:
You are the medical registrar on the oncology ward. A 63-year-old woman receiving her third cycle of chemotherapy for a locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma reports three days of left calf swelling and aching. A compression ultrasound confirms thrombus extending from the popliteal into the superficial femoral vein, with no involvement above the common femoral vein.

She has no chest pain or breathlessness, and her observations are within normal limits. Her platelet count is 96 x10^9/L (150-400), haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155), creatinine 71 micromol/L (45-90) and liver function tests are within normal limits. She has had two episodes of vomiting in the four days since her last cycle and describes intermittent epigastric discomfort, and an endoscopy six weeks ago showed a friable ulcerated tumour at the gastro-oesophageal junction. She takes no antiplatelet agent.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Left calf 4 cm greater in circumference than the right, mild pitting oedema to mid-calf, no chest signs
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 96 x10^9/L (150-400), haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155), creatinine 71 micromol/L (45-90), liver function within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Compression ultrasound: thrombus in left popliteal and superficial femoral veins, common femoral vein patent

lead_in: Which anticoagulation regimen would you start?

options.text: Therapeutic weight adjusted low molecular weight heparin given once daily by subcutaneous injection
Therapeutic oral rivaroxaban using the standard loading schedule then the maintenance dose
Therapeutic oral warfarin bridged with low molecular weight heparin until the target range is reached
Prophylactic dose low molecular weight heparin given the platelet count of 96 x10^9/L
Retrievable inferior vena cava filter insertion with anticoagulation deferred until platelets recover

subtopic_detail: interpreting a positive interferon gamma release assay before starting tumour necrosis factor inhibitor therapy in an asymptomatic patient
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar in a combined clinic with rheumatology. A 44-year-old man who moved from Vietnam eleven years ago has rheumatoid arthritis that has failed methotrexate and leflunomide, and the plan is to start adalimumab. He has no cough, no fever, no night sweats and no weight loss, and he has gained 3 kg over the past year.

His pre-treatment screening shows a positive interferon gamma release assay. A chest radiograph is reported as showing no parenchymal abnormality, no cavitation and no apical scarring. He received bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccination as an infant. Three induced sputum specimens collected for completeness are negative on acid fast smear and remain negative on culture at six weeks. His liver function tests and full blood count are within normal limits, and his alcohol intake is two standard drinks weekly.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical small joint synovitis of the hands, chest clear on auscultation, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Interferon gamma release assay positive, three sputum acid fast smears negative, cultures negative at six weeks, liver function and full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph: no parenchymal abnormality, no cavitation, no apical scarring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management before adalimumab is started?

options.text: Proceed with adalimumab now and monitor symptoms with a chest radiograph every six months
Treat for latent infection with isoniazid and pyridoxine for nine months, starting adalimumab after four weeks
Treat for active disease with four drug therapy for six months, starting adalimumab after completion
Attribute the assay result to prior bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccination and proceed directly to adalimumab
Repeat the assay in three months and defer any decision about adalimumab until that result returns

subtopic_detail: recognising when a rapidly progressive lower limb soft tissue infection requires theatre rather than escalation of intravenous antibiotics
stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, admitted eight hours ago with a red swollen left leg and started on intravenous flucloxacillin, has a marked border that advanced 8 cm.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 92/54 mmHg, T 38.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Dusky calf, two new tense blisters, woody induration, pain out of proportion
data_table.Investigations: White cells 24.1 x10^9/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, creatine kinase 1840 units/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin tazobactam
Measure compartment pressures and elevate the limb
Call the surgical team for immediate operative exploration
Urgent magnetic resonance imaging to confirm fascial involvement
Calculate the laboratory risk indicator score and reassess

subtopic_detail: choice and pace of parenteral blood pressure lowering when very high pressure is accompanied by acute pulmonary oedema
stem: A 66-year-old woman has two hours of severe breathlessness that woke her from sleep and forced her upright. She stopped her amlodipine six weeks ago when the packet ran out.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112 /min, BP 226/128 mmHg, RR 34 /min, SpO2 86% room air
data_table.Examination: Accessory muscle use, crackles to mid zones, third heart sound
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph bilateral alveolar opacification

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Oral captopril 25 mg, repeating the pressure in thirty minutes
Intravenous labetalol boluses to normalise the pressure within the hour
Intravenous morphine with oxygen and her usual amlodipine restarted
Titrated intravenous glyceryl trinitrate with non-invasive ventilation
Intravenous furosemide 80 mg alone with high flow oxygen

subtopic_detail: preparing a patient for aldosterone to renin ratio testing when their current antihypertensives interfere with the result
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar in the hypertension clinic. A 46-year-old woman has had blood pressure above 160/100 mmHg for three years despite perindopril, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide taken together at maximal tolerated doses, and home readings confirm the clinic values. She has had two episodes of muscle cramps and her potassium has twice been recorded at 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2) without any potassium losing illness.

Her sodium is 143 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90) and bicarbonate 30 mmol/L (22-32). Renal artery imaging performed last year was reported as normal, plasma metanephrines were within normal limits, and an overnight dexamethasone suppression test was normal. She has no family history of early stroke and takes no liquorice, no non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and no oral contraceptive. You plan to measure the aldosterone to renin ratio.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 168/104 mmHg, other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No cushingoid features, no abdominal bruit, no radiofemoral delay
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2) on two occasions, sodium 143 mmol/L (135-145), bicarbonate 30 mmol/L (22-32), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90)
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide at maximal tolerated doses

lead_in: How should you prepare her for the test?

options.text: Measure the ratio now on her current three agents without first correcting the potassium
Start spironolactone for the hypokalaemia and measure the ratio once the potassium has normalised
Proceed to adrenal vein sampling first since the biochemical picture already indicates the diagnosis
Collect a twenty four hour urinary aldosterone instead and continue her current three agents unchanged
Replace potassium, stop the thiazide for four weeks and substitute verapamil or prazosin for control

subtopic_detail: switching opioid route and drug when oral morphine causes intolerable toxicity in a patient whose renal function is falling
stem:
You are the palliative care registrar reviewing a 71-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer and painful bone disease in the sacrum and femur. He has been taking slow release oral morphine twice daily with immediate release breakthrough doses, and his pain had been well controlled for two months.

Over the past four days his family report that he twitches at rest, plucks at the bedclothes, and sees a cat at the end of the bed that is not there. He is more drowsy but rousable and his pain score has actually risen from three to seven. His creatinine has risen from 92 to 214 micromol/L (60-110) with a urea of 18 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), and his estimated glomerular filtration rate is 24 mL/min/1.73m2. His calcium corrected for albumin is 2.38 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), sodium and glucose are within normal limits, and he is not febrile. He takes no anticholinergic medication and has had no change in his other drugs.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, multifocal myoclonus at rest, visual hallucinations reported, pupils 2 mm and reactive
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 214 micromol/L (60-110) up from 92, urea 18 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73m2, corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.15-2.60)
data_table.Medications: Slow release oral morphine twice daily with immediate release breakthrough, docusate and senna, no anticholinergics

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to his analgesia?

options.text: Rotate to subcutaneous hydromorphone at a reduced equianalgesic dose and give intravenous fluids
Increase the slow release morphine by fifty per cent because his reported pain score has risen
Add regular oral haloperidol for the hallucinations and continue the morphine at its present dose
Give intravenous naloxone in titrated doses to reverse the sedation and continue the current regimen
Stop all opioid and manage his bone pain with regular paracetamol and a non-steroidal agent

subtopic_detail: distinguishing two antibody mediated causes of proximal weakness when the reflex pattern and the response to exertion disagree with the usual teaching
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar assessing a 64-year-old man referred with four months of difficulty rising from a low chair and climbing the stairs at his farm gate. He has smoked thirty cigarettes daily since his twenties and has lost 6 kg without trying.

He describes a dry mouth that has made him carry water everywhere, and erectile difficulty that started around the same time as the weakness. He denies double vision, and his speech and swallowing are unaffected. On examination his hip flexors and shoulder abductors are graded four out of five, and his knee reflexes are absent on first testing but become detectable after he holds a sustained quadriceps contraction for fifteen seconds. Strength in the hip flexors is slightly better after brief maximal exertion than at rest. There is no ptosis and no fatigable weakness of eye closure. Creatine kinase, thyroid function and inflammatory markers are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Proximal weakness four out of five at hips and shoulders, no ptosis, no ophthalmoplegia, dry oral mucosa
data_table.Reflexes: Knee reflexes absent at rest, detectable after fifteen seconds of sustained contraction
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase, thyroid function and inflammatory markers within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Steroid myopathy from unrecognised exogenous glucocorticoid exposure over recent months
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome associated with an underlying small cell lung carcinoma
Generalised myasthenia gravis with antibodies to the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor
Polymyositis with symmetrical proximal inflammatory muscle involvement of the limb girdles
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with proximal and distal involvement

subtopic_detail: choosing first symptomatic therapy for newly diagnosed parkinsonism in an older patient whose occupation depends on fine motor control
stem:
You are the general physician in a movement disorder clinic. A 74-year-old retired watchmaker who still repairs clocks for a local dealer describes eighteen months of a right hand tremor that is worst when the hand rests in his lap and settles when he reaches for a tool. His wife says his handwriting has shrunk and he no longer swings his right arm when walking.

On examination there is a four hertz rest tremor of the right hand, cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist that increases when he taps his left hand, and decrement in amplitude on repetitive finger tapping. His gait is slightly stooped with reduced right arm swing and normal stride length. There is no early postural instability, no vertical gaze restriction, no cerebellar sign and no orthostatic drop in blood pressure. His Montreal Cognitive Assessment is 28 out of 30 and there are no visual hallucinations. He takes no antiemetic and no antipsychotic, and his symptoms now interfere with his repair work.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits, no postural blood pressure drop
data_table.Examination: Four hertz right hand rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist with contralateral activation, decrementing finger tapping, reduced right arm swing
data_table.Cognition: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 28 out of 30, no hallucinations
data_table.Medications: No antiemetic, antipsychotic or other dopamine blocking drug

lead_in: Which initial symptomatic therapy would you recommend?

options.text: A monoamine oxidase B inhibitor such as rasagiline as monotherapy at the standard daily dose
Deferring drug therapy with physiotherapy and review in six months given his preserved gait
Levodopa with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor, titrated slowly from a low starting dose
A non-ergot dopamine agonist such as pramipexole, titrated slowly from a low starting dose
An anticholinergic such as benzhexol, titrated slowly from a low starting dose for the tremor

subtopic_detail: sequencing haematinic replacement when macrocytic anaemia is accompanied by posterior column signs and both vitamin levels are low
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 58-year-old woman in the assessment unit with three months of tiredness and unsteadiness that is worse in the dark. She has vitiligo and treated hypothyroidism and follows a strict vegan diet begun eleven years ago.

She describes pins and needles in both feet that has crept up to mid-calf. On examination vibration sense is absent at both ankles and reduced at the knees, joint position sense is impaired at both great toes, and Romberg is positive. Reflexes are brisk at the knees with extensor plantar responses. Her haemoglobin is 96 g/L (115-155) with a mean cell volume of 112 fL (80-100), and the film shows hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum vitamin B12 is 84 pmol/L (150-700) and red cell folate is 220 nmol/L (>360). Thyroid function is within normal limits on her current thyroxine dose and there is no alcohol history.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Absent ankle vibration sense, impaired great toe joint position sense, positive Romberg, brisk knee reflexes with extensor plantars
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 112 fL (80-100), hypersegmented neutrophils on film, vitamin B12 84 pmol/L (150-700), red cell folate 220 nmol/L (>360)
data_table.Background: Vegan diet for eleven years, vitiligo, treated hypothyroidism with normal thyroid function

lead_in: How should you start replacement?

options.text: High dose oral cyanocobalamin now with oral folic acid added after the first week of treatment
Transfuse two units of packed red cells now and commence both vitamins once the haemoglobin is safe
Withhold both vitamins until intrinsic factor antibody and gastroscopy results clarify the cause
Intramuscular hydroxocobalamin now with oral folic acid added only after the cobalamin is running
Oral folic acid 5 mg daily now with cobalamin added once the blood count has begun to respond

subtopic_detail: headache with papilloedema in a young woman on a drug that is itself a recognised precipitant of raised pressure
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 27-year-old woman referred by her optometrist. She has had a daily headache for seven weeks that is worse on waking and when she bends forward, and twice this week her vision has greyed out completely for a few seconds when she stood up quickly. She also describes a rhythmic whooshing in her right ear that matches her pulse.

Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2 and she started oral isotretinoin for acne four months ago. Fundoscopy shows bilateral disc swelling with blurred margins and loss of spontaneous venous pulsation. Visual acuity is 6/6 in each eye and formal perimetry shows an enlarged blind spot bilaterally with no other field defect. There is no focal neurological deficit and no fever. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with venography is reported as showing no mass lesion, no hydrocephalus and patent dural venous sinuses.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bilateral papilloedema with absent venous pulsation, visual acuity 6/6 both eyes, no focal deficit, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: Perimetry: bilateral enlarged blind spot only
data_table.Imaging: Magnetic resonance brain with venography: no mass, no hydrocephalus, patent dural venous sinuses

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start acetazolamide and arrange outpatient neurology review in six weeks without further testing
Stop the isotretinoin and review the discs in three months with repeat visual field testing
Arrange urgent computed tomography venography to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
Refer for optic nerve sheath fenestration now given the presence of bilateral disc swelling
Lumbar puncture with measurement of the opening pressure and cerebrospinal fluid analysis

subtopic_detail: separating a delayed multiorgan drug hypersensitivity from the epidermal detachment syndromes when both a rash and a fever follow a new anticonvulsant
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to see a 33-year-old man admitted with fever and a rash. He was started on lamotrigine five weeks ago after a first unprovoked seizure and the dose was escalated over that period.

He has a confluent morbilliform eruption covering about 70 per cent of his body surface with marked facial swelling, particularly periorbital. The rash is not tender, Nikolsky sign is negative, and there are no erosions on the lips, conjunctivae or genitals. His pulse rate is 106 per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air and temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius. Bloods show white cells 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with eosinophils 2.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), alanine aminotransferase 384 units/L (5-40), alkaline phosphatase 180 units/L (30-110), creatinine 138 micromol/L (60-110) and atypical lymphocytes on the film. There is bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 106 per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform rash over 70 per cent body surface, marked periorbital and facial oedema, negative Nikolsky sign, no mucosal erosions, bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: White cells 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), eosinophils 2.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), alanine aminotransferase 384 units/L (5-40), creatinine 138 micromol/L (60-110), atypical lymphocytes on film

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and start systemic corticosteroid with organ monitoring for at least several weeks
Cease lamotrigine and transfer to a burns unit for management of epidermal detachment
Continue lamotrigine at a reduced dose with antihistamine and emollient for a benign drug rash
Cease lamotrigine and start intravenous immunoglobulin as the primary immunomodulatory therapy
Cease lamotrigine and treat empirically for acute Epstein-Barr virus infection with supportive care

subtopic_detail: managing a catecholamine crisis precipitated in a patient already taking a beta blocker before the diagnosis was suspected
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the ward. A 49-year-old woman admitted yesterday for investigation of episodic palpitations, drenching sweats and headaches was started on metoprolol 50 mg twice daily last night by the covering doctor for a presumed tachyarrhythmia. She had a computed tomography of the abdomen with contrast this morning.

Thirty minutes after returning from the scan she became acutely unwell with a crushing headache, pallor and vomiting. Her pulse rate is 128 per minute, blood pressure 248/142 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute, SpO2 92 per cent on room air and temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius. She has bibasal crackles and a third heart sound. The scan report describes a 5 cm right adrenal mass with an unenhanced attenuation of 38 Hounsfield units and marked heterogeneous enhancement. Her plasma free metanephrines, sent yesterday, have just returned at more than six times the upper limit of normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 per minute, blood pressure 248/142 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute, SpO2 92 per cent room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale, diaphoretic, bibasal inspiratory crackles, third heart sound, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Plasma free metanephrines more than six times the upper limit of normal
data_table.Imaging: Computed tomography abdomen: 5 cm right adrenal mass, unenhanced attenuation 38 Hounsfield units, heterogeneous enhancement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological management?

options.text: Start an intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion alone and withhold any further adrenergic blockade
Start intravenous phentolamine and continue the beta blocker once alpha blockade is established
Increase the metoprolol dose and add intravenous furosemide for the pulmonary congestion present
Start intravenous labetalol, relying on its combined alpha and beta receptor blocking activity
Start oral phenoxybenzamine and arrange surgical resection of the adrenal mass within the week

subtopic_detail: deciding on timing of valve surgery when embolic and haemodynamic indications conflict with a very recent cerebral event
stem: A 52-year-old man on day six of benzylpenicillin for viridans streptococcal endocarditis of a bicuspid aortic valve developed left arm and leg weakness this morning.

data_table.Examination: Alert, stable left hemiparesis, bibasal crackles, raised jugular venous pressure
data_table.Imaging: CT brain 2 cm right middle cerebral artery infarct, no haemorrhage
data_table.Echocardiography: 16 mm mobile aortic vegetation, severe regurgitation, premature mitral valve closure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation about valve surgery?

options.text: Avoid surgery and anticoagulate to prevent further embolism
Delay seventy two hours and repeat the brain imaging
Proceed to surgery now despite the recent infarct
Delay four weeks to avoid haemorrhagic transformation
Delay until the antibiotic course is complete

subtopic_detail: responding to a sodium rise that has exceeded the safe daily limit partway through correction of chronic hyponatraemia
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 63-year-old woman admitted eighteen hours ago. She had been drinking heavily for years, eating little, and taking a thiazide started three months ago. Her admission sodium was 104 mmol/L (135-145) with a serum osmolality of 228 mmol/kg, urine osmolality 96 mmol/kg and urine sodium 12 mmol/L. She was confused but had no seizure.

She was given a single 100 mL bolus of hypertonic saline for confusion, the thiazide was ceased, and she then received 1 litre of sodium chloride 0.9 per cent. Over the past few hours her urine output has risen to 380 mL per hour and is dilute. Her sodium is now 121 mmol/L, having risen 17 mmol/L in eighteen hours. She is alert and orientated with no focal neurological deficit, her observations are within normal limits, and her potassium and glucose are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated, no focal neurological deficit, mucous membranes moist, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Admission sodium 104 mmol/L (135-145), current sodium 121 mmol/L, serum osmolality 228 mmol/kg on admission, urine osmolality 96 mmol/kg, urine sodium 12 mmol/L
data_table.Fluid balance: Urine output 380 mL per hour and dilute over the past few hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Give a further 100 mL bolus of hypertonic saline because the sodium remains below 125 mmol/L
Restrict fluid to 800 mL daily and recheck the sodium in six hours without other intervention
Give a tolvaptan dose to control the free water handling and recheck the sodium in four hours
Give desmopressin with 5 per cent dextrose to relower the sodium toward the intended daily target
Continue the current plan unchanged because she is alert with no neurological deficit at present

subtopic_detail: sequencing adjunctive corticosteroid against the first antibiotic dose in suspected adult bacterial meningitis awaiting imaging
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department at 3 am. A 54-year-old man has been brought in by his wife with 12 hours of headache, fever and neck stiffness, and she says he has become progressively harder to rouse over the past two hours.

He opens his eyes to voice, is confused in his speech, and localises to pain. He has no rash, no focal limb weakness and no papilloedema on fundoscopy, but given his reduced conscious level the department protocol requires computed tomography of the head before a lumbar puncture, and the radiographer has been called in from home with an expected delay of about 40 minutes. He takes no immunosuppressive medication, has no history of central nervous system disease and has had no recent overseas travel. Blood cultures have been taken and two cannulas are in place.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112, blood pressure 138/82, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96 per cent in air, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 12, neck stiffness present, no rash, no focal neurological deficit, no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 21.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 248 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 3.1 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2), blood cultures taken
data_table.Logistics: Computed tomography of the head required before lumbar puncture, expected delay approximately 40 minutes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Await the computed tomography and lumbar puncture results before giving any antimicrobial therapy
Give ceftriaxone with intravenous aciclovir now and withhold corticosteroid entirely
Give vancomycin with meropenem now and add dexamethasone after the lumbar puncture is performed
Give dexamethasone with the first dose of ceftriaxone and benzylpenicillin now
Give ceftriaxone and benzylpenicillin now and add dexamethasone once the culture confirms the organism

subtopic_detail: choosing the imaging modality for suspected inflammatory back pain in a young adult whose plain films are normal
stem: A 26-year-old man has four years of low back pain with an hour of morning stiffness. It improves with activity, wakes him after midnight and worsens with rest. He had a painful red eye treated with drops last year.

data_table.Examination: Modified Schober 3.5 cm, tenderness over both sacroiliac joints
data_table.Imaging: Radiographs of the pelvis normal

options.text: Computed tomography of both sacroiliac joints for erosion

Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine for disc disease

Magnetic resonance imaging of both sacroiliac joints with STIR

subtopic_detail: deciding anticoagulation duration after a first pulmonary embolism with no identifiable provoking factor
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 47-year-old man in clinic three months after a segmental pulmonary embolism. He has completed three months of apixaban and is asking whether he can stop.

His embolism followed no surgery, no immobilisation, no long haul flight, no trauma and no hospital admission, and he had no active malignancy on a thorough review including up to date bowel screening. He has had no bleeding on treatment, is fully active and back at work as an electrician, and his exercise tolerance has returned to normal. His full blood count, renal and liver function are within normal limits. There is no family history of venous thromboembolism. His echocardiogram at diagnosis showed a normal right ventricle and he has no residual breathlessness.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no calf swelling or tenderness, no signs of chronic liver disease
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal and liver function within normal limits; no bleeding events on treatment
data_table.Event details: First segmental pulmonary embolism with no surgery, immobilisation, travel, trauma or malignancy identified; normal right ventricle on echocardiography

lead_in: What would you recommend about the duration of his anticoagulation?

options.text: Continue extended anticoagulation indefinitely with periodic review of bleeding risk and benefit
Stop anticoagulation now, since three months is a complete course for a first event
Extend anticoagulation to a total of six months and then stop without further review
Stop anticoagulation and perform a full thrombophilia screen to guide any further treatment
Stop anticoagulation and commence aspirin 100 mg daily as long term secondary prevention

subtopic_detail: choosing between treatment regimens for latent infection in a person about to start a biologic agent
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar in a pre-biologic screening clinic. A 39-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is due to start a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor and has been screened as part of that workup.

She moved to Australia from Vietnam at age 22 and has no history of tuberculosis treatment or known contact. She is entirely asymptomatic with no cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss. Her interferon gamma release assay is positive, and her chest radiograph shows no parenchymal abnormality, no cavitation, no pleural thickening and no calcified nodes. Two sputum samples induced for completeness are smear negative and cultures are pending at six weeks with no growth to date. Her liver function and full blood count are within normal limits, she takes methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid, and she is not pregnant and is using reliable contraception.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no lymphadenopathy, weight stable, synovitis in both wrists
data_table.Investigations: Interferon gamma release assay positive, liver function and full blood count within normal limits, two induced sputum samples smear negative with cultures showing no growth at six weeks
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph with no parenchymal abnormality, cavitation, pleural thickening or calcified nodes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management before she starts the biologic?

options.text: Perform a tuberculin skin test to confirm the result before committing her to any treatment
Treat for latent infection with isoniazid and pyridoxine, with monthly clinical and liver review
Treat with a four drug regimen of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for six months
Proceed with the biologic now and monitor with a chest radiograph every three months
Repeat the interferon gamma release assay in three months and treat only if it remains positive

subtopic_detail: prioritising which of several contributing medicines to withdraw first after recurrent falls in an older adult
stem: An 84-year-old woman has had three falls in two months, the last fracturing her wrist, and feels lightheaded standing at night. She takes amitriptyline 25 mg nightly for eleven years, temazepam 10 mg most nights for six years, perindopril, atorvastatin and paracetamol.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/78 mmHg sitting, 108/62 after 3 minutes standing
data_table.Examination: Timed up and go 18 seconds, dry mouth

lead_in: Which medication change would you prioritise first?

options.text: Cease the atorvastatin, since statin myopathy contributes to falls
Add fludrocortisone daily for the postural hypotension
Taper and cease the amitriptyline for anticholinergic burden
Taper and cease the temazepam, the strongest single drug risk
Cease the perindopril, the usual cause of postural hypotension

subtopic_detail: setting oxygenation and carbon dioxide targets in the first hours after return of spontaneous circulation in a comatose survivor
stem: A 58-year-old man is comatose and ventilated 90 minutes after an out of hospital ventricular fibrillation arrest. His right coronary artery has been stented and he is on low dose noradrenaline.

options.text: Keep the oxygen at 1.0 and increase minute volume further
Reduce the oxygen to normal saturation and increase minute volume
Reduce the oxygen to target saturation 88 to 92 per cent
