subtopic_detail: sequencing blockade before surgery in a patient with episodic hypertension whose beta blocker was started first
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 44-year-old man referred with hypertension resistant to three agents. He describes episodes two or three times a week lasting about 20 minutes in which he sweats through his shirt, his heart pounds and he develops a severe throbbing headache, and he says he feels a sense of doom during them.

His general practitioner started metoprolol 50 mg twice daily nine days ago and he reports that since then the episodes have felt worse, with higher readings on his home monitor. His plasma free metanephrines are four times the upper reference limit on two separate occasions, and computed tomography shows a 4.2 cm right adrenal mass with an unenhanced attenuation of 38 Hounsfield units. Surgery has been discussed with the endocrine surgeons and he has no chest pain, no cardiac failure and a normal echocardiogram.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, blood pressure 178/104, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale and diaphoretic during an episode observed in clinic, no thyroid enlargement, no abdominal bruit, no neurocutaneous stigmata
data_table.Investigations: Plasma free metanephrines four times the upper reference limit on two occasions, potassium and renal function within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Computed tomography shows a 4.2 cm right adrenal mass with unenhanced attenuation of 38 Hounsfield units

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Continue the metoprolol, add phenoxybenzamine, and proceed to surgery once the blood pressure settles
Continue the metoprolol, add amlodipine, and proceed to adrenalectomy within the next week
Cease the metoprolol, arrange metaiodobenzylguanidine scintigraphy, and defer any blockade until it returns
Cease the metoprolol, arrange adrenal vein sampling, and commence spironolactone while awaiting results
Cease the metoprolol, commence phenoxybenzamine, and add a beta blocker later once blockade is established

subtopic_detail: separating two severe cutaneous adverse reactions when the rash appeared six weeks after an anticonvulsant was started
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 36-year-old woman with a widespread rash and fever. She started lamotrigine six weeks ago for bipolar disorder and the dose was escalated more quickly than the recommended schedule.

The rash began on her trunk four days ago and has spread to her limbs and face, and she says her face feels tight and swollen. There is no blistering anywhere, no skin pain and no ulceration of her mouth, eyes or genitals, and Nikolsky sign is negative. Her white cell count is 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) with eosinophils of 1.8 x10^9/L (0.0 to 0.5) and atypical lymphocytes reported on the film. Her alanine aminotransferase is 384 U/L (less than 35) with a bilirubin of 24 micromol/L (less than 20), her creatinine is 118 micromol/L (45 to 90), and her thyroid function is within normal limits today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Widespread confluent morbilliform eruption over trunk, limbs and face with facial oedema; no blistering, no mucosal ulceration, Nikolsky sign negative; cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), eosinophils 1.8 x10^9/L (0.0 to 0.5), atypical lymphocytes on film, alanine aminotransferase 384 U/L (less than 35), creatinine 118 micromol/L (45 to 90)
data_table.Medication: Lamotrigine commenced 6 weeks ago with faster than recommended dose escalation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and commence systemic corticosteroid with monitoring of liver and renal function
Cease lamotrigine and transfer to a burns unit for management of epidermal detachment
Continue lamotrigine with oral antihistamine and topical corticosteroid for a simple drug eruption
Cease lamotrigine and commence intravenous immunoglobulin as the primary treatment
Cease lamotrigine and start broad spectrum antibiotics for presumed sepsis with a reactive rash

subtopic_detail: interpreting pleural fluid biochemistry that meets exudative criteria in a patient already treated with diuretics for heart failure
stem: A 78-year-old woman with heart failure has had intravenous furosemide for four days, losing 5 kg. Her breathlessness has improved but a right pleural effusion persists, and you aspirate it.

data_table.Examination: Stony dullness at the right base, afebrile
data_table.Pleural fluid: Straw coloured, protein 32 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 168 U/L
data_table.Serum: Protein 62 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 290 U/L with upper reference limit 250 U/L, albumin 33 g/L, CRP 4 mg/L

options.text: Withhold diuretic and repeat the aspiration in 48 hours
Calculate the serum to pleural albumin gradient before acting
Refer for thoracoscopic biopsy, as the fluid is exudative
Insert an intercostal catheter to drain the effusion fully

subtopic_detail: distinguishing two neuromuscular junction disorders when strength improves rather than fatigues on repeated effort
stem:
You are the neurology registrar assessing a 63-year-old man with six months of difficulty rising from low chairs and climbing the stairs at home. He has smoked 40 cigarettes a day for 45 years.

He describes a dry mouth that he attributes to his blood pressure tablets and says he has become constipated. His eyelids are not droopy and he has no double vision, no difficulty chewing and no change to his voice or swallowing. On examination his hip flexors and shoulder abductors are graded 4 out of 5, and his knee and ankle reflexes are absent at rest. After he performs 15 seconds of maximal quadriceps contraction, you re-test the knee reflex and it is present, and his hip flexion strength is briefly graded 5 out of 5. His chest radiograph is reported as showing a right hilar fullness of uncertain significance.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Proximal limb weakness graded 4 out of 5 at hip flexors and shoulder abductors, areflexia at rest with reflexes returning after sustained contraction, no ptosis, no ophthalmoplegia, no bulbar weakness, dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase, thyroid function, electrolytes and full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph shows right hilar fullness of uncertain significance

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine to assess for a compressive myelopathy
Nerve conduction studies looking for a demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy
Computed tomography of the chest with voltage gated calcium channel antibody testing
Acetylcholine receptor antibody testing with computed tomography of the mediastinum for thymoma
Muscle biopsy of the vastus lateralis with immunohistochemistry for an inflammatory myopathy

subtopic_detail: Indication for urgent haemodialysis in acute kidney injury with hyperkalaemia refractory to medical therapy
stem: A 68-year-old man on day 4 of admission for pneumonia has acute kidney injury. Perindopril and spironolactone were stopped on day 2. He is breathless with palpitations.

data_table.Fluid status: JVP 6 cm, crackles, urine 20 mL in 4 h
data_table.Bloods: K 6.8 mmol/L (6.2 yesterday), bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, pH 7.20
data_table.ECG: Peaked T waves, QRS 130 ms, bradycardia
data_table.Given in the last 30 min: Calcium gluconate, salbutamol, insulin with dextrose, sodium bicarbonate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent haemodialysis via a femoral vascular catheter
Repeat calcium gluconate and insulin with dextrose in 30 minutes
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g with furosemide 80 mg
Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10 g with calcium gluconate
Continuous nebulised salbutamol with sodium bicarbonate

subtopic_detail: Adult acute pyelonephritis empirical therapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 34-year-old woman with 2 days of right flank pain, rigors, and vomiting. She reports urinary frequency and dysuria since yesterday. She has no medical history, no known allergies, is not pregnant (urine bhCG negative), and takes only the combined oral contraceptive pill.

On examination she is flushed with right costovertebral angle tenderness. Pulse 108, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C. Urinalysis shows leucocytes 3+, nitrites positive, blood 2+. Urine and blood cultures are collected. Full blood count shows white cell count 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), creatinine 82 micromol/L (45 to 90), lactate 1.8 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2). She is able to tolerate oral fluids after antiemetic but still has rigors.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 108/68 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 98% RA, temp 38.9
data_table.Bloods: WCC 16.2 x10^9/L; creatinine 82 micromol/L; lactate 1.8 mmol/L
data_table.Cultures: Urine and blood cultures collected before antibiotics

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen at this point?

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg every 6 hours for 10 days with early GP review at 48 hours
Oral trimethoprim 300 mg once daily for 14 days without empirical intravenous cover
Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus oral fluconazole 200 mg for empirical yeast cover
Intravenous gentamicin 5 mg per kg with amoxicillin 2 g every 6 hours pending culture results
Intravenous meropenem 1 g every 8 hours for broad spectrum cover pending culture results

subtopic_detail: Aortic dissection with atypical presentation
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man with 45 minutes of interscapular pain that woke him from sleep. He describes it as tearing, radiating to the left flank, and he vomited once at home. He has hypertension treated with perindopril 5 mg daily, smoked 20 cigarettes daily for 30 years, and quit 4 years ago. His father died aged 62 of a ruptured aorta.

He is diaphoretic. Vital signs are pulse 96 regular, blood pressure 176/104 mmHg right arm and 138/82 mmHg left arm, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.9. Chest auscultation reveals a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. His left radial pulse is diminished compared with the right. ECG shows sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria; no ST elevation. Chest x-ray shows a widened mediastinum. Bedside troponin is not elevated. High-sensitivity D-dimer is 4.2 mg/L (less than 0.5).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP right arm 176/104, BP left arm 138/82, RR 22, SpO2 96% RA, temp 36.9
data_table.Bedside findings: Diaphoretic; diminished left radial pulse; early diastolic murmur LSE
data_table.ECG: Sinus rhythm; LVH by voltage; no ST elevation
data_table.Investigations: Widened mediastinum on CXR; troponin negative; D-dimer 4.2 mg/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Trans thoracic echocardiogram at the bedside to look for aortic root dilatation and regurgitation
Repeat high-sensitivity troponin at 1 hour and reassess for type 2 myocardial infarction cause
Coronary angiography via right radial access to exclude an unstable ostial coronary lesion
Contrast enhanced computed tomography angiography of the aorta from arch to iliac bifurcation now
Magnetic resonance angiography of the aorta with gadolinium contrast within the next 24 hours

subtopic_detail: Adult sepsis hour-1 bundle sequencing
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68-year-old woman transferred from a nursing home with 8 hours of fevers, rigors, and reduced oral intake. She has type 2 diabetes on metformin and a permanent indwelling urinary catheter for neurogenic bladder. On arrival her Glasgow Coma Scale is 14, she is confused about place, and she has cool mottled knees.

Vital signs are pulse 128, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 94% on 4 L nasal prong oxygen, temperature 39.2. Point-of-care venous lactate is 4.6 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2). Bedside creatinine 168 micromol/L (45 to 90) from a rise of 82 last month. Urinalysis of catheter urine is grossly turbid with leucocytes 4+ and nitrites positive. Chest x-ray shows no consolidation. Two intravenous cannulas are in place.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 82/48, RR 26, SpO2 94% 4L NP, temp 39.2
data_table.qSOFA / signs: Altered mentation; SBP below 100; RR above 22
data_table.Bloods: Lactate 4.6 mmol/L; creatinine 168 micromol/L (from 82 last month)
data_table.Source clues: Turbid catheter urine; leucocytes 4+; nitrites positive; CXR clear

lead_in: Within the first hour of recognition, which sequence best reflects the ANZICS-endorsed sepsis bundle?

options.text: Give empirical antibiotics, then start intravenous fluids, then collect blood cultures once stable
Measure lactate, give a 500 mL fluid bolus, arrange CT abdomen, then collect blood cultures before antibiotics
Measure lactate, collect blood cultures, give empirical broad spectrum antibiotics, and commence 30 mL per kg crystalloid
Start noradrenaline infusion immediately then collect cultures and give antibiotics after stabilisation
Commence 250 mL of 4 percent albumin, transfuse packed red cells for haemoglobin above 100, then give antibiotics

subtopic_detail: Massive transfusion protocol activation criteria
stem:
You are the medical registrar coordinating care for a 58-year-old man with cirrhosis brought to the emergency department by ambulance with a 4 hour history of vomiting fresh red blood. He has vomited 3 more times since arrival, each estimated 300 to 400 mL. Ambulance recorded blood pressure 82/48 mmHg and pulse 128 with two 16 gauge cannulas placed en route and 1000 mL of Hartmann's solution infused.

On arrival pulse 132, blood pressure 78/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 96% on 4 L nasal prong oxygen, temperature 35.4 degrees C. He is confused (GCS 13) and peripheries are cold. Bedside haemoglobin 62 g/L (135 to 175), platelets 68 x10^9/L (150 to 400), INR 2.1, fibrinogen 1.1 g/L (2.0 to 4.0), lactate 6.8 mmol/L. You have called endoscopy and given intravenous terlipressin and ceftriaxone. Two units of emergency O negative packed cells are already infusing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132, BP 78/44, RR 26, SpO2 96% 4L NP, temp 35.4, GCS 13
data_table.Prior resuscitation: 1000 mL Hartmann's; 2 units emergency O negative pRBC infusing

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in his resuscitation?

options.text: Continue two more units of O negative packed cells and reassess response after another 500 mL Hartmann's
Activate the massive transfusion protocol and target packed cells, fresh frozen plasma, platelets, and cryoprecipitate
Give a single unit of platelets alone since platelet count is only mildly reduced at 68 x10^9/L
Give intravenous prothrombinex 25 units per kg to correct INR of 2.1 in place of any plasma or platelets
Delay further transfusion until formal cross match is complete to reduce the risk of a haemolytic reaction

subtopic_detail: Unprovoked VTE anticoagulation duration
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 52-year-old man in outpatients 3 months after a right sided segmental pulmonary embolus. There was no preceding surgery, plaster cast, prolonged immobility, hospitalisation, cancer, oestrogen exposure, or long haul travel. He has no personal or family history of thrombosis. His pulmonary embolism was diagnosed on CT pulmonary angiogram after 3 days of pleuritic chest pain; troponin was negative and echocardiogram normal. He has been on apixaban 5 mg twice daily since diagnosis.

Repeat compression ultrasound of the legs is normal. D-dimer measured today after 4 weeks off treatment (planned trial cessation) is 620 micrograms/L (less than 500). Full blood count, renal function, liver function tests, and coagulation studies are within normal limits. He is a non-smoker, drinks 4 standard drinks weekly, has hypertension controlled with perindopril, and works as a physiotherapist. His HAS-BLED score is 1.

data_table.Anticoagulant: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily since diagnosis
data_table.Post-cessation trial D-dimer: 620 micrograms/L (less than 500) after 4 weeks off treatment

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan from this point?

options.text: Stop apixaban permanently now and rely on daily 100 mg aspirin as long term secondary prevention
Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely without dose reduction at any point in the future
Extend apixaban for a further 3 months only then reassess with repeat D-dimer at that time again
Continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily beyond 6 months as extended low intensity secondary prevention
Switch to warfarin with target INR 2 to 3 for at least 10 years then reassess bleeding risk

subtopic_detail: Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 46-year-old man with 5 days of unsteady gait and double vision. He had 3 days of gastroenteritis 3 weeks ago (self limited, no antibiotics). On examination he is alert with normal cognition. Cranial nerve examination shows bilateral partial abduction failure with limitation of upgaze; pupils are 4 mm and sluggishly reactive. Facial strength and swallow are normal. Limb power is 5 out of 5 throughout with normal tone; deep tendon reflexes are absent at both biceps, triceps, knees, and ankles. Plantar responses are downgoing.

Romberg positive; heel-shin dysmetria bilaterally. Vital signs are pulse 82 regular, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C. Bedside single breath count is 32; forced vital capacity 4.1 L. MRI brain and orbits are unremarkable. CSF from lumbar puncture shows protein 0.9 g/L (0.15 to 0.45), white cell count 3 x10^6/L (less than 5), glucose 3.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Peripheral: Areflexia; power 5/5; sensory loss absent; Romberg positive
data_table.CSF: Protein 0.9 g/L; WCC 3 x10^6/L; glucose 3.8 mmol/L

lead_in: Which single specific antibody test is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Anti aquaporin 4 antibody serum titre to distinguish neuromyelitis optica spectrum from other syndromes
Anti acetylcholine receptor antibody assay to confirm myasthenia gravis at a specialised neuroimmunology lab
Anti myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody to characterise a demyelinating central nervous system syndrome
Anti GQ1b IgG serum antibody to confirm the Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome
Anti Hu paraneoplastic antibody panel to look for an underlying small cell lung cancer in the setting

subtopic_detail: Warfarin over-anticoagulation without bleeding
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 74-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve prosthesis maintained on warfarin 5 mg on alternate days with 4 mg on the other days for the past 6 years. She takes no other regular medications. She rings you because a routine INR taken today shows 8.9 (target 2.5 to 3.5 for mechanical mitral valve). She feels well, has no bruising, no gum bleeding, no melaena, no haematuria, and no headache. She reports she started a 5 day course of clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily 4 days ago for a chest infection.

Baseline vital signs 2 weeks ago were pulse 72 regular, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, and today she reports feeling the same. She has an appointment available with her cardiologist next week and lives 15 minutes drive from a public hospital emergency department. She asks what to do now.

data_table.Warfarin regimen: 5 mg on alternate days with 4 mg on other days for 6 years
data_table.Recent medication: Clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily started 4 days ago
data_table.Bleeding: No overt bleeding or headache reported

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step now?

options.text: Continue current warfarin dose and repeat INR in 2 weeks after clarithromycin course completes
Give a single dose of intravenous vitamin K 10 mg via slow infusion at home to reverse anticoagulation now
Administer prothrombinex 25 units per kg with fresh frozen plasma at the general practice today
Withhold two warfarin doses only, without vitamin K, and repeat INR in 3 days at the practice
Withhold warfarin, give 1 mg oral vitamin K1 (phytomenadione), and repeat INR in 24 hours

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection recognition and surgical urgency
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 63-year-old man admitted 6 hours ago with a red painful right lower leg after minor gardening trauma 24 hours earlier. He has type 2 diabetes on metformin. Since arrival his pain has escalated from 4 out of 10 to 9 out of 10 despite oral oxycodone 15 mg and paracetamol 1 g given 90 minutes ago. He now has a tense, waxy area of swelling above the ankle with 2 haemorrhagic bullae, and the skin overlying appears anaesthetic to pinprick testing.

Vital signs deteriorate: pulse 128, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 39.4 degrees C. Bloods: white cell count 22 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), sodium 129 mmol/L (135 to 145), creatinine 178 micromol/L (from 92 last month), glucose 14.2 mmol/L, CRP 348 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 4.4 mmol/L. His LRINEC score is calculated at 9.

data_table.Local findings: Tense waxy swelling; 2 haemorrhagic bullae; skin anaesthesia to pinprick
data_table.Pain trajectory: Escalated from 4/10 to 9/10 despite opioid analgesia
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 96/58, RR 24, SpO2 96% RA, temp 39.4

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate step in management?

options.text: Give intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours and admit for 48 hours of observation before reassessment
Arrange a magnetic resonance imaging scan of the leg to confirm fascial involvement before surgical review
Elevate the limb, apply topical dressings, and mark the erythematous margin for reassessment in 4 hours
Urgent surgical referral for operative exploration with concurrent broad spectrum antibiotics and resuscitation
Refer to hyperbaric oxygen therapy after intravenous antibiotics have been running for 24 hours

subtopic_detail: Bone protection when long term glucocorticoid treatment begins
stem: A 70-year-old woman starts prednisolone 25 mg daily for giant cell arteritis and will need at least twelve months of treatment. She has never fractured. Densitometry arranged at diagnosis shows a femoral neck T-score of -1.8, and her dairy intake is about 800 mg of calcium daily.

data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.31 mmol/L; vitamin D 78 nmol/L; eGFR 76 mL/min
data_table.Examination: No kyphosis or spinal tenderness; normal temporal arteries after four days of treatment

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start weekly oral alendronate together with the prednisolone
Repeat densitometry in twelve months and treat only if worse
Give calcium and vitamin D supplements as the only bone measure
Defer any bone treatment until the prednisolone dose is below 7.5 mg
Start subcutaneous teriparatide as the anabolic agent of choice

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis recognition on prednisolone taper
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man who was tapered off prednisolone 4 weeks ago after 18 months of 15 to 20 mg daily for pemphigus vulgaris. He was reduced from 5 mg every second day to zero over 3 weeks. He is now on day 4 of an upper respiratory tract infection with fevers to 38.6 and rigors. Today he attended the emergency department after collapsing at home when he stood up quickly.

Examination: he is drowsy but rousable, mucosal pallor, deeply tanned in sun exposed areas. Vital signs are pulse 118, blood pressure 76/44 mmHg (unresponsive to a 500 mL saline bolus already given), respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C. Bloods: sodium 128 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), glucose 3.1 mmol/L, urea 12.4 mmol/L, creatinine 148 micromol/L. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Chest x-ray shows early right lower zone consolidation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 76/44 (unresponsive to 500 mL saline), RR 22, SpO2 96% RA, temp 38.9
data_table.Steroid history: Prednisolone 15 to 20 mg daily x 18 months, tapered off 4 weeks ago
data_table.Bloods: Na 128; K+ 5.4; glucose 3.1 mmol/L; urea 12.4; creatinine 148
data_table.Skin: Deeply tanned in sun exposed areas; mucosal pallor

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g and doxycycline 100 mg for community-acquired pneumonia as primary treatment
Intravenous noradrenaline infusion titrated to mean arterial pressure above 65 mmHg via central line access
Intravenous 3 percent sodium chloride 100 mL bolus to correct hyponatraemia before other interventions
Send a short synacthen test now and defer any glucocorticoid until baseline and 30 minute cortisol return
Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately with concurrent normal saline resuscitation and glucose

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia intravenous iron choice
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 45-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding due to fibroids. She has 6 months of fatigue and shortness of breath climbing stairs. She has trialled two oral iron products (ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily and iron polymaltose 100 mg elemental daily) but stopped both within 2 weeks because of intolerable epigastric pain and constipation. She is on the waitlist for a Mirena insertion in 8 weeks.

Bloods: haemoglobin 82 g/L (115 to 165), MCV 74 fL (80 to 100), ferritin 4 micrograms/L (30 to 200), transferrin saturation 6 percent (16 to 45), CRP 3 mg/L (less than 5). Coeliac serology and faecal occult blood are negative. She has no history of severe allergy or asthma, is not pregnant, and is otherwise well. She weighs 68 kg, and her calculated iron deficit (Ganzoni formula) is approximately 1200 mg.

data_table.Iron studies: Hb 82; MCV 74; ferritin 4; transferrin saturation 6 percent
data_table.Oral iron trial: Ferrous sulfate and iron polymaltose both stopped within 2 weeks for GI intolerance
data_table.Cause of loss: Heavy menstrual bleeding due to fibroids; Mirena in 8 weeks

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step for iron replacement?

options.text: Single dose intravenous ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg over 15 minutes with 15 minutes post infusion monitoring
Restart oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily with a proton pump inhibitor 40 mg to reduce epigastric pain
Transfuse 2 units of packed red blood cells now to correct haemoglobin above 100 g/L rapidly
Prescribe intramuscular iron dextran 100 mg alternate days for 12 weeks in the general practice setting
Delay all iron replacement until the Mirena insertion in 8 weeks resolves the ongoing menstrual loss

subtopic_detail: Pleural effusion Light's criteria interpretation
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68-year-old man with progressive breathlessness on exertion over 8 weeks and left sided pleuritic chest pain. He has a 40 pack year smoking history, quit 2 years ago. On examination he has stony dull percussion and reduced breath sounds over the left lower zone. Chest x-ray shows a moderate left pleural effusion. Bedside ultrasound guided pleurocentesis is performed and 40 mL of straw coloured pleural fluid is aspirated.

Pleural fluid analysis: protein 38 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 320 U/L, glucose 4.1 mmol/L, pH 7.36. Serum protein 62 g/L, serum lactate dehydrogenase 210 U/L (upper limit of normal 240 U/L). Cytology and culture are pending. Bloods: full blood count and creatinine within normal limits, NT-proBNP 82 ng/L (less than 125). Echocardiogram shows normal biventricular function.

data_table.Imaging: Moderate left pleural effusion on CXR

lead_in: How should the pleural fluid be classified using Light's criteria and what is the next step?

options.text: Transudate; initiate loop diuretic therapy and repeat chest x-ray in 2 weeks without further evaluation
Exudate; arrange contrast enhanced CT chest and consider pleural biopsy given smoking history and unilateral effusion
Exudate; initiate empirical broad spectrum antibiotics and arrange chest drain insertion for empyema treatment
Transudate; commence NT-proBNP based heart failure workup and add angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor immediately
Indeterminate; repeat pleurocentesis in 4 weeks with albumin gradient to establish the effusion aetiology later

subtopic_detail: NSTEMI antiplatelet regimen selection in an older patient
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 78-year-old man with new-onset chest pain lasting 4 hours and a high-sensitivity troponin I of 78 ng/L (99th percentile 34) that rose to 220 ng/L 3 hours later. He has known chronic kidney disease with an eGFR of 42 mL/min/1.73 m2, hypertension on perindopril, and takes no antiplatelet at baseline. He weighs 74 kg. He is not on anticoagulation and has no history of intracranial haemorrhage or recent bleeding.

On examination he is comfortable in bed with resolved chest discomfort. Vital signs: pulse 78/min, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97 percent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. ECG shows sinus rhythm with 1 mm ST depression in leads V4 to V6 that has resolved on the current tracing. He has been given aspirin 300 mg and sublingual GTN and the cardiology team has planned a coronary angiogram within 24 hours.

data_table.ECG: Sinus rhythm; 1 mm ST depression V4 to V6, resolved on current
data_table.Given so far: Aspirin 300 mg; sublingual GTN; angiography planned within 24 hours
data_table.Bleeding risk: No ICH history; no recent bleeding; not on anticoagulant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate additional antiplatelet to add now?

options.text: Continue aspirin monotherapy without adding a P2Y12 inhibitor before angiography
Oral prasugrel 60 mg loading dose then 10 mg daily as second antiplatelet
Oral ticagrelor 180 mg loading dose then 90 mg twice daily as second antiplatelet
Commence oral apixaban 5 mg twice daily as an anticoagulant addition to aspirin
Oral clopidogrel 300 mg loading dose then 75 mg daily as part of dual antiplatelet therapy

subtopic_detail: SGLT2 inhibitor indication in chronic kidney disease with albuminuria
stem:
You are the nephrology registrar reviewing a 62-year-old man in the CKD clinic with type 2 diabetes for 12 years, hypertension, and a background of chronic kidney disease. His HbA1c is 7.6 percent on metformin 2 g daily and gliclazide 60 mg daily. He is on perindopril 8 mg daily and rosuvastatin 20 mg. His weight has been stable and his blood pressure is controlled.

Investigations today: eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m2 (stable over 12 months), urinary albumin-creatinine ratio 62 mg/mmol (up from 42 six months ago), sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, HbA1c 7.6 percent (target under 7 for this patient). He has never had diabetic ketoacidosis and has no history of recurrent genital or urinary infections. Ophthalmology screening at 6 months was normal.

data_table.Current meds: Metformin 2 g/day; gliclazide 60 mg/day; perindopril 8 mg; rosuvastatin 20 mg
data_table.Renal function: eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m2 stable; uACR 62 mg/mmol rising from 42
data_table.Screening: No DKA history; no recurrent genital or urinary infection; ophthalmology normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next medication change?

options.text: Reduce metformin to 500 mg twice daily because of the reduced eGFR
Add oral empagliflozin 10 mg daily as an SGLT2 inhibitor for cardiorenal protection
Increase gliclazide to 120 mg daily to further lower HbA1c to under 7 percent
Cease perindopril because of the reduced eGFR and switch to amlodipine
Add oral dulaglutide 1.5 mg weekly injection as a GLP-1 receptor agonist for weight loss

subtopic_detail: Adrenal insufficiency stress-dose glucocorticoid during acute illness
stem:
You are the medical registrar assessing a 48-year-old woman with known Addison's disease on hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking and 10 mg midday plus fludrocortisone 100 microgram daily. She has worn a MedicAlert bracelet for 6 years. She presents with 24 hours of vomiting, cramping abdominal pain, and non-bloody diarrhoea after a work barbecue; her husband has similar mild symptoms. She has taken sips of water and has vomited both her morning and midday hydrocortisone doses.

On examination she is tired but alert with dry mucous membranes. Vital signs: pulse 108/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg with a postural drop to 82/50 mmHg on standing, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 percent, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill is 3 seconds. Point-of-care electrolytes show sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, glucose 4.2 mmol/L. She has not yet used her home emergency hydrocortisone injection.

data_table.Diagnosis: Addison's disease on hydrocortisone 20/10 mg and fludrocortisone 100 microgram
data_table.Illness: 24 hours vomiting, cramping abdominal pain, non-bloody diarrhoea; vomited scheduled doses
data_table.Vitals: HR 108; BP 96/58 supine, 82/50 standing; RR 18; SpO2 99 percent; T 37.6
data_table.POC bloods: Na 132 mmol/L; K 4.5 mmol/L; glucose 4.2 mmol/L
data_table.Emergency plan: MedicAlert bracelet worn; home emergency hydrocortisone not used

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give ondansetron 8 mg intravenous alone and reassess before considering any change to steroid
Give hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenous now followed by 200 mg over 24 hours as continuous or 6 hourly boluses
Double the fludrocortisone dose to 200 microgram daily and continue routine hydrocortisone
Administer intramuscular dexamethasone 4 mg while awaiting adrenal function tests
Give oral hydrocortisone 40 mg as a double dose and observe in the emergency department for 4 hours

subtopic_detail: COPD exacerbation antibiotic indication and choice
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar reviewing a 71-year-old woman with severe COPD (FEV1 42 percent predicted) presenting with 4 days of worsening breathlessness, increased sputum volume, and change in sputum colour from clear to green. She uses tiotropium and a fluticasone-vilanterol preventer with salbutamol as needed. She smokes 10 cigarettes daily. She has no penicillin allergy and is not on immunosuppression.

On examination she is speaking in short sentences with pursed-lip breathing. Vital signs: pulse 108/min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 90 percent on 1 L/min nasal prongs, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius. Chest examination reveals widespread expiratory wheeze with reduced air entry bilaterally. CXR shows hyperinflation without focal consolidation. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.38, PaCO2 48 mmHg (35 to 45), PaO2 62 mmHg (75 to 100), HCO3 30 mmHg (22 to 32). She has already received nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium and oral prednisolone 50 mg.

data_table.Baseline: Severe COPD, FEV1 42 percent predicted; tiotropium plus fluticasone-vilanterol plus salbutamol
data_table.Symptoms: 4 days worsening breathlessness; increased sputum volume; change from clear to green sputum
data_table.Vitals: HR 108; BP 138/82; RR 26; SpO2 90 percent on 1 L/min NP; T 37.2
data_table.Imaging: CXR hyperinflation without focal consolidation
data_table.Given so far: Nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium; oral prednisolone 50 mg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding antibiotic therapy?

options.text: Commence oral azithromycin 500 mg daily for 3 days as first-line antibiotic agent
Commence intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours for broad-spectrum cover
Withhold antibiotics because CRP and white cell count have not returned to guide need
Commence oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days as first-line therapy
Commence oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 5 days as first-line antibiotic agent

subtopic_detail: Hyperacute ischaemic stroke thrombolysis window and blood pressure threshold
stem:
You are the medical registrar on the stroke team called to a 68-year-old woman brought in by ambulance with sudden onset right-sided weakness and expressive dysphasia noted by her husband. Symptom onset was 2 hours and 20 minutes ago as timed by his phone. She has hypertension on amlodipine and is on apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation, last taken 14 hours ago. She has no history of intracranial haemorrhage and has not had recent major surgery.

On examination her NIHSS is 12, GCS 15. Vital signs: pulse 84/min irregular, blood pressure 192/102 mmHg (repeated 190/104 five minutes later), respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Point-of-care glucose is 6.8 mmol/L. Non-contrast CT brain shows no haemorrhage and no established infarct core. CT angiography demonstrates a left middle cerebral artery M1 occlusion. Apixaban level is not available and idarucizumab is not stocked; andexanet alfa is available.

data_table.Time and severity: Onset 2 h 20 min ago; NIHSS 12; GCS 15
data_table.Vitals: HR 84 irregular; BP 192/102 then 190/104; RR 16; SpO2 99 percent; T 36.7
data_table.Bloods: POC glucose 6.8 mmol/L; apixaban level unavailable
data_table.Imaging: Non-contrast CT no haemorrhage or infarct core; CTA left MCA M1 occlusion
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg BD (last dose 14 hours ago); amlodipine
data_table.Reversal availability: Andexanet alfa available; idarucizumab not stocked

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Proceed directly to mechanical thrombectomy without thrombolysis and target blood pressure under 180/105 mmHg
Administer intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg after reversing apixaban with andexanet alfa pre-treatment
Give intravenous tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg without waiting for the apixaban level result today
Lower blood pressure to under 140/90 mmHg with intravenous labetalol before any reperfusion therapy
Commence intravenous heparin infusion to prevent thrombus extension while awaiting thrombectomy

subtopic_detail: Hyponatraemia discrimination SIADH versus cerebral salt wasting post-SAH
stem: A 58-year-old woman is on day 5 after coiling of a ruptured aneurysm. She is drowsy but rousable.

data_table.Weight: 62 kg, down from 66 kg on admission
data_table.Vital signs: HR 108/min, BP 106/62 mmHg supine and 88/54 mmHg standing; dry mucous membranes
data_table.Urine: Sodium 92 mmol/L, output 3.2 L in 24 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: 0.9 per cent sodium chloride at 1 to 2 mL/kg/h
Fluid restriction to 800 mL daily with sodium monitoring
Oral tolvaptan daily to correct the sodium by aquaresis
3 per cent saline 100 mL bolus, repeated as needed
Intravenous furosemide to promote a free water diuresis

subtopic_detail: Warfarin over-anticoagulation with active bleeding reversal strategy
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 76-year-old man on chronic warfarin for mechanical mitral valve replacement (target INR 2.5 to 3.5) who has been brought in by ambulance with 3 hours of melaena and lightheadedness. He takes no other antiplatelet or NSAID. Endoscopy has been requested and will be available within 4 hours.

On arrival he is pale and cool peripherally. Vital signs: pulse 118/min regular, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on 2 L/min nasal prongs, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill is 3 seconds. Investigations: haemoglobin 82 g/L (baseline 138), platelets 210 x 10^9/L, INR 6.4, urea 14.8 mmol/L (2.5 to 7.5), creatinine 108 micromol/L, sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L. Group and hold has been done and 2 units of cross-matched red cells will be available in 15 minutes.

data_table.Indication: Chronic warfarin for mechanical mitral valve, target INR 2.5 to 3.5
data_table.Vitals: HR 118; BP 92/58; RR 22; SpO2 98 percent on 2 L/min NP; T 36.6
data_table.Bleeding: 3 hours of melaena; lightheaded; endoscopy in 4 hours
data_table.Blood products: 2 units cross-matched red cells in 15 minutes; group and hold done

lead_in: What is the most appropriate strategy to correct anticoagulation?

options.text: Withhold warfarin now and repeat the INR in 4 hours before deciding on any specific reversal step
Administer fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg alone without prothrombin complex concentrate to reverse warfarin
Give oral vitamin K 10 mg and hold the next warfarin dose without giving factor replacement now
Give intravenous vitamin K 5 to 10 mg plus 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 25 to 50 IU/kg now
Give recombinant activated factor VII 90 microgram/kg as the primary reversal agent for the bleed

subtopic_detail: Hour one sepsis bundle timing
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 68-year-old man is brought in by ambulance with 12 hours of fever, cough with rusty sputum and confusion. His temperature at triage is 39.4 degrees C. He has a background of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and type 2 diabetes on metformin.

On examination he is drowsy but rousable and confused about the date. He has right basal crackles and dullness to percussion. Peripheries are warm with capillary refill 3 seconds.

Pulse rate 122/min, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg after a 500 mL fluid bolus, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 92% on 4 L per minute via nasal prong, temperature 39.4 degrees C. Lactate 3.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2). Blood cultures have been drawn and a portable chest radiograph shows a right lower lobe consolidation. His weight is 82 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122/min; BP 88/54 mmHg after 500 mL bolus; RR 28/min; SpO2 92% on 4 L/min nasal prong; T 39.4 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy; confused about the date; right basal crackles; dull to percussion; capillary refill 3 sec; warm peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 3.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); CXR: right lower lobe consolidation; blood cultures drawn

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step within the hour one bundle?

options.text: Give intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g and azithromycin 500 mg orally, and reassess response after 2 hours
Give intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g and intravenous azithromycin 500 mg within the hour, plus further fluid resuscitation
Commence noradrenaline peripherally at 5 micrograms per minute before further fluid resuscitation is complete
Perform urgent computed tomography scan of the chest to characterise the consolidation before starting antibiotics
Give intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g monotherapy and add atypical cover only if the patient deteriorates

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic choice for pyelonephritis
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 42-year-old woman with 24 hours of loin pain, rigors and dysuria. She is nauseated but tolerating small sips. She has no vomiting and no drug allergies. She takes no regular medications and has not been in hospital recently.

On examination she looks unwell but not septic. She has right loin tenderness on percussion. Abdomen is otherwise soft.

Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 122/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees C. Urine dipstick leucocytes 3 plus, nitrites positive, blood 1 plus. She is 12 weeks postpartum from a first pregnancy and is not currently breastfeeding. She has no known renal impairment.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96/min; BP 122/72 mmHg; RR 18/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 38.6 C
data_table.Examination: Unwell but not septic; right loin tenderness on percussion; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick leucs 3+, nitrites positive, blood 1+
data_table.History: 12 weeks postpartum; not breastfeeding; no drug allergies; no regular medications; no recent hospital

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Trimethoprim 300 mg orally once daily for 3 days and outpatient review and safety netting for any worsening loin pain or systemic symptoms
Amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid 875 plus 125 mg orally twice daily for 10 days and general practitioner review at 48 hours
Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 10 to 14 days after a urine sample is sent for culture and susceptibility
Intravenous gentamicin 5 mg/kg once and admit for further doses for further intravenous antibiotic therapy on the ward round
Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally 6 hourly for 5 days after a urine sample is sent for further review with the general practitioner in 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Discrimination of necrotising fasciitis from cellulitis
stem: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has a red painful right leg 24 hours after a garden scratch. The pain is out of keeping with the appearance of the skin.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 116 /min, BP 102/60 mmHg, T 38.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Tense erythematous calf, tenderness beyond the margin, dusky area, early blistering
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L, CRP 380 mg/L, Hb 128 g/L, Na 132 mmol/L, creatinine 138 micromol/L, glucose 12.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin with overnight observation and review
Contrast enhanced magnetic resonance imaging of the leg
Aspirate blister fluid for culture and reassess in 4 hours
Urgent surgical debridement, with meropenem, vancomycin and clindamycin
Elevate the limb, mark the margin and reassess in 6 hours

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic differentiation of DKA and HHS
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 78-year-old woman brought in by her son for 4 days of increasing lethargy, thirst and confusion. She has type 2 diabetes on metformin and gliclazide, and hypertension. She has had reduced oral intake since her chest infection started a week ago.

On examination she is drowsy but rousable, with dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor. There is no Kussmaul breathing. Chest reveals right basal crackles.

Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees C. Glucose 42 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), venous pH 7.32 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 20 mmol/L (22-30), ketones 0.6 mmol/L (less than 0.6), sodium 152 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.5 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 180 micromol/L (60-110), calculated osmolality 348 mOsm/kg (285-295).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118/min; BP 96/58 mmHg; RR 22/min; SpO2 96% RA; T 37.8 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy; rousable; dry mucous membranes; reduced skin turgor; no Kussmaul breathing; right basal crackles
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 42 mmol/L (3.5-7.8); venous pH 7.32 (7.35-7.45); bicarbonate 20 mmol/L (22-30); ketones 0.6 mmol/L (<0.6); Na 152 mmol/L (135-145); K 4.5 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); creatinine 180 micromol/L (60-110); osmolality 348 mOsm/kg (285-295)
data_table.History: T2DM on metformin and gliclazide; hypertension; reduced intake for 1 week; chest infection

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state precipitated by pneumonia requiring careful fluid resuscitation and delayed low dose insulin infusion
Diabetic ketoacidosis precipitated by pneumonia requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation and a fixed rate insulin infusion
Euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis from SGLT2 inhibitor use requiring cessation of the SGLT2 inhibitor and dextrose plus insulin infusion
Alcohol induced ketoacidosis requiring supportive care, thiamine and dextrose infusion under monitoring with regular monitoring in a high dependency bed
Lactic acidosis due to metformin accumulation in acute kidney injury requiring supportive care, cessation of metformin and possible haemodialysis

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic choice in infective endocarditis by valve type
stem: A 58-year-old man has three weeks of fever and night sweats. He had a mechanical mitral valve replacement three years ago and no recent procedures. He has no beta lactam allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Splinter haemorrhages, new apical pansystolic murmur
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram 12 mm vegetation on the mitral prosthesis with paravalvular regurgitation; three blood culture sets drawn

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin with gentamicin for six weeks
Intravenous vancomycin, gentamicin and rifampicin with surgical review
Intravenous flucloxacillin with gentamicin for six weeks
Intravenous ceftriaxone alone for streptococcal cover for six weeks
Intravenous daptomycin alone with cardiothoracic surgical review

subtopic_detail: Recognition and management of adrenal crisis on chronic steroids
stem: A 62-year-old woman on prednisolone 15 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica has 2 days of vomiting and weakness and stopped her tablets 3 days ago. She is drowsy with cool peripheries.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128 /min, BP 78/44 mmHg after 1 L of saline, T 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Na 128 mmol/L, K 5.6 mmol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L, cortisol pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral hydrocortisone 50 mg once the glucose is corrected, then reassess
Await the cortisol result before starting steroid replacement
Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg with fluid resuscitation and dextrose
Oral fludrocortisone 0.1 mg to correct the sodium and potassium
Intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg to avoid interfering with the cortisol assay

subtopic_detail: Screening test choice for Cushing's syndrome
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 42-year-old woman with 18 months of weight gain, new hypertension, and violaceous abdominal striae. She has type 2 diabetes diagnosed 6 months ago that is difficult to control on metformin plus dapagliflozin. She takes no steroids and does not use inhaled corticosteroids. She drinks less than 4 standard drinks per week.

On examination she has central obesity, a dorsocervical fat pad, thin skin with easy bruising and proximal muscle weakness. She has striae up to 2 cm wide on her abdomen. She has 3 hospital admissions with vertebral compression fractures in the last year.

Pulse rate 84/min, blood pressure 158/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C. Fasting glucose 9.2 mmol/L, HbA1c 8.4 percent (less than 5.7), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), TSH within normal limits. She does not have a shift work pattern or any recent stress that would perturb her circadian rhythm.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84/min; BP 158/98 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Central obesity; dorsocervical fat pad; thin skin with easy bruising; proximal muscle weakness; 2 cm violaceous abdominal striae
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 9.2 mmol/L; HbA1c 8.4% (<5.7); K 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); TSH within normal limits
data_table.History: 18 months symptoms; new T2DM 6 months on metformin plus dapagliflozin; 3 vertebral fractures in 1 year; no exogenous steroids; no shift work

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial screening test?

options.text: Random serum cortisol drawn at any time of day, with confirmatory ACTH if elevated
Insulin tolerance test with hypoglycaemia challenge to demonstrate cortisol response
Serum ACTH concentration and inferior petrosal sinus sampling to distinguish source
24 hour urinary free cortisol collected on at least two occasions
Adrenal computed tomography scan with contrast to identify a cortisol producing adenoma

subtopic_detail: Reversal of dabigatran in life threatening bleeding
stem: A 78-year-old man on dabigatran 150 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation, last dose 6 hours ago, is brought in after a collapse with dense right hemiparesis and aphasia.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/94 mmHg, NIHSS 22
data_table.CT brain: 45 mL left temporoparietal intracerebral haemorrhage with intraventricular extension and 4 mm midline shift
data_table.Bloods: Creatinine 96 micromol/L, INR 1.4, aPTT 42 seconds, dilute thrombin time prolonged

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reversal strategy?

options.text: Four factor prothrombin complex concentrate 50 units/kg intravenously
Intravenous vitamin K 10 mg with fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg
Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g with platelet transfusion
Urgent haemodialysis without any pharmacological reversal
Intravenous idarucizumab 5 g as two consecutive 2.5 g boluses

subtopic_detail: SMART-COP triage decision for a patient failing outpatient CAP therapy
stem: A 68-year-old man has four days of productive cough, fever and breathlessness with right pleuritic chest pain. He started oral amoxicillin 48 hours ago and has not improved.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9 degrees C, HR 118/min, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 30/min, oriented
data_table.Investigations: Albumin 34 g/L; chest x-ray dense right lower lobe consolidation only; room air gas pH 7.44, PaO2 62 mmHg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge on oral amoxicillin and doxycycline, review tomorrow
Ward admission with intravenous benzylpenicillin and oral doxycycline
High acuity admission with intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin
Ward admission with intravenous meropenem and oral azithromycin
Ward admission with oral moxifloxacin monotherapy and oxygen

subtopic_detail: Rate versus rhythm control in AF of unknown duration
stem: A 72-year-old man has palpitations and breathlessness that began overnight. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. An ECG 6 months ago showed sinus rhythm. He has no chest pain.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138/min irregularly irregular, BP 132/78 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: ECG atrial fibrillation at 138/min with no ischaemic changes; echocardiogram preserved left ventricular function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Intravenous heparin now and direct current cardioversion today, then apixaban
Intravenous amiodarone for pharmacological cardioversion today, then apixaban
Aspirin and oral metoprolol titrated to a rate under 110/min
Apixaban and oral metoprolol titrated to a rate under 110/min
Warfarin bridging, then cardioversion if transoesophageal echo is clear

subtopic_detail: Immediate management of suspected adrenal crisis in a patient on chronic prednisolone
stem: A 58-year-old woman on prednisolone 7.5 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica has 24 hours of vomiting and diarrhoea and has kept nothing down since yesterday.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128/min, BP 82/48 mmHg, T 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Cool mottled peripheries, dry mucous membranes
data_table.Bloods: Na 128 mmol/L (135-145), K 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 148 micromol/L (baseline 72), glucose 3.2 mmol/L, pH 7.29

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Await a serum cortisol result before any parenteral corticosteroid
Oral prednisolone 15 mg with intravenous saline and dextrose
Intramuscular dexamethasone 4 mg with intravenous saline and dextrose
Intravenous fludrocortisone 100 microg with saline and dextrose
Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg with saline and dextrose

subtopic_detail: Escalating stable COPD therapy after a recent exacerbation per COPD X
stem: A 68-year-old ex-smoker with COPD has taken tiotropium alone for 18 months. He was admitted with an infective exacerbation 4 weeks ago and had two others in the past year. His mMRC dyspnoea score is 2.

data_table.Examination: Chest clear, SpO2 96%, inhaler technique correct
data_table.Investigations: FEV1 55 percent predicted post bronchodilator, FEV1/FVC 0.62, blood eosinophils 220 cells per microL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate step up in therapy?

options.text: Substitute a combined long-acting beta agonist and muscarinic antagonist
Add an inhaled corticosteroid as a combination inhaler with tiotropium
Add maintenance azithromycin three times weekly, continuing tiotropium
Commence maintenance oral prednisolone, continuing tiotropium
Commence oral roflumilast, continuing tiotropium maintenance

subtopic_detail: Bisphosphonate selection after low trauma vertebral fracture on background CKD
stem: A 74-year-old woman has had a second low trauma vertebral fracture in 12 months and has never had bone therapy. She has chronic kidney disease and no oesophageal disease, with regular dental care.

data_table.Examination: Kyphotic, intact dentition
data_table.Investigations: T-score lumbar spine -2.9, femoral neck -2.7, eGFR 32 mL/min/1.73m2, calcium 2.34 mmol/L, 25-OH vitamin D 68 nmol/L, PTH 5.8 pmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate bone active therapy today?

options.text: Commence oral alendronate 70 mg weekly, taken fasting
Commence subcutaneous denosumab 60 mg six-monthly
Commence intravenous zoledronic acid 5 mg yearly
Commence subcutaneous teriparatide 20 microg daily
Commence oral raloxifene 60 mg daily, continued indefinitely

subtopic_detail: Refractory adult anaphylaxis on beta blocker requiring adjunct pharmacotherapy
stem: A 62-year-old man on atenolol 50 mg daily has anaphylaxis after a wasp sting. Paramedics gave intramuscular adrenaline 500 microg twice. He is still hypotensive and wheezy with urticaria after 1 L of saline.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82/min, BP 76/48 mmHg, RR 32/min, SpO2 91 per cent on 15 L
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.32, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, preserved left ventricular function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next specific pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Noradrenaline infusion 0.05 microg/kg/min through a central line
Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg with promethazine 25 mg
Intravenous glucagon 1 to 2 mg with an adrenaline infusion
Vasopressin 4 units then 0.02 unit per minute centrally
Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g with ranitidine 50 mg

subtopic_detail: Priority intervention in severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes
stem: A 68-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease, admitted 48 hours ago with pneumonia, remains on ramipril and spironolactone. He is lethargic and oliguric.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 42 /min, BP 108/72 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: K 7.4 mmol/L, creatinine 320 micromol/L (baseline 240), bicarbonate 16 mmol/L
data_table.ECG: Peaked T waves, PR 240 ms, QRS 130 ms with sine wave morphology emerging

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 10 mg to shift potassium intracellularly now
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4 percent 100 mL over 15 minutes
Intravenous furosemide 80 mg with oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate
Intravenous calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL, then insulin 10 units with dextrose
Urgent haemodialysis through a tunnelled line, with continuous cardiac monitoring

subtopic_detail: First line vasopressor after fluid resuscitation in septic shock
stem: A 62-year-old man with pneumonia has had 30 mL/kg of crystalloid, with ceftriaxone and azithromycin given after blood cultures. He remains oliguric with cool peripheries.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128 /min, BP 82/48 mmHg, MAP 58 mmHg, T 39.2 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.28, lactate 4.6 mmol/L; echocardiogram shows a preserved but underfilled left ventricle

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Vasopressin infusion at a fixed rate of 0.03 units per minute
Dopamine infusion at 10 micrograms per kilogram per minute
Adrenaline infusion at 0.05 micrograms per kilogram per minute intravenously
A further 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus before any vasopressor
Noradrenaline infusion titrated to a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg

subtopic_detail: Opportunistic infection prophylaxis thresholds at new HIV diagnosis
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 41-year-old man in the ambulatory clinic two weeks after a new diagnosis of human immunodeficiency virus infection made on serology and confirmed by a second assay. He feels well, has gained no weight recently and has no cough, fever or oral lesions.

He has never taken antiretroviral therapy. He has no allergies, in particular no sulfonamide allergy, and his liver function is within normal limits. His chest radiograph is clear and his cryptococcal antigen is negative. His baseline results are now available and he is keen to begin treatment today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 124/78, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: CD4 count 140 cells/microlitre (500-1500); HIV viral load 82000 copies/mL; cryptococcal antigen negative; chest radiograph clear
data_table.Blood tests: Full blood count, electrolytes and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management to commence today?

options.text: Antiretroviral therapy alone, with prophylaxis added only if the CD4 count falls further
Antiretroviral therapy plus azithromycin weekly for disseminated mycobacterial prophylaxis
Antiretroviral therapy plus daily co-trimoxazole for Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis
Deferred antiretroviral therapy until the CD4 count recovers above 350 cells per microlitre
Antiretroviral therapy plus fluconazole daily for prevention of cryptococcal meningitis

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis treatment selection after a positive interferon gamma release assay
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the refugee health clinic. A 26-year-old man who arrived from Nepal 11 months ago has been referred after a positive interferon gamma release assay performed during a pre employment health check for aged care work.

He is entirely asymptomatic with no cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss. Two sputum samples collected for completeness were negative on smear and on culture at six weeks. His chest radiograph reported today shows clear lung fields with no apical scarring, cavitation or hilar lymphadenopathy. He takes no medication, drinks no alcohol, and has normal liver function with a negative human immunodeficiency virus serology. He asks how long treatment will take because he is due to start work.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Investigations: Interferon gamma release assay positive; chest radiograph clear; sputum smear and culture negative; HIV serology negative
data_table.Blood tests: Liver function and full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for two months then continuation phase
No treatment at present, with a repeat interferon gamma release assay in twelve months
Bacille Calmette Guerin vaccination now with annual symptom review by the general practitioner
Rifampicin daily for four months with baseline and interval liver function monitoring
Pyrazinamide with rifampicin for two months and fortnightly liver function monitoring throughout

subtopic_detail: Antiviral indication and agent choice in influenza with chronic airways disease
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 68-year-old woman during an influenza season. She describes 36 hours of fever, myalgia and a dry cough that began abruptly. A point-of-care nucleic acid test taken this morning is positive for influenza A.

She has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with a forced expiratory volume in one second of 52 per cent predicted and uses a long-acting muscarinic antagonist and a long-acting beta agonist daily. She has had two exacerbations in the last 12 months. She is not hypoxic, her chest is clear of focal crackles and her sputum has not changed colour or volume. Her creatinine and eGFR are within normal limits and she received the seasonal vaccine four weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 132/78, RR 20, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 38.2
data_table.Investigations: Influenza A nucleic acid test positive; chest auscultation clear with no focal crackles
data_table.Blood tests: Creatinine and eGFR within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Symptomatic treatment only, since antivirals are of benefit only within 24 hours of onset
Oral oseltamivir twice daily for five days alongside her usual inhaled maintenance therapy
Inhaled zanamivir twice daily for five days as the preferred agent in chronic airways disease
Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for five days to cover secondary bacterial infection risk
Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for five days as treatment for an infective exacerbation

subtopic_detail: Osteoporosis pharmacotherapy selection with impaired renal function
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 72-year-old woman four weeks after she sustained a T12 vertebral compression fracture while lifting a shopping bag. The fracture was confirmed on plain radiography and her back pain is now settling with simple analgesia.

She is postmenopausal since age 51, has never smoked, and takes no corticosteroid. Her corrected calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone are within normal limits and her serum 25 hydroxyvitamin D is 68 nmol/L after supplementation. A myeloma screen is negative. Her bone mineral density shows a lumbar spine T score of minus 2.8. Her renal function has been stable at this level for two years.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70, BP 132/78, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Lumbar spine T score minus 2.8; T12 vertebral compression fracture on radiography; myeloma screen negative
data_table.Blood tests: eGFR 28 mL/min/1.73m2; corrected calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone within normal limits; 25 hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Subcutaneous denosumab six monthly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation continued
Oral alendronate 70 mg weekly taken fasting with calcium and vitamin D supplementation continued
Intravenous zoledronic acid five milligrams annually with calcium and vitamin D continued
Calcium 1200 mg and colecalciferol 1000 international units daily as the sole ongoing therapy
Subcutaneous teriparatide daily for eighteen months with calcium and vitamin D continued

subtopic_detail: Interpretation of pleural fluid biochemistry using Light criteria
stem:
You are the medical registrar caring for a 64-year-old man admitted with three weeks of progressive breathlessness. A chest radiograph shows a moderate left pleural effusion and you have performed a diagnostic pleural aspiration.

He is a former smoker with a 30 pack year history and takes no diuretic. His jugular venous pressure is not elevated, there is no peripheral oedema, and his echocardiogram yesterday reported normal left and right ventricular function with no valvular abnormality. His serum albumin, liver function and creatinine are within normal limits. The pleural fluid is straw coloured, and Gram stain shows no organisms with a pH of 7.38.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 128/76, RR 22, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Investigations: Pleural fluid protein 42 g/L; serum protein 68 g/L; pleural fluid LDH 310 U/L; serum LDH 380 U/L; pleural fluid pH 7.38; Gram stain no organisms
data_table.Blood tests: Serum albumin, liver function and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence furosemide 40 mg daily and repeat the chest radiograph after five days of treatment
Insert an intercostal catheter for drainage of a complicated parapneumonic collection today
Arrange a contrast enhanced computed tomography of the chest before further pleural intervention
Repeat the diagnostic pleural aspiration in six weeks and send further fluid for cytology
Repeat the transthoracic echocardiogram with contrast to reassess for occult diastolic dysfunction

subtopic_detail: Management of supratherapeutic warfarin anticoagulation without bleeding
stem:
You are the general practitioner contacted by the pathology laboratory about a 76-year-old man on warfarin for a mechanical aortic valve replacement performed six years ago. His target international normalised ratio range is 2.5 to 3.5 and his last three readings were in range.

He completed a course of trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole four days ago for a urinary tract infection. He reports no bruising, mucosal bleeding, dark stool, haematuria or headache. He has had no falls or recent trauma. His blood pressure and pulse are unchanged from his baseline and his haemoglobin today is 138 g/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74, BP 134/80, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 8.6 (target 2.5-3.5); haemoglobin 138 g/L (130-180); platelets within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No bruising, no mucosal bleeding, no abdominal tenderness, no neurological deficit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Withhold warfarin and recheck the international normalised ratio in three days with no other action
Withhold warfarin and give vitamin K1 one to two milligrams orally, rechecking in 24 hours
Withhold warfarin and give prothrombin complex concentrate at fifty units per kilogram now
Withhold warfarin and transfuse two units of fresh frozen plasma with post transfusion coagulation studies
Withhold warfarin and give vitamin K1 ten milligrams intravenously with repeat testing in six hours

subtopic_detail: Blood pressure targets in hypertensive emergency with retinal and renal involvement
stem:
You are the emergency registrar assessing a 52-year-old man who presented with three days of headache and blurred vision. He ran out of his perindopril and amlodipine eight weeks ago when he moved interstate.

He has no chest pain, focal neurological deficit or dyspnoea. Fundoscopy shows bilateral flame haemorrhages and disc swelling. His creatinine was 92 micromol/L when checked nine months ago. His electrocardiogram shows voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy without ischaemic change, his troponin is not raised and his chest radiograph shows a normal cardiac silhouette with clear lung fields. Computed tomography of the brain is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 224/128, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Fundoscopy: bilateral flame haemorrhages with disc swelling; no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110); urinalysis protein 2+ and blood 1+; troponin not raised; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial blood pressure management?

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg repeated as needed until the systolic pressure falls below 160 mmHg
Restart oral perindopril and amlodipine at previous doses with general practitioner review in one week
Intravenous antihypertensive therapy titrated to reach a blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg within one hour
Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to reduce mean arterial pressure by 20 to 25 per cent
Intravenous hydralazine 10 mg by bolus repeated every twenty minutes until symptoms have settled

subtopic_detail: Cortisol testing confounded by oestrogen containing contraception
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 29-year-old woman referred with weight gain, purple abdominal striae wider than one centimetre, proximal muscle weakness on standing from a chair, and new hypertension at 152/96 mmHg.

She takes a combined oral contraceptive pill containing ethinylestradiol and has done so continuously for four years. She takes no corticosteroid in any form, including inhaled, topical and intra-articular preparations, and drinks no alcohol. Her general practitioner performed a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test which returned a morning cortisol of 78 nmol/L, above the suppression threshold of 50 nmol/L. Her potassium and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 152/96, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test: morning cortisol 78 nmol/L (suppression threshold below 50); potassium and thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Purple abdominal striae greater than 1 cm wide; proximal weakness on sit to stand testing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary to identify a corticotroph adenoma
Measure plasma adrenocorticotrophic hormone now to determine whether the excess is dependent
Repeat the same overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test in six weeks for confirmation
Arrange inferior petrosal sinus sampling to localise the source of the cortisol excess
Measure 24 hour urinary free cortisol on two separate collections while she continues the pill

subtopic_detail: Interfering antihypertensives in aldosterone to renin ratio testing
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the hypertension clinic seeing a 44-year-old woman whose blood pressure remains 168/102 mmHg despite three agents at maximum tolerated doses. She has been on perindopril, amlodipine and spironolactone for the last five months.

Her potassium has been persistently low at 3.1 mmol/L on three occasions and she takes no diuretic other than the spironolactone and no liquorice or over the counter preparations. Her renal function and thyroid function are within normal limits, her urinary metanephrines are not raised and a renal artery duplex shows no stenosis. Her general practitioner has sent an aldosterone to renin ratio which came back below the screening threshold. She asks why her potassium keeps dropping.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 168/102, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Investigations: Aldosterone to renin ratio below screening threshold; urinary metanephrines not raised; renal artery duplex no stenosis
data_table.Blood tests: Potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); sodium 142 mmol/L (135-145); creatinine and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease spironolactone for six weeks, substitute verapamil and prazosin, then repeat the ratio
Accept the negative ratio and add a fourth agent such as hydralazine to control the pressure
Proceed directly to adrenal vein sampling to lateralise aldosterone production before any imaging
Arrange computed tomography of the adrenal glands and act on any adenoma that is identified
Perform a saline suppression test now while the current antihypertensive regimen is continued

subtopic_detail: Myasthenic crisis with respiratory compromise
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the ward for a 63-year-old woman with acetylcholine receptor antibody positive myasthenia gravis. She was admitted yesterday for a chest infection and started on azithromycin.

Over eight hours her voice has become nasal, she is pooling saliva and cannot count past 12 in one breath. Her pupils are 3 mm and reactive, with no abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, bronchorrhoea or fasciculation. Her forced vital capacity has fallen from 2.6 litres on admission to 1.1 litres this afternoon. Her oxygen saturation remains 96 per cent on room air and her chest radiograph shows a right basal consolidation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, BP 142/84, RR 26, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 37.6
data_table.Investigations: Forced vital capacity 1.1 L, fallen from 2.6 L on admission; arterial pH 7.36 with pCO2 46 mmHg; chest radiograph right basal consolidation
data_table.Examination: Nasal speech, pooled secretions, single breath count 12, pupils 3 mm reactive, no fasciculation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the pyridostigmine dose and frequency and reassess the vital capacity in four hours
Commence high dose oral prednisolone 60 mg daily as monotherapy and continue ward observation
Transfer to intensive care for airway support and commence plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin
Perform an edrophonium test at the bedside to distinguish myasthenic from cholinergic crisis
Commence azathioprine as a steroid sparing agent and arrange thiopurine methyltransferase testing

subtopic_detail: Early Guillain Barre syndrome with normal initial cerebrospinal fluid protein
stem:
You are the medical registrar assessing a 38-year-old man with five days of progressive leg weakness that has now reached his thighs and is affecting his grip. He had a diarrhoeal illness three weeks ago that settled without treatment.

He has areflexia at the knees and ankles with preserved sensation to pinprick and mild distal paraesthesia. There is no sensory level on the trunk, no back pain, and bladder and bowel function are normal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine performed this morning is unremarkable. His lumbar puncture shows a protein of 0.38 g/L with one white cell per microlitre, and his forced vital capacity is 3.1 litres. His electrolytes, glucose and inflammatory markers are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 138/82, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical proximal and distal lower limb weakness, absent knee and ankle reflexes, no sensory level, normal anal tone
data_table.Investigations: CSF protein 0.38 g/L (0.15-0.45) with 1 white cell per microlitre; MRI whole spine unremarkable; forced vital capacity 3.1 L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat the lumbar puncture in one week and withhold treatment until the protein is elevated
Commence intravenous immunoglobulin over five days with four hourly vital capacity monitoring
Commence intravenous methylprednisolone one gram daily for three days with proton pump cover
Commence plasma exchange and intravenous immunoglobulin together to maximise the treatment effect
Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast before starting any therapy

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulant selection in cancer associated venous thromboembolism
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 61-year-old man with a newly diagnosed right femoral deep vein thrombosis confirmed on compression ultrasound. He was diagnosed six weeks ago with a locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma and started palliative chemotherapy last week.

His endoscopy at diagnosis described a large ulcerated antral tumour that oozed on contact with the scope. His haemoglobin has drifted from 128 to 106 g/L over four weeks and his faecal occult testing was positive. He has no chest pain and no dyspnoea. His platelet count is 168 x10^9/L, his creatinine clearance is 74 mL/min and his liver function is within normal limits. He takes no antiplatelet agent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 122/74, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Compression ultrasound: occlusive right femoral vein thrombus; endoscopy: ulcerated antral tumour with contact oozing
data_table.Blood tests: Haemoglobin 106 g/L (130-180), down from 128; platelets 168 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine clearance 74 mL/min; liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation?

options.text: Oral apixaban at treatment dose for six months with three monthly haemoglobin monitoring
Oral rivaroxaban at treatment dose for six months with a proton pump inhibitor for gastric protection
Oral warfarin bridged with enoxaparin until the international normalised ratio reaches the target range
Subcutaneous enoxaparin at treatment dose for six months with periodic reassessment of the bleeding risk
