Insertion of a retrievable inferior vena cava filter with no systemic anticoagulation commenced

subtopic_detail: Severe cutaneous adverse reaction with eosinophilia and organ involvement
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 34-year-old woman with a widespread rash and fever. She started lamotrigine 24 days ago for bipolar disorder and takes no other new medication.

Her rash is a confluent morbilliform eruption over roughly 60 per cent of her body surface with marked facial swelling. Nikolsky sign is negative, there are no target lesions, no skin detachment and her oral, ocular and genital mucosae are entirely spared. She has palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Her blood film shows an eosinophil count of 1.9 x10^9/L and her alanine aminotransferase is 284 U/L. Her creatinine is 96 micromol/L and blood cultures taken on arrival are negative at 48 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 106, BP 118/70, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.7
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform eruption 60% body surface area with facial oedema; Nikolsky sign negative; mucosae spared; cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 1.9 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5); alanine aminotransferase 284 U/L (5-35); creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90); blood cultures negative at 48 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and commence intravenous immunoglobulin at two grams per kilogram over five days
Cease lamotrigine and commence ciclosporin three milligrams per kilogram daily for seven days
Continue lamotrigine at a reduced dose with daily liver function testing and topical corticosteroid
Cease lamotrigine and commence oral cetirizine with emollients and outpatient dermatology review
Cease lamotrigine and commence systemic prednisolone with thyroid function monitoring for six months

subtopic_detail: Empirical therapy for native valve infective endocarditis
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 58-year-old man with three weeks of fevers, night sweats and lethargy. He is a retired teacher with no prosthetic material, no indwelling lines and no injecting drug use, and he has not been in hospital or aged care in the past year.

He had a dental extraction six weeks ago. A new early diastolic murmur is audible at the left sternal edge and there are splinter haemorrhages in two nail beds. Three sets of blood cultures have been taken from separate sites and are pending. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a 9 mm mobile aortic valve vegetation with mild regurgitation. He has no penicillin allergy and his renal function is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, BP 118/58, RR 20, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 38.4
data_table.Examination: Early diastolic murmur at left sternal edge, splinter haemorrhages, no stigmata of injecting drug use
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C reactive protein 142 mg/L (less than 5); creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110); echocardiogram shows 9 mm aortic vegetation

lead_in: Which empirical antibiotic regimen is the most appropriate to start now?

options.text: Ceftriaxone with oral rifampicin, awaiting blood culture results before escalation
Benzylpenicillin with flucloxacillin and gentamicin, adjusted once cultures return
Vancomycin with gentamicin and rifampicin, adjusted once blood cultures return
Piperacillin with tazobactam, awaiting blood culture results before any escalation
Withhold all antibiotics until the blood culture results are available in 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Timing of dexamethasone and antibiotics in adult bacterial meningitis
stem:
You are the emergency registrar assessing a 43-year-old woman with 12 hours of severe headache, neck stiffness and photophobia. She is drowsy but obeys commands and has a Glasgow coma scale of 13.

Fundoscopy shows blurred disc margins in both eyes, so computed tomography of the head is required before lumbar puncture. The scanner is occupied and the radiographer estimates a 45 minute wait. Two sets of blood cultures have just been taken. She has no allergies, has not travelled overseas and is not immunosuppressed. There is no rash and her coagulation profile is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112, BP 138/82, RR 22, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 38.9
data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 13, neck stiffness, bilateral blurred disc margins, no focal deficit, no rash
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C reactive protein 210 mg/L (less than 5); coagulation profile and platelets within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Wait for the scan and lumbar puncture before starting any antimicrobial treatment
Give ceftriaxone now and add dexamethasone only if the culture grows pneumococcus
Give ceftriaxone and benzylpenicillin now and add dexamethasone after the scan
Give dexamethasone immediately followed by ceftriaxone, then proceed to the scan
Give aciclovir and dexamethasone now and defer antibacterial therapy until the scan

subtopic_detail: Adrenal insufficiency during intercurrent illness
stem:
You are the registrar in an after hours general practice clinic. A 36-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency telephones and then attends with 10 hours of vomiting and watery diarrhoea after a family barbecue.

She normally takes hydrocortisone 20 mg in the morning and 10 mg in the afternoon, plus fludrocortisone 100 mcg daily. She doubled her morning hydrocortisone dose today but vomited within 20 minutes of taking it and has kept nothing down since. She feels dizzy on standing. Her capillary blood glucose is 3.9 mmol/L and her lying to standing blood pressure falls from 104/62 to 84/54 mmHg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 104/62 lying, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.4
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, postural drop to 84/54 mmHg, alert and orientated
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood glucose 3.9 mmol/L (3.0-7.7); point-of-care sodium 131 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 5.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg by intramuscular injection and arrange urgent transfer
Give oral hydrocortisone 40 mg with an antiemetic and review her again in one hour
Double her fludrocortisone dose and encourage oral rehydration solution at home
Take a random serum cortisol and withhold steroid until the result is available
Give intravenous normal saline alone and reassess her postural blood pressure hourly

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis before biologic therapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a rheumatology clinic. A 47-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis has failed methotrexate and leflunomide, and a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor is planned.

She was born in Vietnam and moved to Australia at age 24. She has no cough, no fevers, no night sweats and no weight loss, and she has never been treated for tuberculosis. Her interferon gamma release assay is positive. Her chest radiograph shows no parenchymal opacity, no cavitation and no calcified nodes, and three sputum specimens sent for acid fast bacilli are negative on smear and culture. Her liver function and human immunodeficiency virus serology are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No lymphadenopathy, chest clear on auscultation, active synovitis in both wrists
data_table.Investigations: Interferon gamma release assay positive; chest radiograph clear; sputum smear and culture negative; liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management before starting the biologic agent?

options.text: Start the tumour necrosis factor inhibitor now and monitor her symptoms monthly
Start a four drug antituberculous regimen and continue it for a total of six months
Repeat the interferon gamma release assay in three months to confirm the result
Treat for latent infection and start the biologic once therapy is well established
Perform a tuberculin skin test and treat only if the induration exceeds 15 mm

subtopic_detail: Sequencing the first hour of sepsis management
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the ward for a 68-year-old man who is confused and febrile on day two of an admission for a diabetic foot ulcer. He was fully orientated at the morning round.

His ulcer now has surrounding erythema tracking to the mid calf with foul smelling discharge. He has received no antibiotics so far this admission. He weighs 80 kg, has no known allergies and his creatinine was 82 micromol/L this morning. His venous lactate taken five minutes ago is 4.2 mmol/L and his capillary blood glucose is 14.6 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, BP 88/52, RR 28, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 38.8
data_table.Examination: Confused and disorientated to place, warm peripheries, foot ulcer with spreading erythema and purulent discharge
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 4.2 mmol/L (less than 2.0); capillary blood glucose 14.6 mmol/L (3.0-7.7); white cell count 21.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate sequence of actions?

options.text: Take blood cultures, then give intravenous antibiotics and a fluid bolus within the hour
Give a fluid bolus first, then take blood cultures once his blood pressure has improved
Arrange urgent imaging of the foot, then give antibiotics once the extent is defined
Start a noradrenaline infusion first, then give antibiotics once his pressure is restored
Give intravenous insulin first, then reassess his conscious state and lactate in an hour

subtopic_detail: Opportunistic infection prophylaxis thresholds in human immunodeficiency virus
stem:
You are the medical registrar in an infectious diseases clinic seeing a 41-year-old man newly diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus infection after presenting with oral candidiasis.

He is otherwise well, with no cough, no breathlessness, no headache and no visual symptoms. Antiretroviral therapy is being arranged and will start this week. His toxoplasma immunoglobulin G serology is negative and his chest radiograph is clear. He has no allergy to sulfonamides and his renal function and full blood count are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Oral pseudomembranous candidiasis, chest clear on auscultation, no focal neurological signs, fundi normal
data_table.Investigations: CD4 count 180 cells/microlitre; human immunodeficiency virus ribonucleic acid 84000 copies/mL; toxoplasma immunoglobulin G negative; chest radiograph clear

lead_in: Which additional prophylaxis is indicated at this point?

options.text: Azithromycin weekly for disseminated mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis
Valganciclovir daily for cytomegalovirus retinitis prophylaxis with monthly review
Co-trimoxazole daily for pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis
Fluconazole daily for cryptococcal disease prophylaxis until his count recovers
No additional prophylaxis, since antiretroviral therapy is starting within the week

subtopic_detail: Preparing for aldosterone to renin ratio testing
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 44-year-old man in a hypertension clinic. His blood pressure has remained above target despite perindopril, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide at maximum tolerated doses, and adherence has been confirmed by dispensing records.

His general practitioner added spironolactone 25 mg daily 10 weeks ago, which improved his readings. His potassium was 3.1 mmol/L before the spironolactone was started and is 4.2 mmol/L today. He has no history of snoring or daytime somnolence, no episodic headache or sweating, and his renal artery imaging is unremarkable. Screening for primary aldosteronism is planned.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74, BP 158/96, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide, spironolactone 25 mg daily
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); sodium 141 mmol/L (135-145); creatinine 84 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before the screening test is performed?

options.text: Measure the aldosterone to renin ratio now while he remains on all current agents
Cease perindopril for two weeks and measure the ratio while other agents continue
Cease spironolactone for at least four weeks and substitute verapamil or prazosin
Proceed directly to adrenal vein sampling without any preceding biochemical screen
Arrange computed tomography of the adrenal glands and test according to the findings

subtopic_detail: Preoperative blockade in phaeochromocytoma
stem:
You are the medical registrar asked to review a 39-year-old woman before adrenalectomy. She had episodes of pounding headache, drenching sweats and palpitations lasting 20 minutes, and a 4 cm right adrenal mass was found on imaging.

Her plasma free metanephrines are six times the upper reference limit and the diagnosis is established. Surgery is planned for three weeks' time. Her resting pulse is 92 and her blood pressure is 172/104 mmHg, with a postural drop of 8 mmHg. She takes no regular medication and has no asthma, and her echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular function.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 172/104, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: No goitre, no neurofibromas, no retinal angiomas, postural drop 8 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: Plasma free metanephrines six times upper reference limit; 4 cm right adrenal mass on computed tomography; echocardiogram normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological preparation?

options.text: Commence metoprolol now and add an alpha blocking agent one week before surgery
Commence phenoxybenzamine now and add a beta blocking agent once it is established
Commence perindopril now and titrate the dose against her home blood pressure diary
Commence furosemide now and restrict her dietary sodium intake until the operation
Proceed to surgery without blockade given that her cardiac function is fully preserved

subtopic_detail: Empirical therapy for acute pyelonephritis requiring admission
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 32-year-old woman with two days of right loin pain, rigors and vomiting. She has been unable to keep down oral fluids since yesterday.

She is not pregnant, has no urinary tract abnormality, no indwelling catheter and no antibiotic exposure in the past six months. She has not travelled overseas and has not been hospitalised previously. She has no allergies. Her urine dipstick shows nitrites and leucocytes, urine has been sent for culture, and her creatinine is 88 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate above 90 mL/min/1.73m2. Ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis and no calculus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 116/70, RR 20, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.7
data_table.Examination: Right renal angle tenderness, abdomen otherwise soft, no suprapubic mass
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick nitrites and leucocytes positive; creatinine 88 micromol/L (45-90); white cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); ultrasound shows no obstruction

lead_in: Which empirical antibiotic regimen is the most appropriate?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 14 days with outpatient review in 48 hours
Intravenous gentamicin with intravenous amoxicillin, reviewed once cultures return
Intravenous meropenem, narrowed to an oral agent once she can tolerate fluids
Intravenous vancomycin, narrowed to an oral agent once the urine culture is available
Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 10 days with outpatient review in 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection with a reassuring score
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who has 14 hours of pain and swelling in the left thigh after a minor scratch while gardening.

He rates his pain 9 out of 10 and it is not relieved by 10 mg of intravenous morphine. The overlying skin is erythematous with a poorly defined edge and there is no crepitus, no bullae and no skin necrosis. Light palpation over the mid thigh reproduces severe pain extending well beyond the area of visible erythema, and the tissues feel woody rather than fluctuant. He looks unwell and his observations have deteriorated over the two hours since arrival. His laboratory risk indicator score for necrotising fasciitis is 4.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 126, BP 96/58, RR 26, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 38.5
data_table.Examination: Ill defined erythema, woody induration, pain far beyond erythematous margin, no crepitus or bullae
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C reactive protein 132 mg/L (less than 5); sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145); creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110); haemoglobin 142 g/L (130-180); glucose 11.2 mmol/L (3.0-7.7)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Refer immediately for surgical exploration alongside resuscitation and antibiotics
Start intravenous flucloxacillin and mark the erythema for review in six hours
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the thigh before any surgical referral is made
Repeat the laboratory risk indicator score in six hours and refer if it exceeds 6
Aspirate the affected area and send the fluid for urgent gram stain and culture

subtopic_detail: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after starting antiretroviral therapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 36-year-old man five weeks after starting antiretroviral therapy. He was diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus infection and concurrent pulmonary tuberculosis, and antituberculous therapy was started three weeks before the antiretrovirals.

He improved initially, with resolution of his fevers and a weight gain of 3 kg. Over the past six days he has developed recurrent high fevers, worsening cough and tender enlarging cervical lymph nodes. His sputum cultures taken this week are negative and his antituberculous drug levels are adequate, with adherence confirmed by directly observed therapy. His CD4 count has risen from 42 to 190 cells per microlitre and his viral load has fallen from 620000 to 900 copies per millilitre.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, BP 118/72, RR 22, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 39.1
data_table.Examination: Tender enlarging cervical lymphadenopathy, crackles at the right upper zone, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: CD4 count risen from 42 to 190 cells/microlitre; viral load fallen from 620000 to 900 copies/mL; sputum culture negative; chest radiograph shows increased right upper zone infiltrate and new mediastinal nodes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop the antiretroviral therapy and continue the antituberculous treatment alone
Stop the antituberculous therapy and investigate for a drug hypersensitivity reaction
Continue both treatments unchanged and add a corticosteroid for symptom control
Change to a second line antituberculous regimen for presumed multidrug resistance
Continue both treatments unchanged and observe him without any additional therapy

subtopic_detail: Suspected herpes simplex encephalitis with early normal imaging
stem:
You are the medical registrar caring for a 61-year-old woman admitted 24 hours ago with fever, confusion and two generalised seizures. Aciclovir and ceftriaxone were started in the emergency department.

Her symptoms began three days ago with a change in personality and word finding difficulty noticed by her husband. Cerebrospinal fluid showed 62 lymphocytes per microlitre, protein 0.72 g/L and normal glucose, with negative gram stain and bacterial culture. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain performed this morning is reported as normal. The herpes simplex virus polymerase chain reaction on the initial cerebrospinal fluid has just returned negative. She remains febrile and disorientated.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 134/80, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 38.4
data_table.Examination: Disorientated to time and place, dysphasic, no focal limb weakness, no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: Cerebrospinal fluid lymphocytes 62 per microlitre; protein 0.72 g/L (0.15-0.45); glucose normal; bacterial culture negative; herpes simplex virus polymerase chain reaction negative; magnetic resonance imaging reported normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Cease aciclovir and treat her as having an aseptic meningitis of viral origin
Cease aciclovir and commence high dose corticosteroids for autoimmune encephalitis
Cease aciclovir and arrange an electroencephalogram before making any further change
Continue aciclovir and repeat the imaging in two weeks if she has not improved
Continue aciclovir and repeat the lumbar puncture with polymerase chain reaction testing

subtopic_detail: Immune checkpoint inhibitor hypophysitis
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 63-year-old man who has received four cycles of an immune checkpoint inhibitor for metastatic melanoma.

Over three weeks he has become profoundly fatigued, has lost his appetite and has had daily frontal headaches. He is normotensive lying and standing and his skin shows no increase in pigmentation. His sodium is 126 mmol/L with a normal potassium, and paired morning bloods show a cortisol of 42 nmol/L with an adrenocorticotropic hormone of 4 ng/L. His free thyroxine is low at 8 pmol/L with a thyroid stimulating hormone of 0.9 mIU/L, and magnetic resonance imaging shows a diffusely enlarged pituitary gland.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 118/74 with no postural drop, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.Examination: No hyperpigmentation, no goitre, visual fields full to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 126 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); morning cortisol 42 nmol/L (200-650); adrenocorticotropic hormone 4 ng/L (10-50); free thyroxine 8 pmol/L (10-20); thyroid stimulating hormone 0.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence levothyroxine now and add hydrocortisone if he fails to improve in a week
Commence hydrocortisone replacement now and start levothyroxine several days later
Commence fludrocortisone with a liberal salt intake and repeat the sodium tomorrow
Restrict his fluid intake to 1 litre daily for presumed inappropriate antidiuresis
Refer for urgent transsphenoidal decompression of the enlarged pituitary gland

subtopic_detail: Antiviral indications in seasonal influenza
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department assessing a 72-year-old woman with 36 hours of fever, dry cough, myalgia and headache during the winter respiratory season.

She has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with two exacerbations in the past year and takes inhaled tiotropium and a combination inhaler. She received this year's influenza vaccine six weeks ago. Her chest radiograph shows hyperinflation without consolidation, and a respiratory panel nucleic acid test is positive for influenza A and negative for all other targets. Her creatinine is 92 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 58 mL/min/1.73m2.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 128/76, RR 22, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Examination: Prolonged expiratory phase, scattered wheeze, no focal crackles, no confusion
data_table.Investigations: Influenza A nucleic acid test positive; chest radiograph shows hyperinflation without consolidation; creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90); white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antiviral management?

options.text: Withhold antiviral therapy because she was vaccinated within the past three months
Withhold antiviral therapy because more than 24 hours have elapsed since onset
Commence oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and withhold antiviral therapy entirely
Commence inhaled zanamivir twice daily and continue her usual inhaled therapy
Commence oral oseltamivir at a dose adjusted for her renal function for five days

subtopic_detail: Initial screening for endogenous cortisol excess
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 38-year-old woman referred with 18 months of progressive central weight gain, easy bruising and proximal weakness that makes standing from a chair difficult.

She has developed hypertension requiring two agents and new hyperglycaemia. There are wide purple abdominal striae. She takes no exogenous corticosteroid in any form, including inhaled, topical and joint injections, and no oestrogen containing preparation. She drinks no alcohol and works regular daytime hours with a stable sleep pattern.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, BP 158/98, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Central adiposity, interscapular fat pad, purple abdominal striae wider than 1 cm, proximal myopathy
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 8.1 mmol/L (3.0-5.4); potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); HbA1c 51 mmol/mol (less than 42)

lead_in: Which investigation is the most appropriate first line screening test?

options.text: Random serum cortisol taken during this afternoon clinic appointment
Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test with a morning cortisol measured after
Plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone measured on a morning sample before other tests
Computed tomography of the adrenal glands with contrast to identify an adenoma
High dose 8 mg dexamethasone suppression test performed over two consecutive days

subtopic_detail: Extended spectrum beta lactamase producing organism in pyelonephritis
stem:
You are the medical registrar caring for a 67-year-old woman admitted 48 hours ago with fever, right loin pain and vomiting, treated empirically with intravenous gentamicin and amoxicillin.

She remains febrile with persistent loin pain and her C reactive protein has risen further. Her ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis and no calculus. Her urine and blood cultures have both grown an Escherichia coli producing an extended spectrum beta lactamase. The isolate is reported as resistant to gentamicin, ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin, and susceptible to meropenem, nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin. Her creatinine is 104 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 48 mL/min/1.73m2.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, BP 112/68, RR 20, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Examination: Right renal angle tenderness persisting, abdomen otherwise soft, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Blood and urine cultures grow extended spectrum beta lactamase producing Escherichia coli; resistant to gentamicin, ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin; susceptible to meropenem, nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin; C reactive protein risen from 148 to 210 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: Which antibiotic should she be changed to?

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin, since the isolate is reported as susceptible to that agent
Oral fosfomycin as a single dose, since the isolate is susceptible to that agent
Intravenous ceftriaxone at a higher dose, since resistance can be overcome by dosing
Intravenous meropenem, reviewed with the infectious diseases team for a total duration
Intravenous vancomycin, given the failure of the initial empirical antibiotic regimen

subtopic_detail: Surgical timing in infective endocarditis
stem:
You are the medical registrar caring for a 61-year-old man on day four of intravenous antibiotics for aortic valve endocarditis caused by a viridans group streptococcus that is fully susceptible to benzylpenicillin.

His fevers have settled and his blood cultures taken at 48 hours are sterile. Overnight he has become breathless at rest and cannot lie flat, and he now has bibasal crackles and a raised jugular venous pressure. Repeat echocardiography shows severe aortic regurgitation with premature closure of the mitral valve, a 12 mm vegetation and no aortic root abscess. He has had no embolic event and his neurological examination is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112, BP 104/44, RR 28, SpO2 91% room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Orthopnoea, bibasal crackles, jugular venous pressure 6 cm above sternal angle, wide pulse pressure
data_table.Investigations: Repeat blood cultures sterile at 48 hours; echocardiogram shows severe aortic regurgitation with premature mitral valve closure and a 12 mm vegetation; creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Refer urgently for valve surgery while continuing the current antibiotic therapy
Complete six weeks of antibiotics and reassess the valve at the end of therapy
Add gentamicin for synergy and reassess his fluid status again in 24 hours
Commence intravenous furosemide and defer surgery until the vegetation has shrunk
Commence an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor and repeat the echocardiogram weekly

subtopic_detail: Acute human immunodeficiency virus seroconversion illness
stem:
You are the medical registrar assessing a 27-year-old man with 10 days of fever, sore throat, myalgia and a widespread non itchy maculopapular rash involving his trunk, palms and soles.

He has tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy and two shallow painful ulcers on the buccal mucosa. He reports a new male sexual partner and condomless receptive anal intercourse about four weeks ago, and has taken no pre exposure prophylaxis. His Epstein Barr virus and cytomegalovirus serology show past infection with no acute markers, his monospot is negative and his syphilis serology is non reactive. A fourth generation human immunodeficiency virus antigen and antibody test is negative and his lymphocyte count is 0.9 x10^9/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98, BP 122/74, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.5
data_table.Examination: Maculopapular rash on trunk, palms and soles; tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy; two shallow buccal ulcers
data_table.Investigations: Fourth generation antigen and antibody test negative; lymphocytes 0.9 x10^9/L (1.0-4.0); platelets 128 x10^9/L (150-400); alanine aminotransferase 78 U/L (less than 40); syphilis serology non reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat the fourth generation antigen and antibody test again in three months
Send a throat swab for bacterial culture and treat empirically for streptococcal pharyngitis
Request a human immunodeficiency virus ribonucleic acid quantitative viral load now
Request a lymph node biopsy to exclude a lymphoproliferative disorder as the cause
Request a CD4 count to assess the degree of his immune suppression before testing further

subtopic_detail: Blood culture negative endocarditis
stem:
You are the medical registrar caring for a 55-year-old man with three months of fever, weight loss and lethargy. Transoesophageal echocardiography shows a 10 mm vegetation on a bioprosthetic aortic valve inserted four years ago.

He works on a sheep and cattle property in western Queensland and assists with lambing each season. Six sets of blood cultures taken over four days, before any antibiotic was given, have shown no growth at 10 days of incubation. His serum has been held by the laboratory. He has no dental disease, no indwelling lines and no injecting drug use, and his renal function is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 94, BP 124/76, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 38.2
data_table.Examination: Soft early diastolic murmur, splenomegaly 3 cm below the costal margin, no peripheral stigmata
data_table.Investigations: Six sets of blood cultures negative at 10 days; C reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5); haemoglobin 102 g/L (130-180); transoesophageal echocardiogram shows a 10 mm prosthetic aortic valve vegetation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Send serology for Coxiella burnetii and Bartonella species on the stored serum
Repeat a further six sets of blood cultures with extended incubation for four weeks
Request computed tomography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis to search for malignancy
Request an antinuclear antibody and antiphospholipid antibody panel on stored serum
Proceed directly to valve replacement and send the explanted valve for culture only

subtopic_detail: Corticosteroid indication in acute respiratory viral infection
stem:
You are the medical registrar assessing a 58-year-old man on day five of a confirmed severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 infection. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension and is not immunosuppressed.

He reports fever, dry cough and fatigue but says he can walk to the bathroom without stopping. He has had three doses of vaccine, the most recent 14 months ago. His chest radiograph shows patchy bilateral peripheral opacities. His oxygen saturation is 96 per cent on room air at rest and falls to 95 per cent after walking 40 metres on the ward, and his respiratory rate does not rise above 20 during that walk.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 136/82, RR 18, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 37.9
data_table.Examination: Chest clear to auscultation, no accessory muscle use, saturation 95 per cent after a 40 metre walk
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5); lymphocytes 1.1 x10^9/L (1.0-4.0); creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110); chest radiograph shows patchy bilateral peripheral opacities

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his corticosteroid therapy?

options.text: Commence dexamethasone 6 mg daily for 10 days because of his radiographic changes
Commence dexamethasone 6 mg daily for 10 days because of his diabetes and hypertension
Withhold corticosteroids and reassess if he develops a requirement for oxygen
Withhold corticosteroids and commence inhaled budesonide twice daily for 14 days
Commence dexamethasone 6 mg daily and add tocilizumab if his markers rise further

subtopic_detail: Coeliac disease testing after self-initiated gluten avoidance
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 34-year-old woman referred with eight months of bloating and loose stools. She has iron deficiency anaemia that has not corrected despite six months of documented adherence to oral ferrous sulfate, and her gastroscopy request has not yet been triaged.

After reading about her symptoms online she removed all gluten from her diet seven weeks ago and reports her bowels have settled. She has no red flag features, no family history of bowel cancer and menstruates normally with a cycle she describes as light. Coeliac serology has not previously been performed.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21 kg/m2, abdomen soft and non-tender, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155); ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-200); C-reactive protein and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?

options.text: Request HLA DQ2 and DQ8 typing and manage according to the result
Request tissue transglutaminase IgA and total IgA on the current diet
Reintroduce gluten for at least six weeks, then test transglutaminase and total IgA
Proceed directly to gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies while she avoids gluten
Continue gluten avoidance and give intravenous ferric carboxymaltose now

subtopic_detail: Helicobacter pylori eradication with penicillin hypersensitivity
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 47-year-old man in the gastroenterology clinic after a gastroscopy performed for three months of epigastric pain. The endoscopist found a 1 cm clean based duodenal ulcer and rapid urease testing on antral biopsies was positive.

At age nineteen he developed a widespread urticarial rash with lip swelling within an hour of an amoxicillin dose and has avoided all penicillins since. He has never taken a macrolide and has not travelled outside Australia. He takes no regular medicines and stopped ibuprofen four weeks ago when the pain began.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mild epigastric tenderness, no guarding, no mass
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 138 g/L (130-175); renal and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: Which eradication regimen is most appropriate to prescribe?

options.text: Esomeprazole with clarithromycin and metronidazole twice daily for seven days
Esomeprazole with amoxicillin and clarithromycin twice daily for seven days
Esomeprazole twice daily alone for eight weeks and repeat the gastroscopy
Esomeprazole with levofloxacin and amoxicillin twice daily for ten days
Esomeprazole with clarithromycin and metronidazole twice daily for three days
